description: Dragon's Lair is a 1983 laserdisc arcade game featuring hand-drawn animation by Don Bluth, former Disney animator, that was unlike anything ever seen in an arcade. Players guide the knight Dirk the Daring through a castle filled with monsters and hazards by pressing directional buttons at precisely the right moments, triggering pre-animated sequences of success or death. The animation quality was astonishing for the era — far beyond the pixel graphics of contemporary games — and lines of players formed around the block to play it for a dollar a quarter. Dragon's Lair was so popular it was credited with revitalising the declining arcade industry in 1983.
longDescription: Dragon's Lair was the brainchild of game designer Rick Dyer, who licensed the animation work to Don Bluth Studios following Disney. The game stored its 45 minutes of animation on a laserdisc player housed inside the cabinet, with the game engine triggering specific scenes based on player input. The result was cinematic quality that no other game could approach at the time. The game cost 50 cents per play — double the standard — yet had lines around the block. It was simultaneously a commercial triumph and a critical controversy, with many arguing it was more a movie than a game since player interaction was limited to timing button presses. Two sequels followed — Dragon's Lair II and Space Ace — and the game was selected for preservation by the U.S. Library of Congress in 2015 for its cultural significance.
trivia: Dragon's Lair cost 50 cents to play in 1983, double the standard arcade price — players paid for the premium animation quality.
Don Bluth had walked out of Disney with 11 other animators in 1979 over creative disagreements — Dragon's Lair was his statement that hand-drawn animation still had a future.
The LaserDisc containing the game footage cost more than most arcade game hardware, making the cabinet extremely expensive to manufacture.
Dragon's Lair's failure rate was high — the LaserDisc mechanism was fragile and machines broke down constantly, infuriating operators.
devStory: Dragon's Lair was created by Rick Dyer and animated by Don Bluth, a former Disney animator who had left the studio in 1979. The game used a LaserDisc to play pre-animated cartoon footage, with players pressing directional buttons or the sword button at specific moments to trigger the correct action sequence. It cost twice as much to play as a standard arcade game (50 cents versus 25) and still had queues around the block.

description: 1942 (1984) is Capcom's vertically scrolling WWII shooter: fly a P-38 across the Pacific and loop out of danger with a limited barrel roll.
longDescription: 1942 sends a P-38 Lightning through 32 stages over the Pacific, shooting down waves of enemy aircraft and collecting power-ups carried by formations of red planes. A limited number of loop manoeuvres per stage let the plane roll away from danger. Designed by Yoshiki Okamoto, it was Capcom's first big arcade hit and began the 194X series, followed by 1943: The Battle of Midway.
trivia: 1942 was Yoshiki Okamoto's first game for Capcom, after he had made Time Pilot and Gyruss at Konami.
The barrel roll mechanic — a brief dodge with temporary invincibility — became standard in shoot-em-ups and appeared in Star Fox 64.
Players controlled an American P-38 Lightning shooting down Japanese Zero fighters, an unusual perspective for a Japanese-made game.
The game launched a series: 1943, 1943 Kai, 1941, and 19XX followed through the 1990s.
devStory: 1942 was designed by Yoshiki Okamoto at Capcom in 1984. It was a vertical-scrolling shoot-em-up set in the Pacific Theatre of World War II — players flew a Lockheed P-38 Lightning on a mission to reach Tokyo. The game introduced the "roll" barrel roll manoeuvre — pressing a button triggered a short invincibility roll that dodged incoming fire. It was Capcom's first major arcade hit and launched a long-running series.

title: Punch-Out!!
description: Punch-Out!! (1984) is Nintendo's arcade boxing game on two stacked screens, in which each opponent's attacks are signalled by tells to learn.
longDescription: Punch-Out!! views the fight from behind the player's green-haired boxer, with a second monitor above showing the score and fighters. Each opponent — Glass Joe, Piston Hurricane, Bald Bull and others — has distinct habits and a tell that warns of each attack, so winning is about reading patterns more than raw reflexes. Designed by Genyo Takeda, it led to the NES Punch-Out!! starring Little Mac.
trivia: Punch-Out!! used two stacked monitors: the lower screen showed the fight, while the upper one displayed the score, timer and fighters' stamina.
Each opponent had a specific tell (a facial tic, a sound cue, or a wind-up animation) that signalled their attack — pattern recognition over reflexes.
The NES version replaced the original's boxer with Little Mac and became one of the platform's most beloved games.
devStory: Punch-Out!! was designed by Genyo Takeda at Nintendo in 1984. The game used two stacked monitors — the lower one for the fight, seen from behind the player's boxer, and the upper one for scores and stats. Punch-Out!! introduced the pattern-recognition mechanic that would define boxing games: each opponent had a specific tell before attacking.

title: Ghosts 'n Goblins
description: Ghosts 'n Goblins (1984) is Capcom's notoriously hard platformer: Arthur fights demons to rescue the princess, losing his armour after one hit.
longDescription: Sir Arthur fights through graveyards, forests and castles full of zombies, demons and dragons to rescue the princess. One hit strips his armour and leaves him in his boxer shorts; a second kills him. Weapons swap as players collect them, some far worse than others. Designed by Tokuro Fujiwara, it is famously difficult — and finishing it once reveals that the victory was a trick, sending the player back to beat the whole game a second time for the real ending.
trivia: Completing Ghosts 'n Goblins once revealed it was an illusion — players had to complete the entire game a second time to see the real ending.
Arthur loses his armour on the first hit from any enemy, fighting in boxer shorts for the rest of the life — an absurdist image that became beloved.
The game's difficulty was legendary — it regularly appears on "hardest games ever" lists, even decades after release.
Tokuro Fujiwara designed the mechanic of requiring two playthroughs as a deliberate challenge to dedicated players.
Ghouls 'n Ghosts (1988) was considered a worthy sequel, and the series continued with Super Ghouls 'n Ghosts on the Super Nintendo.
devStory: Ghosts 'n Goblins was designed by Tokuro Fujiwara at Capcom and released in 1984. It was notorious for its extreme difficulty and for requiring players to complete the game twice — finishing once revealed the game was an illusion, and the true ending required a second complete playthrough. The image of Arthur losing his armour and continuing in heart-patterned boxer shorts became iconic.

title: Karate Champ
description: Karate Champ (1984) is Data East's one-on-one karate tournament game, an early template for fighting games, with moves set by two joysticks.
longDescription: Karate Champ stages point-based karate bouts judged by a referee, awarding full or half points for clean strikes, with bonus rounds of breaking bricks and dodging objects between matches. Instead of buttons, the player combines the directions of two joysticks to produce different kicks, punches and blocks — an early form of the move inputs that later fighting games adopted. It set out much of the one-on-one format that games such as Street Fighter built on.
trivia: Karate Champ is the direct ancestor of Street Fighter, Mortal Kombat, and every one-on-one fighting game — it established the format in 1984.
The dual joystick control system mapped combinations of stick movements to specific attacks — an early version of the input notation that defines fighting games.
A referee judged each exchange and awarded points, mirroring real martial arts competition scoring.
Data East sued Epyx in 1987, claiming its World Karate Championship copied Karate Champ; Data East won at trial, but the verdict was overturned on appeal.
devStory: Karate Champ was developed by Data East in 1984. It was one of the first one-on-one fighting games and established the format — two players in a dojo, fighting in rounds, with a judge awarding points. The dual-joystick control system mapped different combinations to different attacks. Karate Champ directly influenced Street Fighter (1987) and every one-on-one fighting game that followed.

title: Paperboy
description: Paperboy (1984) is Atari's bicycle delivery game: steer with real handlebars, throw papers to subscribers and dodge the hazards of a hostile suburb.
longDescription: Paperboy rides a bike down a diagonal suburban street, throwing newspapers into subscribers' mailboxes while dodging cars, dogs, break-dancers and lawnmowers. Missed deliveries cost subscribers, while non-subscribers' houses are fair game for broken windows. Each day ends with a bonus obstacle course. The cabinet's handlebar controller made it one of the most physical arcade games of its era, designed by John Salwitz, Dave Ralston and colleagues at Atari Games.
trivia: Paperboy featured a genuine bicycle handlebar as its controller — one of the most elaborate physical controllers in arcade history.
Non-subscriber houses could be attacked and vandalised — windows broken, flowerpots smashed — without penalty.
Subscribers who missed their paper cancelled their subscription, reducing the points available in future runs.
The training course at the end of each route was an obstacle course that offered bonus points and was often more enjoyable than the main delivery.
devStory: Paperboy was designed by John Salwitz, Dave Ralston, Wilfredo Aguilar, and Carl Bedard at Atari Games in 1984. Players rode a bicycle delivering newspapers to subscribers while avoiding hazards and vandalising non-subscribers' property. The handlebar controller was a genuine innovation — a physical bicycle handlebar that players steered and pedalled. The game's suburban American setting and dark humour (the non-subscriber deaths were comedic) made it memorable.

title: King's Quest
description: King's Quest (1984) is Roberta Williams' Sierra adventure for the IBM PCjr, the first graphic adventure with a hero players walk around an animated world.
longDescription: King's Quest: Quest for the Crown sends Sir Graham across the kingdom of Daventry to recover three stolen treasures and earn the throne. Players type commands into a parser but walk Graham freely around each screen, a first for graphic adventures, and the world is full of hazards that can end the game in an instant. IBM commissioned it to show off the PCjr; the computer flopped, but the game launched Sierra's most successful series, which ran to eight instalments.
trivia: King's Quest was commissioned by IBM as a showcase for the PCjr — a computer that failed commercially, while the game it spawned became a decade-long franchise.
Characters could be killed by falling into pits, being eaten by a dragon, or dozens of other hazards — adventure game deaths were Roberta Williams' signature.
Williams and her husband Ken founded Sierra On-Line in their living room in 1979, building one of the most important game companies of the 1980s.
The King's Quest series ran to eight games, with the eighth released in 1998 — a 14-year franchise spawned from an IBM showcase demo.
devStory: King's Quest was designed by Roberta Williams at Sierra On-Line in 1984. It was created as a showcase for IBM's PCjr computer and was the first graphical adventure game with an animated protagonist who moved around the screen. Williams had designed Mystery House (1980) with her husband Ken, one of the first graphical text adventures. King's Quest transformed adventure games from text parsers into visual worlds and launched Sierra's most successful franchise.

title: Elite
description: Elite (1984) is Braben and Bell's open-ended space trading game: fly between 2,048 procedurally generated star systems, trading, fighting and chasing the Elite rank.
longDescription: Elite gives the player a Cobra Mk III, 100 credits and no set goal. Trade goods between planets, hunt pirates, turn pirate yourself or mine asteroids, all in wireframe 3D combat, while climbing the combat ranks towards 'Elite'. Written by David Braben and Ian Bell as Cambridge students, it fits eight galaxies of 256 systems each into a BBC Micro by generating them from a mathematical seed rather than storing them. It shaped the space trading and open-world games that followed.
trivia: Elite's entire universe of 2048 star systems was stored in just 22 kilobytes using procedural generation — a mathematical miracle of compression.
Braben and Bell fell out after Elite's release and did not speak publicly to each other for decades, despite creating one of gaming's most beloved worlds together.
The BBC Micro version was delivered on a cassette tape — the game's universe was generated mathematically from the same seed every time.
Achieving "Elite" status required destroying 6,400 enemy ships — a grind that took dedicated players hundreds of hours.
Elite directly inspired Wing Commander, Privateer, No Man's Sky, and the entire space trading/exploration genre.
devStory: Elite was designed by David Braben and Ian Bell while they were students at Cambridge University and released in 1984. The game created a procedurally generated universe of 2048 star systems in just 22KB of code — using a mathematical seed to regenerate the same universe from a seed without storing it. Elite was arguably the first open-world game and directly influenced every space trading and exploration game since.

title: Boulder Dash
description: Boulder Dash (1984) is First Star's cave-digging puzzle game: tunnel for diamonds while boulders fall and roll, triggering chain reactions.
longDescription: Rockford digs through the earth of each cave collecting a quota of diamonds before time runs out, but digging disturbs everything around him: boulders and diamonds fall when their support is removed and roll off rounded surfaces, crushing whatever is below. Fireflies and butterflies explode when hit, the latter into diamonds, and a spreading amoeba must be contained. Designed by Peter Liepa with Chris Gray, it was ported to many systems and widely imitated.
trivia: The boulder physics — objects rolling off rounded surfaces and triggering chain reactions — were the game's central puzzle mechanic and required spatial planning.
Boulder Dash was ported to over 20 platforms, making it one of the most ported games of the 8-bit era.
The firefly enemies exploded into diamonds when trapped — a mechanic that rewarded creative problem-solving over direct confrontation.
Amoeba growth was time-limited — if not contained it filled an entire cave, turning the level into a lose state.
devStory: Boulder Dash was designed by Peter Liepa and Chris Gray and published by First Star Software in 1984. Players dug through earth collecting diamonds while avoiding falling boulders and amoebas. The physics of falling objects was the core mechanic — boulders rolled off rounded objects, creating chain reactions that players could trigger or avoid. The game was immediately and widely cloned, spawning a genre sometimes called "digger" or "boulder-dash-like."

title: Impossible Mission
description: Impossible Mission (1984) is Epyx's C64 action-puzzle game: search Elvin Atombender's rooms for puzzle pieces while somersaulting over robots.
longDescription: A secret agent infiltrates the underground complex of Professor Elvin Atombender, searching furniture room by room for puzzle pieces and codes while dodging patrolling robots — 'Another visitor. Stay a while… stay forever!' greets him in synthesised speech. The pieces must be assembled into a password to reach Atombender, and the puzzles are shuffled each game. Designed by Dennis Caswell, it was famous for its fluid, lifelike animation of the agent's run and somersault.
trivia: "Another visitor. Stay a while... stay FOREVER!" became one of the most quoted villain speeches in gaming history.
The protagonist's animation was among the smoothest ever seen on an 8-bit home computer, achieved through carefully crafted sprite sequences.
The game's puzzle mechanic — searching rooms for puzzle pieces to assemble a password — was a completely original structure.
Each game had a randomised puzzle, meaning the same room layout could require different puzzle pieces each play.
devStory: Impossible Mission was designed by Dennis Caswell at Epyx in 1984. The game is famous for its synthesised speech — "Another visitor. Stay a while... stay FOREVER!" — delivered when the player's spy character was killed by a security robot. The smooth animation of the protagonist, achieved through rotoscoping-influenced sprite work, was exceptional for a home computer game of 1984.

title: Duck Hunt
description: Duck Hunt (1984) is Nintendo's NES light-gun game, played with the Zapper: shoot ducks or clay pigeons while a dog laughs at every miss.
longDescription: Duck Hunt was one of the games that showed off the NES Zapper. Ducks flap out of the grass one or two at a time and the player has three shots to bring them down; a hunting dog retrieves the kills and snickers at the misses. A third mode swaps birds for clay pigeons. The Zapper registers a hit by blanking the screen and flashing white boxes where the targets are, a trick that relies on CRT televisions and does not work on modern flat screens.
trivia: The laughing dog became so hated by players that when it appeared as a fighter in Super Smash Bros. for Wii U in 2014, players reported great satisfaction finally being able to defeat it.
The Zapper detected hits by briefly displaying white squares where the targets were — the gun's sensor triggered on the bright flash, not the duck sprite itself.
Clay Shooting mode featured flying discs instead of birds — a calmer alternative that some players preferred.
The NES Zapper does not work on modern flat-screen televisions due to differences in display technology from CRT screens.
devStory: Duck Hunt was designed by Nintendo Research & Development 1 and released with the NES in 1985 alongside a Zapper light gun peripheral. The game used the Zapper's light sensor technology to detect when the gun was pointed at the screen during the moment a duck sprite was displayed. The laughing dog — who mocked players who missed — became one of gaming's most divisive characters.

title: Excitebike
description: Nintendo's 1984 side-scrolling motocross racer, where managing engine heat and landing jumps cleanly matters as much as speed — and players could build their own tracks.
longDescription:
Excitebike was developed and published by Nintendo for the NES in 1984. Later that year it was adapted for arcades on Nintendo's VS. System, and a Famicom Disk System version followed in 1988.

Riders race across side-on tracks full of ramps and mud, and the game's depth comes from controlling the bike in the air and managing the engine's temperature, which overheats if the turbo is used too long. A built-in editor let players design their own courses. Excitebike became one of the best-selling NES games in North America and was the first entry in Nintendo's Excite series.
trivia: Excitebike included a full track editor, making it one of the earliest games with a level creation tool on a home console.
The heat management system — overusing the turbo caused the bike to overheat and stall — was a novel resource mechanic for a racing game.
Saved custom tracks required the Famicom Data Recorder peripheral, making them effectively inaccessible to most players.
devStory: Excitebike was designed by Shigeru Miyamoto and released by Nintendo in 1984. The game featured a track editor mode where players could design and save their own motocross circuits — one of the earliest track creation tools in a console game. The heat management mechanic — the bike overheated if the turbo was overused — added strategic depth to the racing.

title: Jet Set Willy
description: Jet Set Willy (1984) is Matthew Smith's sequel to Manic Miner: explore Willy's 60-room mansion collecting items before bed, in a sprawling Spectrum platformer.
longDescription: After the party, Miner Willy's housekeeper won't let him go to bed until every item left lying around his mansion has been tidied up. Unlike Manic Miner's separate caverns, the more than sixty rooms connect into one explorable house. It was a big commercial success, but it shipped with bugs that made it impossible to finish, and players traded fixes through magazines. It was Matthew Smith's last major game before he left the industry.
trivia: Jet Set Willy shipped with game-breaking bugs that made several rooms impossible to complete — players discovered workarounds through the gaming press.
Software Projects offered a £1,000 prize for the first player to finish the game, but the bugs made this technically impossible.
The game featured over 60 rooms in Willy's mansion, each with its own hazard layout and personality.
Matthew Smith's disappearance after the game's release became a minor gaming legend — he resurfaced periodically in interviews over the following decades.
devStory: Jet Set Willy was written by Matthew Smith in 1984 as the sequel to Manic Miner. It expanded the house of eccentric millionaire Willy across over 60 rooms and was an enormous commercial success. However, the game shipped with several bugs — including at least one room that was impossible to clear — that prevented players from finishing it. Smith disappeared from the games industry shortly after and his whereabouts were the subject of speculation for years.

title: Kung-Fu Master
description: Kung-Fu Master (1984) is Irem's side-scrolling martial arts game: fight up five floors of a temple to rescue Sylvia, defeating a boss on each floor.
longDescription: Thomas battles across the five floors of a temple to rescue his girlfriend Sylvia, punching and kicking through waves of grabbers and knife-throwers, with a different boss guarding the end of each floor. The setup draws on Bruce Lee's Game of Death. Designed by Takashi Nishiyama, who later created Street Fighter, it is an early form of the side-scrolling beat-'em-up refined by Double Dragon and Final Fight.
trivia: Kung-Fu Master was designed by Takashi Nishiyama, who later created the original Street Fighter — the fighting game genre's lineage runs directly through him.
In Japan it was released as Spartan X, a tie-in with the Jackie Chan film Wheels on Meals, though its climb up a guarded tower borrows from Bruce Lee's Game of Death.
Five distinct floor bosses each required different tactics, introducing the concept of themed boss encounters to beat-em-ups.
The side-scrolling brawler format created here was refined by Double Dragon and perfected by Streets of Rage and Final Fight.
devStory: Kung-Fu Master was developed by Irem in 1984, designed by Takashi Nishiyama who would later design Street Fighter. In Japan it was a tie-in with the Jackie Chan film Wheels on Meals, released as Spartan X, while its structure echoes Bruce Lee's Game of Death. Players fought through five floors of enemies using punches, kicks, and jumps. The side-scrolling beat-em-up format it established influenced virtually every fighting game of the following decade.

title: Pac-Land
description: Pac-Land (1984) takes Pac-Man out of the maze into a side-scrolling platform world, with parallax backgrounds and a fairy to escort home.
longDescription: Pac-Land shows Pac-Man side-on for the first time, running and jumping through towns, forests and deserts to return a lost fairy to Fairyland and then find his way home to his family. The familiar ghosts return in cars, planes and buses, and power pellets still turn the tables. Players run by alternately tapping buttons. With its colourful, multi-layered scrolling backgrounds, it was an influential early side-scrolling platformer.
trivia: Pac-Land was the first game to show Pac-Man from the side, revealing he had legs — a revelation for players who only knew him as a circular sprite.
The game featured multiple parallax scrolling layers, creating a sense of depth that influenced platformers throughout the late 1980s.
Pac-Man's wife and daughter appeared in the game, giving the character a domestic life players had never considered.
Pac-Land directly inspired the creators of Super Mario Bros., who cited its smooth side-scrolling as a technical benchmark.
devStory: Pac-Land was developed by Namco in 1984. It reinvented Pac-Man as a side-scrolling platformer — the first time the character had left his original maze format. The game's animation was fluid and colourful, featuring Pac-Man returning a fairy to Fairyland and then making his way home. It was notable for being one of the first games with multiple looping background layers creating parallax depth.

title: Bomb Jack
description: Bomb Jack (1984) is Tehkan's floaty platformer: glide around famous landmarks collecting bombs, taking the lit ones in order for the best scores.
longDescription: Bomb Jack leaps and floats around single-screen scenes set before the Sphinx, the Acropolis and other landmarks, collecting all 24 bombs while dodging birds, mummies and other enemies. Taking the lit bombs in sequence earns large bonuses, which gives the game a hidden layer of planning. Jack can glide and steer in the air with unusual control for 1984, and enemy patterns can be learned. It was made by Tehkan, later Tecmo.
trivia: Collecting flashing bombs rather than regular ones multiplied point values — managing bomb priority under enemy pressure was the game's hidden depth.
Bomb Jack's floating physics allowed players to drift across the screen with fine trajectory control, unusual for 1984 arcade games.
The game's global settings — defusing bombs on the Pyramids, the Parthenon, and Tower Bridge — gave it a cinematic, exotic feel.
Enemy patterns were scripted and memorisable, rewarding players who treated the game as a puzzle rather than a reflex challenge.
devStory: Bomb Jack was developed by Tehkan (later Tecmo) in 1984. The superhero Bomb Jack flew around defusing bombs on monuments, pyramids, and cityscapes while collecting them in a specific order for bonus points. The game's physics — Jack floated down slowly and could control his trajectory — were distinctive. The order in which bombs were collected was critical; taking lit (flashing) bombs first multiplied the score.

title: Spy vs. Spy
description: Spy vs. Spy (1984) is First Star's split-screen game based on the Mad comic: the black and white spies set booby traps while racing to escape.
longDescription: Two spies search an embassy for a set of secret items and a briefcase to carry them out before the timer runs out, each on their own half of the screen. Along the way they rig furniture and doors with bombs, springs and buckets of water for the other to trigger — and can fight hand to hand when they meet. Based on Antonio Prohías's strip in Mad, it was designed by Mike Riedel and remains a model of slapstick competitive play.
trivia: Spy vs. Spy was one of the earliest split-screen competitive games — both players saw the full environment but from their own perspective.
Traps were set in objects around the map — briefcases, filing cabinets, doors — and triggered when the opponent interacted with them.
The game's tone perfectly matched the Mad magazine comic strip it was based on: slapstick violence with no lasting consequences.
It was one of the first games to be based on a magazine property, years before the era of licensed games from films and TV.
devStory: Spy vs. Spy was developed by Mike Riedel at First Star Software in 1984, based on the Mad magazine cartoon strip. Two spies set traps for each other in a split-screen environment. The game was one of the first to use a divided screen to show both players simultaneously in a competitive game, and the booby trap mechanic — setting spring-loaded surprises for the opponent — was genuinely creative.

title: Tetris
description: Tetris is a 1984 puzzle game created by Soviet computer scientist Alexey Pajitnov at the Dorodnitsyn Computing Centre of the Soviet Academy of Sciences in Moscow. Players rotate and position falling geometric pieces called tetrominoes to form complete horizontal lines, which then disappear — incomplete lines accumulate until they fill the screen and end the game. The game's design is deceptively simple but endlessly captivating, embodying what Pajitnov called the human instinct to impose order on chaos. Tetris is the best-selling paid video game of all time with over 520 million copies sold, and its bundling with the Game Boy in 1989 established Nintendo's handheld dominance.
longDescription: Pajitnov created Tetris in his spare time on a Soviet Elektronika 60 computer, drawing inspiration from the pentomino puzzle game Pentominoes. He shared it freely with colleagues, and it spread through Soviet research networks before being smuggled to the West. The rights became entangled in a complex international dispute involving British publisher Mirrorsoft, Nintendo, and the Soviet state agency ELORG. Robert Stein of Andromeda Software smuggled a copy to the West and the resulting legal battle — documented in the book The Tetris Effect — was one of the most complex in entertainment history. Nintendo secured handheld and console rights and bundled it with the Game Boy in 1989, a decision credited with making the Game Boy the dominant handheld. Research has shown Tetris is uniquely effective at preventing PTSD flashbacks by occupying the brain's visual processing centres.
trivia: Pajitnov received no royalties for Tetris until 1996 — the rights were owned by the Soviet government, which licensed them to Western companies.
The Game Boy version, bundled with the handheld in most markets, sold more than 35 million copies.
Pajitnov named the game by combining "tetra" (four, the number of blocks in each piece) with "tennis," his favourite sport.
The fight over the rights involved Nintendo, Atari's Tengen, Mirrorsoft and the Soviet agency Elorg, and ended in 1989 with Nintendo holding the console and handheld rights.
Tetris Effect — a real psychological phenomenon — causes players to see falling blocks when they close their eyes after extended play.
devStory: Tetris was designed by Alexey Pajitnov at the Soviet Academy of Sciences in Moscow in 1984. Pajitnov created it on an Electronika 60 — a text-based terminal — and the game spread through Soviet scientific institutions on floppy disk before Western companies discovered it. The resulting legal battle over rights — involving Nintendo, Atari, Mirrorsoft, and the Soviet government — became one of the most complex licencing disputes in gaming history.

title: Yie Ar Kung-Fu
description: Yie Ar Kung-Fu (1984) is Konami's one-on-one fighting game, in which Oolong faces a line of opponents, each with a signature weapon or style.
longDescription: Yie Ar Kung-Fu pits Oolong against a series of fighters, each with a distinct weapon or technique — nunchaku, a staff, throwing stars, a chain, fire breath — so every bout calls for a different approach. Health bars and a roster of varied characters made it one of the forerunners of the modern fighting game, and Street Fighter's designers set out to build on its example.
trivia: Yie Ar Kung-Fu featured opponents of different genders, body types, and fighting styles — diversity in game characters unprecedented for 1984.
Each opponent had a unique special move or weapon, requiring the player to adapt strategy for every fight.
devStory: Yie Ar Kung-Fu was developed by Konami in 1984. It was a one-on-one fighting game where players faced a series of opponents each with a distinct fighting style, weapon, or special ability. The variety of opponents — including a female fighter, a nunchaku user, and a bo staff expert — was greater than any fighting game before it. It directly influenced Street Fighter and established the "unique opponent roster" format.

title: Space Harrier
description: Space Harrier (1985) is Yu Suzuki's pseudo-3D rail shooter for Sega, flying a jet-powered hero at speed through surreal landscapes on Super Scaler hardware.
longDescription: Space Harrier's hero runs and flies into the screen through the Fantasy Zone, shooting dragons, mammoths and geometric oddities while dodging pillars and trees rushing past. Sega's Super Scaler hardware resized sprites fast enough to create a convincing sense of 3D speed, and a deluxe sit-down cabinet moved with the controls. Yu Suzuki followed it with Out Run and After Burner, a run of spectacular arcade games that defined Sega in the late 1980s.
trivia: Space Harrier used Sega's Super Scaler hardware to enlarge sprites rapidly, creating the illusion of moving through 3D space at high speed.
The sit-down cabinet featured a moving seat that tilted and vibrated in sync with on-screen action — early force feedback.
Yu Suzuki designed Space Harrier, OutRun, and After Burner in consecutive years, establishing Sega's reputation for arcade spectacle.
devStory: Space Harrier was designed by Yu Suzuki at Sega in 1985. Suzuki used Sega's Super Scaler hardware — which could scale sprites rapidly to simulate 3D movement — to create a pseudo-3D rail shooter that ran at a smooth framerate. The sensation of flying at high speed through a fantastic landscape was unlike anything in arcades before it. Suzuki followed Space Harrier with OutRun and After Burner, creating a trilogy of Sega 'super-scaler' spectaculars.

title: Commando
description: Commando (1985) is Tokuro Fujiwara's Capcom run and gun, in which Super Joe fights alone through enemy territory with a rifle and a limited supply of grenades.
longDescription: Super Joe's rifle never runs out and fires in eight directions, while grenades are rationed and thrown forward to clear obstacles and groups of enemies. The arcade game has eight levels. It popularised the run and gun and inspired many imitators, including SNK's Ikari Warriors.
trivia: Its Japanese title, Senjō no Ōkami, means "Wolf of the Battlefield".
Rob Hubbard reportedly wrote the Commodore 64 version's music in under 12 hours.
devStory: Fujiwara designed it and Tamayo Kawamoto composed the music. Released in May 1985, it was the UK's highest-grossing arcade game of the year and among the top three in the US. The NES version sold about 1.14 million copies, and the sequel, Mercs, followed in 1989. It is unrelated to the 1985 film.

title: Gradius
description: Gradius (1985) is Konami's side-scrolling shooter built around a power-up meter: collect capsules and choose your upgrade — speed, missiles, lasers or Options.
longDescription: The Vic Viper flies through volcanoes, stone heads and alien cells, ending each stage against a battleship boss. Its innovation is the power meter: each capsule collected moves a cursor along a bar of upgrades, and the player decides when to cash it in — speed-up, missiles, double shot, laser, the glowing Option pods that copy the ship's fire, or a shield. That choice made building a loadout part of the play and launched one of Konami's most enduring series.
trivia: The Gradius power-up selection bar was a completely new mechanic — players chose which upgrade to apply from a menu, making loadout strategy part of the game.
The 'Konami Code' was created by Kazuhisa Hashimoto while converting Gradius to the NES — he found the game too hard to test and added a secret input that granted full power-ups.
Option pods — orbiting weapons that mirrored the player's fire — were a visual innovation that became a series trademark.
Big Core, the armoured battleship that guards the stages, became one of the most recognisable bosses in shooting games.
devStory: Gradius was designed by Hiroyasu Machiguchi at Konami in 1985. The game's power-up system was its central innovation: players collected power capsules and applied them to a selection bar to choose which upgrade to apply — speed, missiles, double shot, laser, or option pods. The system required strategic planning before play even began. Gradius established Konami's most enduring shooting game series.

title: Gauntlet
description: Gauntlet (1985) is Atari's four-player dungeon crawler: Warrior, Valkyrie, Wizard and Elf fight through mazes of monsters as their health drains away.
longDescription: Up to four players choose a hero — Warrior, Valkyrie, Wizard or Elf — each with different strengths, and fight through maze-like dungeons where monster generators spawn enemies until destroyed. Health ticks down constantly, so food and more coins keep a hero alive, and a synthesised narrator comments ('Elf needs food badly!'). Designed by Ed Logg, the four-player cabinet was a huge commercial success and a template for co-operative action games.
trivia: "Elf needs food badly!" became one of the most recognisable game voice lines of the 1980s.
Gauntlet was designed as a four-player game from the start — the cabinet had four sets of controls built in from day one.
Health decreased continuously over time, making more coins (and thus more health) a core part of the business model.
Monster generators could spawn enemies indefinitely — destroying them was often more important than fighting individual enemies.
Gauntlet earned so much revenue that some operators reported it paid for itself in days rather than the usual weeks.
devStory: Gauntlet was designed by Ed Logg at Atari Games in 1985. It supported up to four simultaneous players — Warrior, Valkyrie, Wizard, and Elf — in a dungeon-crawl adventure with a continuous supply of enemies generated by monster generators. The speech synthesiser directed players ("Elf needs food badly!") and the coin-operated mechanic of paying to restore health created a completely new business model. Gauntlet was a massive financial success.

title: Where in the World Is Carmen Sandiego?
description: Where in the World Is Carmen Sandiego? (1985) is Broderbund's geography detective game, chasing V.I.L.E. thieves around the world using a real almanac.
longDescription: As a rookie detective, the player follows the trail of a thief from Carmen Sandiego's V.I.L.E. gang from city to city, interviewing witnesses whose clues point to the next destination, gathering a description for an arrest warrant, and making the collar before time runs out. The game came with a World Almanac for looking up the clues, so learning geography was the path to winning. It grew into a long-running educational franchise and a PBS television show.
trivia: The game shipped with a physical World Almanac — players had to consult the real book to find geographical clues, making it a genuinely educational tool.
Carmen Sandiego was the first computer game character to have her own television show, which ran for five seasons on PBS.
The red coat and wide-brimmed hat made Carmen one of the most visually distinctive game characters of the 1980s.
Players were apprentice detectives working their way up through ranks — V.I.L.E. henchmen at first, with Carmen as the ultimate quarry.
The series expanded to history, time, Europe, and the USA, creating a franchise of educational titles that spanned decades.
devStory: Where in the World Is Carmen Sandiego? was designed by Broderbund in 1985, conceived by Gene Portwood and Lauren Elliott. The educational adventure game required players to look up real geographical facts in an included World Almanac to track the thief Carmen Sandiego across countries. The PBS television show (1991–1996) starring Lynne Thigpen as the Chief reached millions of children. Carmen Sandiego became one of the most recognisable educational game brands in history.

sources.title: Where in the World Is Carmen Sandiego? (1985 video game)

title: Super Mario Bros.
description: Super Mario Bros. is the 1985 NES platformer by Nintendo that single-handedly revitalised the North American video game industry after the crash of 1983. Designed by Shigeru Miyamoto and Takashi Tezuka, it follows Mario and Luigi as they traverse the Mushroom Kingdom to rescue Princess Toadstool from King Bowser. With 32 levels across 8 worlds, an iconic musical score, and hidden secrets and warp zones, the game set the standard for platform game design that endures to this day. Super Mario Bros. has sold over 40 million copies, making it one of the best-selling individual games ever produced.
longDescription: Super Mario Bros. was designed to showcase the NES hardware and shipped as a bundle with the console, becoming the game that defined a generation. Miyamoto and Tezuka built the game around the principle of teaching through play — the first level, World 1-1, is a masterclass in game design that introduces every core mechanic through environmental cues without a single word of text. The underground pipe shortcuts, flagpole timing bonuses, mushrooms and fire flowers, and the final Bowser-bait switch are all constructed to reward exploration and skill. The game's music by Koji Kondo is among the most recognised musical works in history. Super Mario Bros. established a franchise that has sold over 800 million games total across all titles, making it the best-selling video game franchise of all time.
trivia: Super Mario Bros. is the best-selling video game of all time for most of its existence — it was bundled with the NES and sold over 40 million copies.
The Minus World is an endless underwater level reached through a glitch in World 1-2 — players discovered it soon after release, and Nintendo Power later explained how to reach it.
Miyamoto designed World 1-1 specifically to teach every game mechanic without text — the first mushroom, the first enemy, the first pit were all precisely placed.
The entire game was created in under a year, with Miyamoto and Tezuka working in the same room and handing sprites back and forth.
Mario's appearance — hat, moustache, overalls — was designed to minimise the number of pixels needed for animation, not for any aesthetic reason.
devStory: Super Mario Bros. was designed by Shigeru Miyamoto and Takashi Tezuka at Nintendo in 1985. It became the showcase title for the NES in North America, where it was bundled with the console. Miyamoto designed the world as a series of discoveries — each mechanic introduced gradually so players learned through play rather than instructions. The game's structure, pacing, and teaching philosophy remain studied in game design courses today.

title: Rush'n Attack
description: Rush'n Attack (1985), Green Beret in Europe, is Konami's Cold War side-scroller: a knife-wielding commando raids an enemy base to free prisoners.
longDescription: A lone commando infiltrates an enemy base armed only with a knife, fighting through soldiers who leap, charge and fire from every direction. Defeating certain enemies drops a flamethrower, rocket launcher or grenades with a few shots, a brief respite from close-quarters combat. The four stages lead to the rescue of prisoners of war. Its Cold War setting was explicit, and the title's pun on 'Russian attack' was dropped in Europe in favour of Green Beret.
trivia: Rush'n Attack's name was a deliberate pun on "Russia and Attack" — Konami's Cold War theme was explicit.
The knife as the primary weapon was deliberately unusual — close-range combat in a side-scroller required different player behaviour than shooting.
Collecting enemies' weapons temporarily added variety: rocket launchers, flamethrowers, and grenades were all available briefly.
The European title "Green Beret" was considered more marketable than the pun, which didn't translate.
devStory: Rush'n Attack (known as Green Beret in Europe) was developed by Konami in 1985. Players used a knife as the primary weapon — unusually close-range for a military action game — and had to disarm enemies to collect their weapons temporarily. The Cold War theme, pitting an American soldier against Soviet forces, was direct and unsubtle by the standards of any era.

title: The Oregon Trail
description: The Oregon Trail (1985) is MECC's educational strategy game: lead a wagon party west in 1848, managing supplies, river crossings and disease.
longDescription: Players outfit a wagon in Independence, Missouri, buying oxen, food and spare parts, then lead their party two thousand miles to Oregon's Willamette Valley. Along the way they hunt, ford rivers, trade and decide how hard to push, while broken axles, snakebites and dysentery claim the unprepared. First created in 1971 by student teacher Don Rawitsch and colleagues, its 1985 Apple II version was distributed so widely in American schools that it became one of the most-played educational games ever.
trivia: When the 1971 class ended, Don Rawitsch deleted the program but kept a printout of the code; in 1974 he typed it back in for MECC.
"You have died of dysentery" became one of gaming's most quoted lines, a dark joke about the game's brutal health system.
The game taught by allowing failure — players could lose to typhoid, broken wagon wheels, drowning, or starvation, learning historical realities through defeat.
MECC distributed the Apple II version through US school systems so widely that a generation of American children grew up playing it.
The game still has active communities creating fan versions, mods, and spiritual successors — its cultural impact has outlasted its educational context.
devStory: The Oregon Trail was originally created in 1971 by student teacher Don Rawitsch and two colleagues to teach US history, programmed on a teletype machine at a middle school in Minnesota. It was donated to MECC (Minnesota Educational Computing Consortium) in 1974 and republished for the Apple II in 1985. The Apple II version became one of the most-played educational games in American history, installed in virtually every school computer lab.

title: Arkanoid
description: Arkanoid (1986) is Taito's block breaker descended from Breakout, in which the Vaus paddle bounces a ball through walls of bricks towards the boss, DOH.
longDescription: The player moves the Vaus with a control knob, bouncing the ball into bricks. Some bricks release power-ups, and the final round pits the Vaus against DOH. The NES and MSX versions came with their own paddle controller.
trivia: It was Japan's top-grossing table arcade game of 1987.
Computer and Video Games called it "a lovely game".
devStory: Akira Fujita and Hiroshi Tsujino designed it, with music by Hisayoshi Ogura. Taito released it in Japan in July 1986, and Romstar in North America. It was the highest-grossing arcade conversion kit in the US in 1987, and sequels began with Revenge of Doh (1987).

title: Bubble Bobble
description: Bubble Bobble (1986) is Taito's co-operative platformer: Bub and Bob trap monsters in bubbles and pop them across 100 single-screen levels.
longDescription: Bub and Bob, two boys turned into bubble-blowing dragons, fight through 100 single-screen levels to rescue their girlfriends. Monsters trapped in bubbles are popped for fruit and points, and linking pops together multiplies the score; dawdle too long and an invincible pursuer appears. Designed by Fukio Mitsuji, it is built around two players working together — the true ending can only be reached by finishing the game with both.
trivia: Bubble Bobble has two endings: a false ending for solo players and a true ending that could only be seen by completing the game with two players simultaneously.
The 100 levels were each a contained puzzle with specific bubble trajectories and enemy behaviour — flow state design at its finest.
Bub and Bob were humans transformed into dinosaurs — the narrative motivation was rescuing their human girlfriends and breaking the curse.
The Baron Von Blubba boss appeared in certain levels as an indestructible pursuer if players were too slow — the first example of a patience mechanic in the series.
The game's catchy theme music became one of the most recognisable video game melodies of the 1980s.
devStory: Bubble Bobble was designed by Fukio "MTJ" Mitsuji at Taito in 1986. Mitsuji was known for his eccentric personality and unconventional design ideas. The game featured two simultaneous players as bubble-blowing dinosaurs on a 100-level adventure to rescue their girlfriends. The true ending required completing the game in two-player mode — solo players saw a fake ending. Bubble Bobble became one of the most beloved co-operative arcade games ever made.

title: Out Run
description: Out Run (1986) is Yu Suzuki's Sega driving game: cruise a red convertible through branching European scenery to one of five goals, with a choice of radio tunes.
longDescription: Out Run is about the drive rather than beating rivals. A red Ferrari Testarossa convertible, with a passenger beside the driver, races the clock through traffic, and at the end of each stage the road forks — so any single run passes through five of fifteen stages, finishing at one of five destinations. Players pick their music from three tracks by Hiroshi Kawaguchi on the car radio. Built on Sega's sprite-scaling hardware, with a deluxe hydraulic cabinet, it became the definitive feel-good racing game.
trivia: Suzuki drove across Europe in a Ferrari Testarossa specifically to research Out Run's visual style and road feel.
The branching route system — five different endings — was the first racing game to offer genuine choice of destination.
Players chose their soundtrack from three Sega original compositions at the start — unprecedented player control over game music.
The car is unmistakably a Ferrari Testarossa, but Sega did not license it — Ferrari's name appears nowhere in the original arcade game.
Out Run's "travel as lifestyle" concept — driving with a blonde passenger, choosing scenic routes — was revolutionary compared to competitive racing games.
devStory: Out Run was designed by Yu Suzuki at Sega in 1986. Suzuki drove across Europe for research, photographing roads, landscapes, and architecture for the game's backdrops. The game was the first to offer a branching route system — five different finish lines reached by choosing at each fork. A radio-cassette player in the cockpit let players choose between three musical tracks at the start. Out Run became the definitive "feel-good" racing game.

title: Rampage
description: Rampage (1986) is Bally Midway's three-player monster game: George, Lizzie and Ralph climb and smash city skyscrapers while the army fights back.
longDescription: Three giant monsters — George the ape, Lizzie the lizard and Ralph the wolf, all humans transformed by experiments — tour North American cities tearing down buildings, eating the fleeing residents and swatting helicopters and tanks. Up to three players take part at once and can punch each other as readily as the army. Designed by Brian Colin and Jeff Nauman, its gleeful destruction made it an instant hit, and it was eventually adapted into a 2018 film.
trivia: Rampage's monsters were legally distinct from King Kong and Godzilla, but their designs were clearly influenced by those characters.
Players could eat soldiers, people, and even each other — friendly fire between monsters was not only allowed but encouraged.
George, Lizzie, and Ralph were originally humans transformed by scientific experiments — a nod to the monster movie genre.
A feature film adaptation was released in 2018, starring Dwayne Johnson — 32 years after the original game.
devStory: Rampage was designed by Brian Colin and Jeff Nauman at Bally Midway in 1986. Three giant monsters — George (gorilla), Lizzie (lizard), and Ralph (werewolf) — destroyed cities while being shot at by the military. The three-player simultaneous format let friends each control a monster and compete to eat the most food and destroy the most buildings. The game's anarchic destruction fantasy was immediately popular.

title: Castlevania
description: Castlevania (1986) is Konami's gothic action platformer: Simon Belmont whips his way through Dracula's castle past movie monsters to face the Count.
longDescription: Simon Belmont climbs through six stages of Dracula's castle with a leather whip that can be upgraded into a chain, plus limited sub-weapons — axe, dagger, holy water, boomerang cross, stopwatch — powered by hearts found in candles. Bosses drawn from horror cinema, including Medusa, the Mummy, Frankenstein's monster and Death, guard the way to Dracula himself. Stiff, deliberate jumps and knockback that sends Simon into pits make it famously tough. Directed by Hitoshi Akamatsu, it began one of Konami's longest-running series.
trivia: Castlevania's enemies were drawn from Universal Monster films — Medusa, Frankenstein's Monster, the Mummy, and the Grim Reaper all appeared before Dracula.
The whip had a specific arc that couldn't hit enemies directly below the player — the game's most famous frustration was the medusa heads that knocked players into pits.
Candles throughout the castle hid sub-weapons and hearts — destroying them was habitual for players who mapped the game.
The staircase sections had fixed movement — players couldn't jump while climbing stairs, making them uniquely vulnerable.
Castlevania's gothic horror aesthetic, combined with action game mechanics, created a genre template that endured through 35 years of sequels.
devStory: Castlevania was designed by Hitoshi Akamatsu at Konami in 1986. Simon Belmont's quest through Dracula's castle was structured as a series of rooms with specific enemy placements and sub-bosses leading to confrontations with classic Universal Monsters — Medusa, Frankenstein's Monster, and the Grim Reaper — before the final battle with Dracula. The sub-weapon system added variety to Simon's primary whip attack.

title: Metroid
description: Metroid (1986) is Nintendo's non-linear sci-fi adventure: explore the caverns of planet Zebes, gaining abilities that open new paths.
longDescription: Bounty hunter Samus Aran lands on Zebes to destroy the Metroids and the Mother Brain of the Space Pirates. The planet is one interconnected labyrinth, and items such as the Morph Ball, missiles, bombs and the Ice Beam open routes that were closed before — the exploration structure later called 'Metroidvania'. Finishing quickly reveals that Samus is a woman, one of gaming's first famous twists. Produced by Gunpei Yokoi's R&D1, it launched a major Nintendo series.
trivia: Completing Metroid in under 5 hours revealed that Samus Aran was a woman — in 1986, this was one of gaming's most shocking reveals.
The Metroid creatures — jellyfish-like beings that drained energy — were designed to be immune to everything except Ice Beam followed by Missiles.
The non-linear world, where later-game abilities unlocked paths in earlier areas, created an entirely new design philosophy now called "Metroidvania."
Samus's power suit was designed to make her appear male specifically to enable the gender reveal — the helmet never came off during gameplay.
The game has no save system on NES — passwords regenerated exact game states, but Samus's equipment and map progress had to be reconstructed.
devStory: Metroid was developed by Nintendo Research & Development 1 under producer Gunpei Yokoi in 1986. The game's non-linear structure — a world where players needed abilities from later areas to access earlier ones — created the "Metroidvania" genre. The shocking reveal that the protagonist Samus Aran was a woman, shown only when players completed the game quickly enough, was one of gaming's first major plot twists.

title: Kid Icarus
description: Kid Icarus (1986) is Nintendo's mythological platformer: the angel Pit climbs from the Underworld to the sky palace to rescue the goddess Palutena.
longDescription: Pit escapes the Underworld and fights his way up through vertically scrolling stages, across the Overworld and into the Sky World, before a final side-scrolling shoot-'em-up assault on Medusa. Fortresses between areas are mazes to map, and hearts collected from enemies buy items and strength upgrades. Pit starts very weak, making the early stages punishing. Developed by R&D1 alongside Metroid, it was revived in 2012 with Kid Icarus: Uprising.
trivia: Kid Icarus and Metroid were developed simultaneously by the same team, sharing engine code — the games launched within months of each other.
Pit began the game extremely weak — the starting areas were intentionally brutal, designed to be replayed after earning upgrades.
The three environmental phases — underworld (bottom-scrolling), overworld (side-scrolling), sky world (horizontal shooting) — kept the game visually fresh.
Pit appeared in Super Smash Bros. Brawl in 2008, reviving interest in the character and leading to Kid Icarus: Uprising in 2012.
devStory: Kid Icarus was developed by Nintendo Research & Development 1 simultaneously with Metroid, sharing engine components. Designer Satoru Okada and producer Gunpei Yokoi wanted two contrasting games — Metroid's dark horizontal exploration and Kid Icarus's vertical ascending structure. Pit's journey from the underworld upward to Olympus provided the visual variety of three distinct environments.

title: Fantasy Zone
description: Fantasy Zone (1986) is Sega's pastel-coloured shooter: the winged ship Opa-Opa destroys enemy bases and spends coins in a shop between stages.
longDescription: Fantasy Zone replaced the dark space of most shooters with bright pastel worlds. Opa-Opa, a sentient ship with wings and feet, flies left or right through looping stages, and each level ends only after every enemy base is destroyed, triggering a boss. Defeated enemies drop coins spent in balloon shops on engines, bombs and weapons, an early in-game economy. Its cheerful look earned it an early 'cute-'em-up' reputation.
trivia: Fantasy Zone was nicknamed "the cute-em-up" for its pastel colours and cheerful aesthetics in contrast to the militaristic shooter norm.
Opa-Opa had legs and walked between flying — this physical detail made him one of the most characterful game protagonists of 1986.
A shop appeared between levels where players could buy weapons with coins collected from destroyed enemies — an early in-game economy.
The level could not be completed until every enemy base was destroyed — exploration was mandatory rather than optional.
devStory: Fantasy Zone was developed by Sega in 1986, designed by Akira Nishino. The game reversed the conventional shooter aesthetic: instead of dark space and military vessels, it featured pastel colours, balloons, walking coin pouches, and a shopkeeper who sold weapons between levels. Players controlled Opa-Opa, a sentient spacecraft with legs, in a horizontally scrolling world that looped indefinitely until all enemies were destroyed.

title: Solomon's Key
description: Solomon's Key (1986) is Tecmo's puzzle platformer: the wizard Dana creates and destroys blocks to reach each room's key and door.
longDescription: Each of Solomon's Key's rooms is a puzzle. Dana can conjure a stone block beside him or break one away, and must use that single power to build routes to the key and then the exit door, while enemies roam and a timer counts down. Hidden bonuses, fairies and secret rooms reward exploration. Tecmo's design makes it far more puzzle than platformer, and its later rooms demand precise sequences.
trivia: Creating and destroying blocks was the core mechanic — the same button alternated between modes based on context.
Hidden fairies in certain levels granted access to a bonus stage called "The Room of Solomon" with powerful items.
Every level had a hidden "Dana" figurine — collecting all of them across multiple playthroughs was a near-impossible completionist challenge.
The game was extremely difficult for a puzzle game — later levels required nearly perfect execution in a specific order.
devStory: Solomon's Key was developed by Tecmo in 1986. Players controlled Dana, a wizard who could create and destroy blocks to navigate puzzles, reach a key, and find a door. Each of the 50 levels was a contained block-manipulation puzzle requiring specific sequences of actions. Hidden rooms containing fairies and secret items rewarded thorough exploration. The game was more puzzle than platformer.

title: Rolling Thunder
description: Rolling Thunder (1986) is Namco's spy action game: agent Albatross fights the Geldra organisation, ducking into doorways for cover and managing scarce ammo.
longDescription: Agent Albatross of the Rolling Thunder espionage unit infiltrates the Geldra organisation to rescue a captured fellow agent. Its hooded Masker soldiers pour from doorways, and Albatross can duck into doors himself to wait out gunfire — an early take on cover. Ammunition is limited and restocked from doors marked for bullets or a machine gun, so resource management matters as much as aim. Its spy-film style made it stand out in 1986.
trivia: Rolling Thunder was one of the first action games with a spy thriller setting — tuxedo-clad Albatross fighting a criminal organisation felt genuinely cinematic.
Ducking into doors provided temporary cover — the first true cover mechanic in a side-scrolling action game.
Ammunition was limited and had to be replenished by entering specific doors — managing both health and ammo was constant.
The game's difficulty and resource management made it more tactical than most 1986 arcade games.
devStory: Rolling Thunder was developed by Namco in 1986. Players controlled secret agent Albatross in a spy-thriller setting — a rare realistic human-scale action game at a time when most games featured fantasy or science fiction settings. The ability to hide behind doors while shooting was a novel cover mechanic. The game's difficulty was high and the ammunition limited, requiring careful resource management.

title: Life Force
description: Life Force (1986), Salamander in Japan, is Konami's Gradius spin-off, a shooter that alternates horizontal and vertical stages, with two-player co-op.
longDescription: Life Force takes the ships and weapons of Gradius into a campaign that switches between horizontally and vertically scrolling stages. Two players can fly together, and power-ups are collected directly rather than from Gradius's selection meter. The stages pass through organic terrain, flaming solar flares and a skeletal fortress, and the Western release reframed the whole mission as a journey inside a living creature.
trivia: In the Japanese version (Salamander), players flew through giant living organisms — the levels were literally inside a creature's body.
Life Force was one of the first shoot-em-ups to mix vertical and horizontal scrolling stages within the same game.
The two-player mode shared a power-up bar — both players collected toward the same upgrades, creating co-operative dynamics.
The bone stage, navigating through a giant skeleton, was one of the most visually distinctive levels in any 1986 arcade game.
devStory: Life Force (known as Salamander in Japan) was developed by Konami in 1986 as a spin-off from Gradius. The game mixed vertical and horizontal scrolling stages and featured a two-player co-operative mode with shared power-up collection. In Japan, the game was set inside a living organism — the stages represented organs and arteries. This visceral premise was partially changed for Western releases.

title: Ikari Warriors
description: Ikari Warriors (1986) is SNK's vertically scrolling run-and-gun for two, with rotary joysticks for aiming and tanks to commandeer.
longDescription: Two commandos, Ralf and Clark, fight up a jungle battlefield with machine guns and grenades, and can climb into abandoned tanks for heavier firepower. The arcade cabinet's rotary joysticks turn to aim independently of movement, so soldiers can strafe while firing. Its style owed much to Rambo-era action films, and its co-operative play made it one of SNK's biggest hits of the decade.
trivia: The heroes, Ralf and Clark (renamed Paul and Vince in some Western versions), later returned as fighters in SNK's The King of Fighters series.
Its rotary joysticks let players aim independently of movement — an idea SNK had already used in TNK III.
Tanks scattered around the levels could be boarded and driven, providing temporary heavy firepower.
The continue system asked players to input a code — one of the earliest examples of limited continues gated by player knowledge.
devStory: Ikari Warriors was developed by SNK in 1986. Players controlled two soldiers, Ralf and Clark, fighting through enemy territory using guns and grenades. The rotary joystick allowed players to aim in one direction while moving in another — an early form of twin-stick shooter control. The two-player co-operative mode was popular.

title: The Legend of Zelda
description: The Legend of Zelda is a 1986 Nintendo NES game that created the action-adventure genre, challenging players to explore an open world, find hidden items, and complete nine increasingly complex dungeons to rescue Princess Zelda from the villain Ganon. Unlike contemporary games, Zelda had no lives, a battery save system for recording progress — a first for home console games — and a non-linear structure that let players explore freely. Its enormous, secret-filled overworld rewarded curiosity and experimentation, establishing exploration and discovery as core pillars of game design. The franchise has since produced over 20 sequels and is one of the most critically acclaimed game series in history.
longDescription: Miyamoto designed Zelda as a digital miniature garden — a world to explore and return to, inspired by his childhood adventures exploring caves and forests near Kyoto. The game's battery-backed save system (the first in a Nintendo cartridge) allowed for a long, complex adventure without starting over each session. Nine underground dungeons, each with a unique layout and boss, were distributed across the overworld map, requiring items from earlier dungeons to access later ones. The second quest — a remixed, harder version unlocked after completing the game — doubled the content. The gold cartridge distinguished it visually on store shelves. The franchise went on to produce landmark titles including A Link to the Past, Ocarina of Time (widely considered the greatest video game ever made), Breath of the Wild, and Tears of the Kingdom, each redefining what games could be.
trivia: Zelda was the first NES game to use battery-backed save memory — the gold cartridge contained a coin battery that preserved game data without password systems.
Miyamoto designed the game based on his childhood memories of exploring caves and forests near his home, famously describing it as "a miniature garden that you can put inside a drawer."
The second quest — a harder remix of the game unlocked after completing it — doubled the playtime and rewarded dedicated players.
Link was named "Link" because he was meant to be a link between the player and the game world — a vessel for player projection.
The Legend of Zelda's "thinking outside the box" puzzle design — burning bushes, bombing walls — trained an entire generation to question every surface.
devStory: The Legend of Zelda was designed by Shigeru Miyamoto and Takashi Tezuka at Nintendo in 1986. Miyamoto drew inspiration from exploring the forests and caves near his childhood home in Sonobe, Japan. The game shipped with a gold cartridge — the first NES game to use battery-backed save memory — allowing players to preserve progress. The open-world structure with no explicit tutorial was revolutionary.

title: Double Dragon
description: Double Dragon (1987) is Technos Japan's beat-'em-up: Billy and Jimmy Lee fight through city gangs to rescue Marian, with grabs, throws and weapons.
longDescription: Brothers Billy and Jimmy Lee brawl through city streets, a factory, a forest and a hideout to rescue Marian from the Black Warriors gang. Grabbing enemies allows knees, headbutts and throws, and dropped baseball bats, whips and knives can be picked up. Two players fight side by side and can hit each other too. Created by Yoshihisa Kishimoto, it turned the side-scrolling beat-'em-up into a commercial force and set up the genre's boom.
trivia: Double Dragon allowed two players to fight simultaneously but also to punch each other — accidental friendly fire was common, deliberate betrayal possible.
The grappling system — grabbing an enemy to headbutt, knee, or throw them — gave the game a physicality rare in 1987 arcade games.
Enemies dropped their weapons when knocked down — picking them up gave players access to baseball bats, whips, and knives.
In two-player games, beating the final boss is not the end: the brothers must then fight each other to decide who wins Marian.
Double Dragon directly inspired Streets of Rage, Final Fight, and the entire beat-em-up genre's commercial golden age of 1987–1994.
devStory: Double Dragon was developed by Technos Japan in 1987. Designers Yoshihisa Kishimoto and Koji Ogata created a beat-em-up where two players co-operated to rescue a kidnapped woman. The game's grappling system — grabbing enemies to headbutt or knee them — was a significant mechanical advance over simple punch-kick games. Double Dragon was massively successful and essentially launched the beat-em-up genre as a commercial force.

title: Mega Man
description: Mega Man (1987) is Capcom's NES action platformer: pick any of six Robot Masters to fight, and take each boss's weapon for the next.
longDescription: Mega Man must stop Dr. Wily's rogue robots. A stage select lets players tackle Cut Man, Guts Man, Ice Man, Bomb Man, Fire Man and Elec Man in any order, and each defeated master gives up a weapon that is especially effective against one of the others. The order becomes part of the puzzle. Designed by Akira Kitamura, with the character designed by Keiji Inafune, it sold modestly but launched one of Capcom's most enduring series.
trivia: Players could complete the six Robot Master stages in any order — a non-linear structure rare in 1987 action games.
Each Robot Master weapon was specifically effective against one other Robot Master, creating a rock-paper-scissors chain that rewarded discovery.
The first game sold modestly, and Capcom agreed to a sequel only if the team made it alongside their other work — Mega Man 2 went on to make the series one of Capcom's biggest.
Mega Man's visual design — blue colour, arm cannon, helmet — was created by Keiji Inafune, who went on to become the series' creative director.
devStory: Mega Man was designed by Akira Kitamura at Capcom in 1987. The core innovation was the stage-select screen allowing players to tackle six Robot Masters in any order — each defeated boss surrendered their weapon, usable against other bosses with specific vulnerabilities. Kitamura designed each Robot Master with a clear thematic identity (Cut Man, Bomb Man, Guts Man) that communicated their attack patterns visually.

title: R-Type
description: R-Type (1987) is Irem's horizontal shooter: the R-9 fights the alien Bydo with the Force, a detachable pod that blocks shots and fires on its own.
longDescription: The R-9 Arrowhead flies eight stages against the Bydo empire. Its signature is the Force, an indestructible pod that can attach to the front or back of the ship or be launched to fight independently, blocking bullets and adding firepower. Holding fire charges the Wave Cannon. Enemy patterns are fixed and punishing, so the game rewards memorisation. Stage 3, a battle along a single colossal warship, is among the most celebrated stages of any shooter.
trivia: The Force pod — detachable, attachable, reflective — was one of gaming's most original weapon mechanics and was never successfully replicated by another game.
R-Type required pattern memorisation rather than reflexes — dying and learning was the intended design philosophy.
The Bydo — the game's antagonist organism — was later revealed in sequels to be a future version of humanity transformed into a weapon.
Stage 3's giant battleship, which players flew through from the outside to the inside, was one of the most ambitious level designs of 1987.
R-Type's demanding difficulty and puzzle-like structure gave it a cult status that persisted long after most contemporaries were forgotten.
devStory: R-Type was developed by Irem in 1987. The Force pod — a reflective orb that attached to the front or rear of the ship — was a completely original mechanic. The pod blocked bullets, reflected certain enemy fire, and served as an independent weapon. Unlike most shooters, R-Type required precise memorisation of enemy patterns rather than reflexes — every stage was a puzzle with a specific solution.

title: Metal Gear
description: Metal Gear (1987) is Hideo Kojima's MSX2 stealth game: Solid Snake infiltrates Outer Heaven, avoiding guards rather than fighting them.
longDescription: Solid Snake is sent into the fortress of Outer Heaven to rescue a captured agent and destroy Metal Gear, a nuclear-armed walking tank. Guards see only in front of them, and being spotted raises the alarm, so Snake sneaks, hides and gathers equipment and keycards rather than fighting. The mission's final twist reveals who has really been directing it. Hideo Kojima's first game, it set out the 'tactical espionage action' formula; a Famicom version by a different team followed.
trivia: Metal Gear was Kojima's first major game — he was assigned to create it as a junior designer and turned it into an anti-war philosophical work.
The NES port of Metal Gear was made by a different team without Kojima's involvement — he has publicly criticised it.
Big Boss, the final antagonist, was revealed to be the player's commanding officer who had been sending them into a trap.
The game's stealth mechanics were designed around MSX2 hardware limitations — the enemy could only see in a straight line due to processing constraints.
Metal Gear Solid (1998) made Kojima a household name, but Metal Gear (1987) established every core concept he would refine for the following three decades.
devStory: Metal Gear was designed by Hideo Kojima at Konami in 1987 for the MSX2 home computer. Kojima wanted to make an anti-war game where combat was the failure state — sneaking past enemies was always preferred over fighting. The game introduced the "tactical espionage action" concept, where players gathered intelligence, used environment, and avoided conflict. Kojima had been assigned to create the game as a junior designer; it became his defining work.

title: Shinobi
description: Shinobi (å¿) is a 1987 hack and slash video game developed and published by Sega for arcades on the Sega System 16 board.  The player controls ninja Joe Musashi, who must stop the Zeed terrorist organisation from kidnapping students of his clan.
longDescription: Shinobi (å¿) is a 1987 hack and slash video game developed and published by Sega for arcades on the Sega System 16 board.  The player controls ninja Joe Musashi, who must stop the Zeed terrorist organisation from kidnapping students of his clan.
trivia: Shinobi's hostage-rescue mechanic gave every stage a secondary objective — players couldn't just survive, they had to find every captive child.
The ninjutsu magic was a screen-clearing power — but players had a fixed number of uses that didn't replenish, so saving them for bosses was critical.
The third level boss was a ninja gang leader who used his own children as hostages — a moment of moral pressure unusual in 1987.
The Master of Shinobi bonus rounds required throwing stars at enemies under strict time pressure — an arcade skill-challenge format.
devStory: Shinobi was developed by Sega in 1987. Players controlled Joe Musashi, a ninja rescuing kidnapped children from the criminal organisation Zeed. The game's hostage-rescue mechanic added consequence to every stage — children had to be freed before completing the level. The ninjutsu magic system provided powerful screen-clearing attacks limited by resource management. Shinobi became one of Sega's most successful arcade franchises.

title: After Burner
description: Sega's 1987 jet-fighter rail shooter, developed by Yu Suzuki's team: fly an F-14 Tomcat through 18 stages of missile lock-ons, ideally from a hydraulic cockpit that rolls with the plane.
longDescription:
After Burner was developed by Sega's Studio 128 and released in arcades in 1987. The player flies an F-14 Tomcat through 18 stages, shooting down waves of enemy aircraft with a machine gun and a limited supply of heat-seeking missiles.

Like Sega's earlier Space Harrier (1985) and Out Run (1986), it uses a third-person view from behind the player's vehicle, and it ran on the Sega X Board, hardware capable of rotating sprites and surfaces to sell the sense of speed and banking. Its most elaborate cabinet was a hydraulic "taikan" motion simulator — the fourth Sega game to use one, and more sophisticated than its predecessors — that tilted the seated player as the jet rolled.
trivia: The hydraulic cabinet version of After Burner physically tilted the entire cockpit — one of the most elaborate arcade experiences ever built.
After Burner used a real F-14 Tomcat as its visual basis, capitalising on the Top Gun film released the previous year.
Machine-gun fire was unlimited, but missiles ran low and were restocked by mid-air refuelling between stages.
Suzuki directed the production like a film — the missions followed a narrative arc with specific enemy formations for each stage.
devStory: After Burner was designed by Yu Suzuki at Sega in 1987. The third-person aerial dogfighting game used Sega's Super Scaler hardware at its most impressive — hundreds of enemy aircraft scaled and rotated at 60fps to simulate aerial combat. The hydraulic cabinet moved the entire cockpit in sync with the on-screen action. After Burner grossed more per machine than almost any game before it.

title: Operation Wolf
description: Operation Wolf (1987) is Taito's military gun game: aim a mounted Uzi with recoil at soldiers and vehicles while rescuing hostages.
longDescription: Operation Wolf mounts a replica Uzi on the cabinet, with a motor that kicks back as it fires. Players shoot soldiers, helicopters and boats across six missions, managing limited magazines and rocket grenades, and must avoid hitting civilians and hostages. Its realistic military setting and physical gun made it a sensation and helped start the boom in gun games of the late 1980s.
trivia: Operation Wolf's mounted UZI gun peripheral had a recoil motor that vibrated when fired — early force feedback in an arcade context.
The game required players to rescue hostages from each area — shooting civilians reduced the hostage count and increased mission difficulty.
The ammunition management system — grenades and machine gun bullets were both limited — created resource pressure across the entire game.
Operation Wolf was one of the first games to achieve the "gun-in-hand" physical sensation that light gun games had always promised.
devStory: Operation Wolf was developed by Taito in 1987. Players used a mounted gun peripheral to shoot at enemies in a series of military missions, aiming to rescue hostages. The game was one of the first light gun games to use a realistic military setting and free-aim rather than screen-limited targeting. Its popularity triggered the "gallery shooter" genre boom of the late 1980s.

title: Contra
description: Contra is a 1987 Konami arcade and NES run-and-gun game that became one of the defining multiplayer action games of the 8-bit era.
