Players control commandos Bill and Lance as they battle through jungles, fortresses, and alien bases to stop an extraterrestrial invasion, firing constantly and jumping with split-second precision. The NES version introduced the famous Konami Code — Up Up Down Down Left Right Left Right B A — which granted 30 extra lives and became the most famous cheat code in gaming history. Contra's cooperative two-player mode, relentless pace, and demanding difficulty made it a beloved classic that still defines the genre.
longDescription: Contra was heavily inspired by the 1980s action film aesthetic — specifically Predator, Aliens, and The Terminator — with its two muscular commandos, dense jungle settings, and alien antagonists. The arcade version featured a mix of side-scrolling and behind-the-back third-person shooting stages, while the NES port streamlined the experience into pure side-scrolling with superior level design. Weapon pickups — spread guns, rapid fire, lasers, and flamethrowers — changed gameplay dramatically and were hotly contested in co-op play. The game's difficulty was brutal by design, but the Konami Code made it accessible to casual players while retaining challenge for purists. The franchise spawned over a dozen sequels and the term 'Contra-style' became shorthand for a specific type of demanding but satisfying run-and-gun action.
trivia: The heroes' first names, Bill and Lance, are often said to nod to Aliens actors Bill Paxton and Lance Henriksen.
The Konami Code (Up Up Down Down Left Right Left Right B A) gave players 30 lives — the most famous cheat code in gaming history.
The spread gun was considered so overpowered that experienced players deliberately avoided power-ups rather than risk losing it when hit.
The two-player mode was completely simultaneous — one player's death didn't stop the other, and the game continued even if one player ran out of lives.
The alien boss designs were directly inspired by H.R. Giger's Alien artwork — Konami did not have a licence.
devStory: Contra was developed by Konami in 1987. The two-player run-and-gun game was explicitly inspired by Predator and Aliens. Bill Rizer and Lance Bean fought through alien-infested jungles and military bases using five weapon types. The spread gun was so powerful that most experienced players kept it for the entire game rather than risking death.

title: Street Fighter
description: Street Fighter is the 1987 Capcom arcade game that launched one of the most successful fighting game franchises in history, though the sequel Street Fighter II would far surpass it in influence. Players control Ryu (or Ken in two-player mode) through a world fighting tournament, facing opponents from across the globe in one-on-one combat. The game introduced the special move system — quarter-circle and half-circle joystick motions combined with button presses that produced fireballs, uppercuts, and hurricane kicks — which became the foundation of all fighting games that followed. Street Fighter established the template that Street Fighter II perfected into a global phenomenon four years later.
longDescription: Street Fighter was designed by Takashi Nishiyama and Hiroshi Matsumoto and was notable for its pneumatic button cabinet, which could detect punch force and vary the attack strength accordingly — though this proved fragile and was replaced by six standard buttons in production. The game featured eight opponents across five countries, each with distinct fighting styles. The special move system — requiring specific joystick patterns to trigger signature attacks — was revolutionary but poorly documented, leading many players to discover moves by accident. The game was a moderate hit but the team recognised the fighting genre's potential. The lessons learned directly informed Street Fighter II's 1991 design, which became one of the most successful arcade games ever made, revitalised the arcade industry, and created the competitive fighting game community that continues to thrive today.
trivia: The deluxe cabinet used two large pressure-sensitive pads — hit harder for stronger attacks — while a conventional six-button version was also sold.
The hadouken (fireball) and shoryuken (dragon punch) special moves introduced the input notation that still defines fighting game design.
Street Fighter II's success was so disproportionate to the original that most players don't know the first game exists.
Opponents came from Japan, the United States, England, China and Thailand — a world-tour format Street Fighter II expanded.
devStory: Street Fighter was designed by Takashi Nishiyama and Hiroshi Matsumoto at Capcom in 1987. The game introduced the special move input system — specific joystick motions combined with button presses triggered powerful attacks. The two-player format and the roster of international opponents established the one-on-one fighting game template. Street Fighter II (1991) refined these concepts into a cultural phenomenon, but the original created the foundation.

title: Pirates!
description: Sid Meier's Pirates! (1987) is MicroProse's open-world Caribbean adventure, in which a privateer duels, battles ships, trades and plunders across a lifetime.
longDescription: The player starts in an era from 1560 to 1680 as a privateer for Spain, the Dutch Republic, England or France, and may turn pirate. Sword duels, sea and land battles mix with decisions such as whom to marry and how to divide the plunder. Relations between nations shift as the game goes on, and the character ages and eventually retires.
trivia: Its copy protection asked when treasure fleets arrived; a wrong answer made the game much harder.
Computer Gaming World named it Action Game of the Year for 1988.
devStory: Meier designed it, with art by Michael Haire. It came out on the Commodore 64 in 1987 and sold over a million copies. It was remade as Pirates! Gold (1993) and again in 2004.

title: Maniac Mansion
description: Maniac Mansion (1987) is Lucasfilm Games' comedy adventure: pick three teenagers to rescue Sandy from Dr. Fred's house — and debut the SCUMM engine.
longDescription: Dave's girlfriend Sandy has been kidnapped by the Edisons and taken into their mansion. Players choose two companions from six teenagers with different skills, and the choice changes which puzzles can be solved and how — leading to several possible endings. Commands are built by clicking verbs and objects, replacing typed commands. Ron Gilbert and Gary Winnick wrote the SCUMM scripting system for it, which went on to power Lucasfilm's adventures from Monkey Island to Day of the Tentacle.
trivia: SCUMM (Script Creation Utility for Maniac Mansion) was the engine Ron Gilbert invented for this game — it went on to power Monkey Island, Indiana Jones, and Day of the Tentacle.
Dave is joined by two teenagers chosen from six, each with different skills — different combinations open different solutions.
Maniac Mansion featured multiple different endings depending on which characters survived and which goals were completed.
The game could be "broken" by feeding a hamster to a microwave — triggering a game-ending consequence deliberately included as player choice.
A sequel, Day of the Tentacle (1993), featured Maniac Mansion playable in its entirety as a game within the game.
devStory: Maniac Mansion was designed by Ron Gilbert and Gary Winnick at LucasArts (then Lucasfilm Games) in 1987. Gilbert invented the SCUMM scripting engine specifically for this game, which allowed complex adventure game logic without requiring constant reprogramming. The point-and-click interface replaced the text parser, making adventure games accessible to players who weren't typists. Gilbert and Winnick based the mansion on a real house in San Rafael, California.

title: Road Blasters
description: Road Blasters (1987) is Atari's armed driving game: blast enemy cars along 50 rallies, collecting fuel globes and special weapons to keep going.
longDescription: Road Blasters puts a weapon-equipped car on a road stretching to the horizon, shooting enemy vehicles and mines while fuel runs down. Collecting fuel globes keeps the run alive, and power-ups dropped from above add attachments such as the UZ Cannon and Nitro Injector. Fifty rallies of increasing difficulty gave players a long campaign by arcade standards. It was one of Atari Games' last big driving hits.
trivia: Road Blasters offered 50 levels — an unusually large amount for an arcade game, designed to give location operators weeks of sustained play.
Fuel management was central — missiles and bombs from enemy aircraft reduced fuel, while refuelling cars provided it back.
The weapon attachment system — collecting UZ Cannons and Nitro Injectors that attached to the car — gave the game a customisation element.
The game's forced perspective road was a technical achievement using Atari's hardware to maintain frame rate across 50 distinct environments.
devStory: Road Blasters was developed by Atari Games in 1987. Players drove an armed car through 50 levels of increasingly difficult traffic and enemies, collecting fuel to continue. The game used a combination of sprite-scaled graphics and a fixed horizon to create a convincing sense of speed. It was one of the last major games developed at Atari before the company's decline.

title: Rastan
description: Rastan (1987) is Taito's barbarian action game: a sword-wielding warrior fights through six stages of fantasy monsters, each ending in a boss.
longDescription: Rastan, a barbarian warrior in the Conan mould, fights through six rounds of dungeons, castles and wilderness with a sword that can be swapped for axes and maces. Swings take time and hits knock him back, giving the combat weight, while vines, ropes and pits make the stages platforming challenges too. Each round ends with a large boss. It was one of Taito's notable action games of the late 1980s.
trivia: Rastan was explicitly inspired by the Conan the Barbarian film and character — the muscular barbarian warrior with a broadsword was Taito's direct homage.
Stamina decreased over time and had to be replenished by collecting potions — a survival mechanic unusual in 1987 action games.
Enemies had significant knockback — being hit threw the player across the screen, making wall positioning critical.
The six stages each ended with a large boss encounter that required specific attack patterns to defeat efficiently.
devStory: Rastan was developed by Taito in 1987. Players controlled a barbarian warrior in a fantasy world, using a sword to fight enemies across six stages. The game was designed with a weighty, physical feel — attacks had swing time, enemies knocked the player back significantly, and stamina decreased during play. The barbarian aesthetic, explicitly inspired by Conan, was popular in mid-1980s entertainment.

title: Mike Tyson's Punch-Out!!
description: Mike Tyson's Punch-Out!! (1987) is Nintendo's NES boxing game: Little Mac works through a circuit of fighters to take on Mike Tyson.
longDescription: Little Mac climbs through the Minor, Major and World circuits against a roster of caricatured boxers — Glass Joe, King Hippo, Soda Popinski, Bald Bull — ending with a dream fight against Mike Tyson. Every opponent has tells that signal each attack, so victory comes from dodging, reading and countering rather than button-mashing. Tyson can floor Mac in a single punch. After the licence ended, the game was reissued with the fictional Mr. Dream in Tyson's place.
trivia: Mike Tyson was licensed at the peak of his career — Nintendo paid $50,000 for the three-year licence.
Tyson's first-round knockdown required frame-perfect timing — he could knock down Little Mac with a single punch, and his blink was the tell.
Each opponent's tell — the facial tic, sound cue, or animation that signalled their attack — was designed to be learnable through repeated play.
The game had no way to punch while dodging — movement and attacking were separate, making defensive play a prerequisite for offence.
After Tyson's licence expired in 1990, Mr. Dream replaced him with identical stats and behaviour — the same fight, different face.
devStory: Mike Tyson's Punch-Out!! was designed by Genyo Takeda and Makoto Wada at Nintendo in 1987 for the NES. It featured eleven opponents in the World Video Boxing Association circuit, several fought twice, each with patterns that had to be read and countered. Mike Tyson himself was licensed and featured as the final opponent — virtually unbeatable without precise timing of his first-round knockdowns. After the licence expired in 1990, Tyson was replaced by "Mr. Dream."

title: Bionic Commando
description: Bionic Commando (1987) is Capcom's arcade action game in which the hero cannot jump, swinging across gaps with an extendable bionic arm instead.
longDescription: Bionic Commando's soldier has no jump button. Instead he fires a grappling arm diagonally or straight up to latch onto platforms and ledges, swinging and climbing through the vertical stages of an enemy base while shooting soldiers. Mastering the arm's reach and swing is the whole game. Designed by Tokuro Fujiwara, it was followed by a very different NES version with a longer story and a map of areas to visit.
trivia: Bionic Commando removed the ability to jump entirely — a deliberate design choice that forced players to rethink every traversal challenge.
The grappling arm could grab ledges, enemies, and even bullets in some cases — mastering its physics was the whole game.
The later Famicom/NES version, a very different game, made a resurrected Hitler its final villain — renamed 'Master-D' for Western releases.
The NES version added radio conversations and a map of areas to visit, turning the arcade game into a longer adventure.
devStory: Bionic Commando was designed by Tokuro Fujiwara at Capcom in 1987. The central innovation was removing the ability to jump — the soldier used a bionic arm with a grappling hook to swing across gaps. This forced entirely new spatial thinking compared to conventional platformers. A reworked NES version followed in 1988 with a longer story.

title: Dragon Spirit
description: Dragon Spirit (1987) is Namco's fantasy vertical shooter: fly a dragon breathing fire at air enemies and bombs at ground targets, growing extra heads.
longDescription: Dragon Spirit swaps the usual spaceship for a blue dragon. Fire breath hits flying enemies while a separate attack targets creatures and structures on the ground, the dual-target idea familiar from Namco's Xevious. Power-up eggs let the dragon grow up to three heads for a wider spread of fire, or shrink it when it takes damage. Its fantasy landscapes gave the vertical shooter a fresh look in 1987.
trivia: Dragon Spirit was one of the first shooters to use a fantasy setting — replacing spacecraft with a dragon gave the genre fresh visual vocabulary.
The dragon's fire evolved with power-ups — growing additional heads increased the width of the fire breath attack.
Ground enemies and aerial enemies required different fire types, creating simultaneous dual-target management.
devStory: Dragon Spirit was developed by Namco in 1987. Players controlled a dragon rather than a spacecraft — a fantasy setting that gave the vertical shooter a different visual language. The dragon could breathe fire at ground targets and a separate breath weapon at air targets, mirroring Xevious's dual targeting. Power-ups evolved the dragon's appearance and abilities, with multiple head growth stages providing wider fire coverage.

title: Altered Beast
description: Altered Beast (1988) is Sega's mythological beat-'em-up: a resurrected centurion collects spirit balls to transform into beasts — and came bundled with the Genesis.
longDescription: Summoned from the grave by Zeus — 'Rise from your grave!' — a Roman centurion fights through the underworld to rescue Athena. Collecting spirit balls from white wolves makes him more muscular, and a third transforms him into a beast for the level's end: a werewolf, weredragon, werebear, weretiger or golden werewolf. Two players can fight together. As the pack-in game with the Sega Genesis in North America, it was the first game many owners of the console played.
trivia: "RISE FROM YOUR GRAVE!" and "WELCOME TO YOUR DOOM!" became instantly recognisable voice samples due to the game's Genesis bundle status.
Altered Beast was the first game most Genesis owners played, making it one of the most culturally significant games of the 16-bit era despite mixed reviews.
Two-player co-op let one player control the hero and the other a clone — both could transform independently.
devStory: Altered Beast was developed by Sega in 1988. Players collected spirit balls to transform into powerful beasts — werewolf, werebear, weretiger, weredragon, and golden wolf — for boss fights. The transformation power fantasy, with accompanying voice samples ("RISE FROM YOUR GRAVE!"), made it memorable. Altered Beast was the pack-in game bundled with the Sega Genesis/Mega Drive in North America, ensuring it was played by millions.

title: Mega Man 2
description: Mega Man 2 (1988) is Capcom's NES sequel with eight Robot Masters, a password system and a celebrated soundtrack — the game that made the series.
longDescription: Mega Man 2 expands the original to eight Robot Masters — Metal Man, Air Man, Bubble Man, Quick Man, Crash Man, Flash Man, Heat Man and Wood Man — each tackled in any order and each yielding a weapon for the others. Passwords let players continue their progress, easier difficulty options helped newcomers, and utility items built paths across gaps. Made by a small team after the first game's modest sales, it was a critical and commercial success, and Takashi Tateishi's music became some of the NES's best known.
trivia: Mega Man 2 was developed by a skeleton crew working overtime on a rejected project — Capcom's management had minimal faith in the sequel.
The game introduced the password system, allowing players to continue from any point — essential for a game with eight long stages.
Composer Takashi Tateishi created the game's iconic soundtrack in his spare time alongside his regular job — it became one of the most beloved game soundtracks ever.
The eight Robot Master selection — Metal Man, Air Man, Bubble Man, Quick Man, Crash Man, Flash Man, Heat Man, Wood Man — created the template for every subsequent Mega Man game.
Mega Man 2 is consistently rated among the greatest NES games ever made, despite being made with little confidence from its own publisher.
devStory: Mega Man 2 was designed by Akira Kitamura and Keiji Inafune at Capcom in 1988. After the original Mega Man's modest sales, Capcom was reluctant to make a sequel. The development team worked on it as a side project with minimal budget. The resulting game — with eight Robot Masters, a password system, and expanded music by Takashi Tateishi — was critically praised and commercially successful, saving the franchise.

title: Ghouls 'n Ghosts
description: Ghouls 'n Ghosts (1988) is Capcom's arcade sequel to Ghosts 'n Goblins: Sir Arthur, golden armour and magic, and a second loop for the true ending.
longDescription: Sir Arthur sets out again, this time to rescue the princess from Loki. He can now fire up and down, and chests hold the golden armour, which charges a magic attack specific to the weapon he carries. The stages throw earthquakes, rising water and collapsing ground at him on top of the demons. Designed by Tokuro Fujiwara, it keeps its predecessor's cruel twist: beating the game once only reveals a second, harder loop, and the final boss can only be damaged with a special weapon.
trivia: Ghouls 'n Ghosts retained its predecessor's brutal mechanic: completing the game triggers a cutscene revealing it was a trick, requiring a second full playthrough.
The golden armour provided magic attacks but was fragile — losing it meant losing the magic system until another was found.
The game's music, composed by Tamayo Kawamoto, was considered one of the finest in 16-bit gaming.
The Mega Drive version was technically impressive and helped establish the console's "arcade-perfect port" reputation.
devStory: Ghouls 'n Ghosts was designed by Tokuro Fujiwara at Capcom in 1988 as the sequel to Ghosts 'n Goblins. The game introduced the two-layer armour system (golden armour unlocked magic attacks) and the Psycho Cannon — the only weapon that can harm the final boss. Like its predecessor, completing the game once revealed it was an illusion, requiring a second playthrough for the true ending.

title: Super Mario Bros. 3
description: Super Mario Bros. 3 (1988) is Nintendo's NES platformer of eight themed worlds, a world map, and suits including the flying Raccoon Mario.
longDescription: Super Mario Bros. 3 sends Mario and Luigi across eight themed worlds — grassland, desert, sea, giant-sized, sky, ice, pipes and Bowser's dark land — navigated on a map with branching paths, mini-games and roaming enemies. Its power-ups transformed the series: the Raccoon suit's tail lets Mario fly, and Frog, Tanooki and Hammer suits add more. Designed by Shigeru Miyamoto and Takashi Tezuka, and staged like a theatre production, it is one of the best-selling and most acclaimed games ever made.
trivia: Super Mario Bros. 3 was revealed to American audiences in the 1989 film The Wizard, months before its US release — generating extraordinary anticipation.
The game appeared to take place on a stage set — certain elements looked like theatrical props, and the ending credits confirmed this staging metaphor.
Miyamoto designed the Raccoon suit to give players flight capability but limited its duration to prevent the whole game being skipped by air.
Super Mario Bros. 3 sold 17 million copies worldwide and is consistently ranked among the greatest video games ever made.
Each of the eight worlds had its own theme: Grass Land, Desert Land, Water Land, Giant Land, Sky Land, Ice Land, Pipe Land and Bowser's Dark Land.
devStory: Super Mario Bros. 3 was designed by Shigeru Miyamoto and Takashi Tezuka at Nintendo in 1988. The game introduced the world map, power-up inventory, and a variety of new suits — Raccoon (flight), Frog (swimming), Tanooki (stone form), Hammer Brother (throwing hammers). The development team structured each of the eight worlds around a distinct theme, treating them as separate experiences rather than a single escalating progression.

title: Ninja Gaiden
description: Ninja Gaiden (1988) is Tecmo's NES ninja platformer: Ryu Hayabusa avenges his father through a cinematic story told in cutscenes, and brutal difficulty.
longDescription: Ryu Hayabusa leaves Japan for America to find his father's killer and uncovers a plot involving an ancient demon. The story unfolds in anime-style cinematic cutscenes between acts, far richer storytelling than most NES action games offered. Ryu slashes, wall-jumps and climbs, using ninja arts powered by collected items. Its difficulty is legendary, especially the final act, where dying against the last bosses sends the player back to the start of the act. (Tecmo's arcade game of the same name is a different, beat-'em-up design.)
trivia: Ninja Gaiden used manga-style panel cutscenes to tell a complex revenge story — narrative depth unprecedented in NES action games.
Losing to any of the three final bosses sends the player back to the start of Act 6 — one of the most notorious difficulty decisions on the NES.
Ryu can cling to walls and jump between them — a traversal move that shaped the game's vertical stages.
The soundtrack, composed by Keiji Yamagishi, is considered one of the finest in NES gaming.
devStory: Ninja Gaiden was designed by Hideo Yoshizawa at Tecmo in 1988. The game was notable for its extensive use of cutscenes — between-level cinematic panels that told a story about Ryu Hayabusa's mission to avenge his father. These were the most sophisticated narrative sequences seen in an NES game to that point. The game's difficulty was legendary, particularly the final stages which reset players to an earlier point after the last few bosses.

title: Blaster Master
description: Blaster Master (1988) is Sunsoft's NES action game: pilot the tank SOPHIA through side-scrolling caverns, then leave it to explore overhead dungeons on foot.
longDescription: In the Western version, Jason follows his pet frog down a hole into an underground world of mutants, where he finds the combat tank SOPHIA. Side-scrolling areas are explored in the tank, which gains the ability to hover, climb walls and drive underwater as it is upgraded; Jason climbs out to enter overhead dungeons on foot and fight the bosses. The two styles make it feel like two games in one, and Naoki Kodaka's score is among the NES's most admired.
trivia: Blaster Master switched between side-scrolling tank sections and overhead-view dungeon exploration — two distinct gameplay modes in one game.
SOPHIA III could cling to walls and ceilings, allowing platforming sequences unlike any other tank in gaming.
The music, by Naoki Kodaka, is considered among the best on the NES — Area 1's theme in particular is frequently cited.
The Western plot (a boy chases his pet frog into a radioactive hole) was a complete rewrite of the Japanese story (a future warrior battles against mutants).
devStory: Blaster Master was developed by Sunsoft in 1988. Players controlled a tank (SOPHIA III) that could jump, cling to walls, and enter overhead-view dungeon sections where the protagonist fought on foot. The switching between side-scrolling tank combat and top-down dungeon exploration created a hybrid that felt like two games in one. The game was known for its excellent music, composed by Naoki Kodaka.

title: Bad Dudes vs. DragonNinja
description: Bad Dudes vs. DragonNinja (1988) is Data East's two-player beat-'em-up: 'Are you a bad enough dude to rescue President Ronnie?'
longDescription: After ninjas kidnap the President of the United States, two street brawlers, Blade and Striker, fight across rooftops, highways, sewers and a moving truck and train to rescue him. Punches, kicks and charged attacks take down waves of ninjas, with knives and nunchaku to pick up and bosses at the end of each stage. Its deadpan opening line and the celebratory burger at the end made it a cult favourite; home versions followed on many platforms.
trivia: "Are you a bad enough dude to rescue the President?" is one of gaming's most absurd and beloved opening questions.
The game was set during the presidency of Ronald Reagan — the manual explicitly names him as the kidnapped president.
Successfully rescuing the President results in eating hamburgers with him — one of the most anticlimactic endings in arcade history.
Bad Dudes was explicitly designed as an American-flavoured response to Japanese martial arts games — Data East's celebration of US culture.
devStory: Bad Dudes vs. DragonNinja was developed by Data East in 1988. Two street fighters rescue the US President from ninjas — a premise so absurd it became legendary. The opening text "Are you a bad enough dude to rescue the President?" became one of gaming's most memorable questions. The hamburger reward at the game's end was equally iconic.

title: Toobin'
description: Toobin' (1988) is Atari's river-tubing game: paddle an inner tube down rivers, dodging obstacles and throwing cans at enemies along the banks.
longDescription: Biff and Jet float down rivers in inner tubes, including the Colorado, the Nile and the Styx, steering through gates for points and around branches, rocks and whirlpools. Cans thrown at alligators, fishermen and other pests clear the way, and currents push the tubes around. Players control each arm separately to paddle and turn. Its relaxed summer premise stood out in arcades full of combat and racing.
trivia: Toobin' was one of the few arcade games with a genuinely relaxing premise — summer tubing rather than combat or racing.
The can-throwing weapons (Pepsi cans in the original, generic in some releases) could be used to hit floating enemies or boost speed.
Current and eddies in the river affected tube movement — physics simulation in a 1988 arcade game.
The two-player competitive format let friends race down the same river, throwing cans at each other as readily as at enemies.
devStory: Toobin' was developed by Atari Games in 1988. Players navigated rubber inner tubes down river courses, throwing cans at enemies and collecting items. The gentle, summery aesthetic was a counterpoint to the military and fantasy games dominating arcades. The controls used separate buttons to paddle each arm forward or backward, steering the tube. It was one of Atari Games' last genuinely successful arcade productions.

title: Strider
description: Strider (1989) is Capcom's arcade hack and slash, in which the ninja Hiryu climbs walls and ceilings and cuts through a dystopian 2048 with a plasma sword.
longDescription: Hiryu slashes with his plasma sword, cartwheels, slides under obstacles and climbs walls and ceilings with a hook. Robot companions called options help him through five stages. Junko Tamiya's music shifts with each stage and situation.
trivia: Capcom and the manga studio Moto Kikaku planned it alongside a Strider Hiryu manga and an NES game; the three were made separately.
The Genesis version won Electronic Gaming Monthly's 1990 Game of the Year.
devStory: Kouichi Yotsui directed it and co-designed it with Tokuro Fujiwara and Shinichi Yoshimoto, on Capcom's CP System board. It was a UK best-seller for three months in early 1989. Most home versions cut its graphics and music.

title: Golden Axe
description: Golden Axe (1989) is Sega's fantasy beat-'em-up: a barbarian, an Amazon and a dwarf ride beasts and cast magic to defeat Death Adder.
longDescription: Ax Battler, Tyris Flare and Gilius Thunderhead fight through Yuria to defeat Death Adder, who has taken the royal family captive and seized the Golden Axe. Each hero has their own magic, strengthened by potions kicked loose from thieving gnomes, and the heroes can ride enemy mounts that bite, swipe or breathe fire. Two players fight together. Designed by Makoto Uchida, whose previous game was Altered Beast, it became one of Sega's defining arcade series.
trivia: Three playable characters had different magic systems: Ax Battler summoned a dragon, Tyris Flare called a full-screen inferno, Gilius Thunderhead commanded lightning.
Magic power was obtained by hitting gnomes who carried potion bags — gnome-kicking became a notable and satisfying gameplay sub-activity.
The Mega Drive port was exceptionally faithful, demonstrating the console's growing muscle for arcade conversions.
devStory: Golden Axe was developed by Sega in 1989. The fantasy beat-em-up starred three warriors — Ax Battler (barbarian), Tyris Flare (Amazon), and Gilius Thunderhead (dwarf) — each with distinct magic attacks powered by collectable potions.

title: Final Fight
description: Capcom's 1989 arcade brawler set in Metro City, in which Mayor Mike Haggar, Cody and Guy fight the Mad Gear gang — the game that set the template for the scrolling beat 'em up.
longDescription:
Final Fight was released in arcades by Capcom in 1989. It is set in Metro City, a crime-ridden city later tied into the Street Fighter universe, where the Mad Gear gang has kidnapped the mayor's daughter. Mayor Mike Haggar, a former wrestler, sets out to rescue her with her boyfriend Cody and his friend Guy.

Up to two players fight through side-scrolling streets, subways and factories against waves of gang members, using punches, throws and weapons picked up along the way. Its large, detailed characters and satisfying combat made it the defining beat 'em up of its generation, and it began a series that had sold 3.2 million units by June 2023.
trivia: Final Fight was originally planned as Street Fighter '89 — it became a separate IP mid-development when the design moved away from one-on-one combat.
Haggar pile-driving enemies while wearing his suit became one of gaming's most iconic images — a politician who solved problems with his body.
The Super Nintendo port controversially removed the two-player co-op mode and a playable character — Guy was absent from the initial SNES release.
Poison, a female enemy in the original, became the subject of decades-long debate about her canonical gender — Capcom has given deliberately inconsistent answers.
Final Fight launched a series that continued through three numbered sequels and influenced every beat-em-up of the 1990s.
devStory: Final Fight was designed by Akira Nishitani and Akira Yasuda (Akiman) at Capcom in 1989. Originally conceived as Street Fighter '89 — a sequel to Street Fighter — the game evolved into its own IP during development. Mayor Mike Haggar, his daughter Jessica, and her boyfriend Cody fought through six stages of Metro City to rescue Jessica from the Mad Gear gang. Final Fight became the definitive beat-em-up of its era.

title: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles
description: Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles (1989) is Konami's four-player arcade beat 'em up based on the cartoon, in which the Turtles rescue April O'Neil and Splinter from Shredder.
longDescription: Each player takes one of the four Turtles and fights the Foot Clan, Shredder and Krang to free April and Splinter. Outside Japan it was sold mainly as a dedicated four-player cabinet; Japan got a two-player conversion kit.
trivia: It was the highest-grossing dedicated arcade game of 1990 in the US and Konami's highest-grossing arcade game.
The NES version, retitled Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles II: The Arcade Game, added two levels and new bosses and sold over a million copies.
devStory: Konami released it in North America in October 1989, drawing on the 1987 animated series. About 25,000 cabinets had sold by May 1990. In Europe it was called Teenage Mutant Hero Turtles.

title: SimCity
description: SimCity (1989) is Will Wright's city-building simulation, with no way to win, which grew out of the level editor he built for Raid on Bungeling Bay.
longDescription: Players zone land, build roads and power, and set taxes, while floods, tornadoes, fires, earthquakes and a monster threaten the city. There is no winning condition, though time-limited scenarios were added at Broderbund's suggestion.
trivia: Its working title was Micropolis, the name its source code took when it was released as open source in 2008.
The 1991 Super NES version added a Bowser disaster and an adviser called Dr. Wright.
devStory: Wright worked on it from 1985. Broderbund declined to publish it, so it came out through Jeff Braun's small company Maxis, with Broderbund later distributing it. It came out on the Amiga and Mac in February 1989, won Computer Gaming World's Game of the Year, and started the city-building genre.

title: Batman
description: Batman (1989) for the NES is Sunsoft's take on the Tim Burton film: a demanding action platformer built on wall-jumping, with a celebrated soundtrack.
longDescription: Sunsoft's Batman takes the film as a starting point and builds its own game: Batman fights through Gotham's streets, a chemical plant, sewers and the cathedral to face the Joker. Its signature move is the wall jump, kicking off one surface to reach the next, and ammunition powers the Batarang, Batdisk and spear gun. Tight, demanding controls and Naoki Kodaka's music made it one of the most respected licensed games of its era. It is a different game from Ocean's home-computer adaptation of the film.
trivia: Sunsoft's Batman is regularly cited as one of the best licensed games ever made — it succeeded as a game first, with the licence secondary.
The wall-jump mechanic — bouncing between walls to climb sheer surfaces — was more sophisticated than most contemporary platformers.
Sunsoft's soundtrack, composed by Naoki Kodaka, is considered among the finest on the NES.
The game bore minimal resemblance to the film — Sunsoft created an original Batman story rather than adapting the movie's plot.
devStory: Batman for the NES was developed by Sunsoft in 1989, timed to the Tim Burton film release. Unlike most licensed games of the era, Sunsoft's Batman was genuinely well-designed — tight controls, excellent wall-jumping mechanics, and a superb soundtrack. The game bore only superficial resemblance to the film but stood on its own merits as one of the best NES action games of 1989.

title: DuckTales
description: DuckTales (1989) is Capcom's NES platformer: Scrooge McDuck pogos on his cane through five treasure-hunting stages, including the Moon.
longDescription: Scrooge McDuck sets out to become the world's richest duck by finding five legendary treasures, visiting the Amazon, Transylvania, the African Mines, the Himalayas and the Moon in any order. His cane doubles as a pogo stick for bouncing on enemies and over spikes, and as a golf club for swinging at rocks. Stages hide secrets and alternate endings depend on the fortune collected. The Moon stage's music became one of the most loved pieces of NES music.
trivia: DuckTales' Moon theme, composed by Hiroshige Tonomura, became one of the most beloved pieces of video game music — it has been covered thousands of times.
The pogo stick mechanic — bouncing on enemies with a cane — was a completely original traversal and attack system.
The five worlds could be completed in any order — a non-linear structure that rewarded different strategies on different playthroughs.
Capcom was given unusual creative freedom by Disney, resulting in a better game than most licensed titles of the era.
A remastered version, DuckTales: Remastered, was released in 2013 and featured voice acting from the original cartoon cast.
devStory: DuckTales was developed by Capcom in 1989, designed by Tokuro Fujiwara. Despite being a Disney licensed game, Capcom was given significant creative freedom and created one of the NES's best platform games. The pogo stick mechanic — using Scrooge's cane to bounce on enemies and objects — was novel. The five non-linear levels and the Moon theme music made it iconic.

title: Klax
description: Klax (1989) is Atari's puzzle game: catch coloured tiles tumbling down a conveyor and stack them into matching rows, columns and diagonals.
longDescription: Tiles tumble down a conveyor toward a paddle at the bottom; the player catches them, holds up to five, and drops them into five bins to form rows, columns and diagonals of the same colour, called Klaxes. Drop too many tiles and the wave is lost. Each of the 100 waves sets a different goal, such as a number of diagonals or points. Designed by Mark Stephen Pierce with programming by Dave Akers, it is easy to learn and hard to master.
trivia: Klax's 100 waves each had distinct objectives — sometimes clear X tiles, sometimes make Y Klaxes, sometimes survive without spilling — creating sustained variety.
Tiles could be thrown back up the ramp, but only five at a time — managing the discard pile was a secondary resource challenge.
The game's advertising tagline "It is the nineties, and there is time for Klax" became one of gaming's more baffling marketing slogans.
Klax was designed to be immediately learnable but deeply masterable — a 30-second tutorial was possible, but mastery took hours.
devStory: Klax was designed by Mark Stephen Pierce and Dave Akers at Atari Games in 1989. Coloured tiles fell down a ramp and had to be caught in a paddle, then arranged into matching columns or diagonals to clear them. The game had a sequence of 100 waves with different objectives — specific numbers of Klaxes to complete, or tiles to prevent from spilling. Klax was one of the most thoughtfully structured puzzle games of its era.

title: Prince of Persia
description: Prince of Persia (1989) is Jordan Mechner's cinematic platformer: escape the Sultan's dungeons in one hour to save the princess, with rotoscoped animation.
longDescription: A young man thrown into the Sultan's dungeons by the vizier Jaffar has sixty minutes to escape and rescue the princess. Twelve levels of traps, crumbling floors, gates and sword-fights test timing, and the one-hour limit runs across the whole game. Jordan Mechner filmed his brother running and jumping and traced the footage to animate the hero with a realism no computer game had shown, giving every leap and fall real weight. It was ported to many platforms and became a long-lived series.
trivia: Mechner rotoscoped his brother David's movements by filming him and tracing each frame onto animation cells — creating animation unlike anything in 1989 games.
The one-hour time limit was global — players who spent too long on any puzzle sequence ran out of time for later ones, requiring holistic time management.
Mechner kept a detailed journal throughout development, published decades later — one of the few primary source documents of 1980s game creation.
The original Apple II version took four years to develop — an unusually long timeline that Mechner balanced against other projects.
Prince of Persia was ported to 25 platforms and inspired the modern platformer's emphasis on physics-based, weighty character movement.
devStory: Prince of Persia was designed by Jordan Mechner in 1989 over four years of development. Mechner used rotoscoping — tracing over video footage of his brother David running, jumping, and falling — to create the most realistic human animation seen in a home computer game. The one-hour time limit created tension across the entire game. Mechner documented the entire development process in journals later published as "The Making of Prince of Persia."

title: Space Quest
description: Space Quest (1986) is Sierra's comic science-fiction adventure, in which janitor Roger Wilco saves the day after the Sariens seize his ship.
longDescription: Roger Wilco, a janitor on the research ship Arcada, finds it captured by the Sariens, who steal the Star Generator. He escapes in a pod and eventually destroys the device aboard their ship, the Deltaur.
trivia: It sold over 100,000 copies early in its life.
A 1991 remake added VGA graphics and replaced typing with icons.
devStory: Mark Crowe and Scott Murphy designed it on Sierra's AGI engine, and it came out in October 1986. Computer Gaming World's Scorpia called it "a middle-of-the-road game".

title: Ultima IV
description: Ultima IV (1985) is Richard Garriott's role-playing game about virtue: become the Avatar by living by eight virtues, not by defeating a villain.
longDescription: Ultima IV: Quest of the Avatar has no great villain to slay. The player's aim is to become a model of eight virtues — Honesty, Compassion, Valor, Justice, Sacrifice, Honor, Spirituality and Humility — and the game tracks behaviour: lying to a merchant, fleeing a fight or killing fleeing foes all count against you. Only then can the Codex of Ultimate Wisdom be reached. Richard Garriott built it in response to the realisation that his earlier games rewarded killing and stealing, and it remains one of the most ambitious RPGs of its era.
trivia: Ultima IV has no final villain — the goal is to achieve virtue, making it one of the only major RPGs where the "enemy" is your own moral failing.
Garriott designed the eight virtues system as a direct response to critics who called earlier Ultima games ethically bankrupt.
The "Avatar" concept — a player character who achieves moral perfection — was entirely Garriott's invention and influenced RPG design for decades.
Every NPC in the game had a schedule, a home, and a personality — depth unprecedented in 1985 RPGs.
devStory: Ultima IV was designed by Richard Garriott at Origin Systems in 1985. After criticism that earlier Ultima games glorified killing and looting, Garriott made an entirely different kind of RPG — the goal was not to defeat a villain but to achieve moral perfection across eight virtues. There was no final boss. Garriott later called this game his first attempt to build ethics into game design, and it remains one of the most philosophically ambitious RPGs ever made.

sources.title: Ultima IV: Quest of the Avatar

title: Microsoft Flight Simulator
description: Microsoft Flight Simulator (1982) brought subLOGIC's flight simulation to the IBM PC: fly a light aircraft between real airports in real time.
longDescription: Microsoft Flight Simulator grew from Bruce Artwick's subLOGIC Flight Simulator, which began as a demonstration of 3D graphics on early microcomputers. The IBM PC version put players at the controls of a light aircraft over areas around real US cities, with working instruments, weather settings and the freedom to fly between airports. Because it pushed hardware hard, it became an informal test of PC compatibility and speed. The series has continued ever since, one of the longest-running in software.
trivia: Flight Simulator grew out of Bruce Artwick's work on real-time 3D graphics; subLOGIC's first version ran on the Apple II in 1979.
Microsoft's series ran from 1982 to 2006, then returned in 2020 — one of the longest-lived names in software.
The game was used as a benchmark for computer hardware performance for years — if a machine ran Flight Simulator smoothly, it was considered fast.
Early versions were used by actual student pilots for familiarisation training, a real-world application no other game could claim.
devStory: Microsoft Flight Simulator was originally developed by subLOGIC and programmer Bruce Artwick, who created it as a technical demonstration of 3D graphics rendering for early personal computers. Microsoft licensed the FS1 Flight Simulator in 1982. It became the longest-running software franchise in Microsoft's history and is still published today. Artwick was one of the first programmers to create real-time 3D rendering on consumer hardware.

title: Police Quest
description: Police Quest (1987) is Sierra's police adventure by former officer Jim Walls: patrol Lytton as Sonny Bonds, where following procedure is the puzzle.
longDescription: Police Quest: In Pursuit of the Death Angel casts the player as officer Sonny Bonds, working patrol and then narcotics to bring down a drug dealer in the town of Lytton, California. Designer Jim Walls, a former California Highway Patrol officer, built real procedure into the puzzles: checking the patrol car, reading suspects their rights and handling evidence correctly are essential, and carelessness can end the game. It was one of the first adventures to aim for realism rather than fantasy.
trivia: Jim Walls was a real police officer before designing Police Quest, and authentic police procedure was enforced — ignoring protocol ended the game.
Players who forgot to buckle their seatbelt before driving could be killed in an accident — realistic consequence taken to an extreme.
The game required players to holster and unholster their weapon correctly — gun safety procedure as puzzle mechanic.
Walls left Sierra during work on Police Quest 3; the fourth game, Open Season, was made with former Los Angeles police chief Daryl Gates.
devStory: Police Quest was designed by Jim Walls and Ken Williams at Sierra On-Line in 1987. Walls was a retired California Highway Patrol officer who brought authentic police procedure into game design — players had to follow actual law enforcement protocols or the game would end. Forgetting to buckle your seatbelt, failing to check your weapon, or violating procedure could all kill the player indirectly.

sources.title: Police Quest: In Pursuit of the Death Angel

title: Leisure Suit Larry
description: Leisure Suit Larry (1987) is Al Lowe's comedy adventure for Sierra: hapless Larry Laffer tries to find love in Lost Wages in one night.
longDescription: Leisure Suit Larry in the Land of the Lounge Lizards follows 40-year-old Larry Laffer, in his white polyester suit, as he tries to find romance in the city of Lost Wages before the night is over. Players type commands to explore bars, a casino and a hotel, with plenty of embarrassment along the way. Al Lowe reworked it from the text game Softporn Adventure, and a quiz of trivia questions at the start was meant to keep children out. It became one of Sierra's most notorious and successful series.
trivia: Larry Laffer was deliberately designed as pathetic and endearing rather than suave — a loser in a white leisure suit was funnier than a genuine lothario.
The age verification quiz asked questions like "In what year was the Korean War?" — questions many adults couldn't answer either.
Al Lowe was in his 40s when he designed the game, older than almost any other game designer working at the time.
The series ran to eight official games, with Larry's romantic failures in increasingly exotic locations.
devStory: Leisure Suit Larry in the Land of the Lounge Lizards was designed by Al Lowe at Sierra On-Line in 1987, based on an earlier text adventure called Softporn Adventure. Lowe updated the game with graphics and expanded the humour. An age verification quiz (questions about 1980s pop culture) was included to deter minors. The game became Sierra's most controversial and, for a period, best-selling title.

title: Head Over Heels
description: Head Over Heels (1987) is Jon Ritman and Bernie Drummond's isometric puzzle adventure: two mismatched heroes who can split up or combine.
longDescription: Head and Heels are spies sent to free the planets of the Blacktooth empire, captured separately and exploring hundreds of isometric rooms. Head jumps high, glides and can fire doughnuts; Heels runs fast and can carry objects in a bag. Many puzzles need one or the other, and once reunited the two can stack into a single, far more capable character. Built on the isometric approach of the pair's earlier Batman, it is regarded as one of the finest games on the ZX Spectrum.
trivia: Head Over Heels had two protagonists with different abilities — the game could be played with either character, but combining them unlocked the full experience.
The isometric 3D world was one of the largest ever created for the ZX Spectrum, with hundreds of interconnected rooms.
Head can glide and fire doughnuts from a hooter; Heels runs fast and can carry objects in a bag — two very different heroes in one game.
Jon Ritman and Bernie Drummond's previous game, Batman (1986), established the isometric engine they perfected in Head Over Heels.
devStory: Head Over Heels was designed by Jon Ritman and Bernie Drummond at Ocean Software in 1987. Two characters — Head (who could jump and shoot) and Heels (who could run fast and carry items) — solved puzzles independently or combined into a single character. The isometric 3D world was vast and full of interconnected rooms. It won numerous awards and is considered one of the finest ZX Spectrum games ever made.

title: Jackal
description: Jackal (1986) is Konami's overhead jeep game: drive into enemy territory, rescue prisoners and fire both a machine gun and grenades or rockets.
longDescription: Jackal puts one or two players in armed jeeps driving up through enemy territory. A forward-firing machine gun handles soldiers while a lobbed grenade — upgraded to rockets by rescuing prisoners — works in any direction and hits armour. Freed prisoners ride in the jeep until they are dropped off at a helicopter pad, and helicopters and fortified bases block the way. The arcade game was known as Top Gunner in some markets, and the NES version kept its co-operative mayhem.
trivia: Jackal's jeep had two functions: a forward cannon for the driver and a grenade launcher for the passenger — co-operation used both simultaneously.
Rescued prisoners upgraded the jeep's firepower by riding in the back — a risk-reward mechanic for filling the vehicle.
Helicopter bosses required targeting with both weapons simultaneously — some enemies were only vulnerable to the passenger's grenades.
The NES version was considered an exceptionally faithful port of the arcade original.
devStory: Jackal was developed by Konami in 1986, released in arcades as Top Gunner and later on NES as Jackal. Players drove a jeep through enemy territory rescuing prisoners of war, with a passenger who could fire in all directions while the driver aimed the mounted cannon forward. The two-player co-operative mode was intense and chaotic.

title: Castlevania II: Simon's Quest
description: Castlevania II: Simon's Quest (1987) turns Konami's series into an open-world action RPG: Simon gathers Dracula's remains to lift a curse.
longDescription: Cursed after defeating Dracula, Simon Belmont must find the Count's scattered body parts in five mansions and burn them in the ruins of the castle. Transylvania is open to explore, with towns where villagers sell items and offer clues, and a day–night cycle in which towns fill with monsters after dark. Experience and hearts level Simon up and buy better whips. Its cryptic, sometimes misleading hints — and puzzles solved by kneeling with the right item — are notorious, but its open structure foreshadowed later Castlevania games.
trivia: Simon's Quest introduced an open world to Castlevania — players explored freely rather than moving through predetermined levels.
The day-night cycle made certain NPCs disappear at night and caused stronger enemies to appear — one of the first dynamic time systems in a console RPG.
NPC hints were deliberately misleading or cryptic in the English translation — "What a horrible night to have a curse" became iconic for its unhelpfulness.
The game required players to kneel with a specific item in certain locations to progress — solutions that required either trial and error or outside guidance.
devStory: Castlevania II: Simon's Quest was designed by Hitoshi Akamatsu and Toshiyasu Yanagisawa at Konami in 1987. It transformed the linear castle format of the original into an open-world RPG — players explored multiple towns and regions, gathering clues from NPCs and assembling Dracula's body parts. The day-night cycle changed NPC behaviour and made certain enemies appear. The deliberately cryptic clues and obtuse puzzles frustrated many players.

title: Mega Man 3
description: Mega Man 3 (1989) is Capcom's NES sequel that adds the slide, the robot dog Rush and the mysterious Proto Man to eight new Robot Masters.
longDescription: Mega Man 3 brings eight new Robot Masters, from Needle Man to Shadow Man, plus a new slide move for ducking under attacks and squeezing through gaps. The robotic dog Rush replaces the previous game's items, transforming into a springboard, a jet and a submarine. After the first eight bosses, the Doc Robot stages revisit Mega Man 2's masters in copied form, and the whistling Proto Man appears as a rival whose loyalties are left unclear.
trivia: Rush the robotic dog introduced a transforming companion that could become a springboard, submarine, or jet — the mechanical pet concept proved enduringly popular.
The Doc Robot stages revisit four earlier levels, where Doc Robot copies the attacks of Mega Man 2's eight bosses.
Proto Man appeared as a mysterious recurring character — his identity and motivation were deliberately kept ambiguous throughout the game.
The game's development was rushed due to time pressure — Capcom later acknowledged that Mega Man 3 needed more polish before release.
devStory: Mega Man 3 was designed by Yoshinori Takamatsu at Capcom in 1989. The game introduced Rush, Mega Man's robotic dog companion who could transform into a springboard, a submarine, and a jet. Eight new Robot Masters were joined by the returns of all eight from Mega Man 2, accessible via Doc Robot stages. The game was the first in the series where Proto Man appeared as a recurring ambiguous ally.

title: Chip 'n Dale Rescue Rangers
description: Chip 'n Dale Rescue Rangers (1990) is Capcom's two-player Disney platformer, in which the chipmunks throw crates, apples and each other at enemies.
longDescription: Chip and Dale set out to foil Fat Cat, working across a city seen from a rodent's-eye view. They pick up crates, apples and other objects to throw at enemies, hide inside boxes for protection, and in two-player mode can pick up and throw each other. A map allows some choice of route. Made by the team behind Capcom's DuckTales, it is among the best of the company's Disney games on the NES.
trivia: Players could pick up and throw each other — a mechanic that was both a co-operative tool and a source of deliberate mischief between friends.
The game was based on the Disney Afternoon cartoon, carrying over the Rescue Rangers' personalities and villains.
Capcom's run of Disney NES games — DuckTales, Chip 'n Dale Rescue Rangers, TaleSpin and Darkwing Duck — is remembered as a high point for licensed games.
The bosses were Fat Cat's henchmen — the game faithfully adapted the cartoon's antagonists rather than creating original enemies.
devStory: Chip 'n Dale Rescue Rangers was developed by Capcom in 1990, designed by the same team that created the acclaimed DuckTales NES game. The two-player co-operative game allowed players to pick up and throw boxes, enemies, and each other — the ability to throw your partner at enemies was both practical and comedic. Capcom's Disney output in this period was consistently excellent despite the licensed game stigma.

title: Battletoads
description: Battletoads (1991) is Rare's NES action game starring three toads, mixing brawling, vehicle and climbing stages — and infamous for its difficulty.
longDescription: Battletoads sends Rash and Zitz after the Dark Queen to rescue their fellow toad Pimple and Princess Angelica. Each stage changes the rules: beat-'em-up brawling with exaggerated 'smash hits', the high-speed obstacles of the Turbo Tunnel, rappelling down a chasm, racing on snakes and unicycles. Two players can join in, and they can hurt each other. Rare built it partly to rival the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, and its punishing difficulty became legendary.
trivia: Battletoads was explicitly created to compete with Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles — Rare wanted their own anthropomorphic animal franchise.
The Turbo Tunnel level (Level 3) was so difficult that many players never saw Level 4, despite the game having 12 levels.
Two-player co-op had friendly fire enabled — punching your partner was entirely possible, and the hit stun was just as severe as from enemies.
The game's difficulty became legendary — asking if someone "beat Battletoads" became shorthand for asking about extreme gaming skill.
devStory: Battletoads was designed by Mark Betteridge and Michael Wiley at Rare in 1991. The three anthropomorphic toad warriors — Rash, Zitz, and Pimple — were explicitly created to compete with the Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles franchise. The game was notorious for extreme difficulty and friendly fire in two-player mode. The turbo tunnel level became one of gaming's most infamous challenges.

title: Xenon
description: Xenon (1988) is the Bitmap Brothers' vertical shooter for the Amiga and Atari ST, switching between a ground tank and an aircraft.
longDescription: Xenon's pilot can transform his craft at will between a ground tank, which can fire in several directions, and a faster aircraft, each suited to different enemies. Power-ups upgrade the weapons, and each level ends with a guardian. Its crisp visuals and polish made it the Bitmap Brothers' breakthrough; its sequel, Xenon 2: Megablast, became even better known for its Bomb the Bass soundtrack.
trivia: Bitmap Brothers games were known for their visual style as much as their gameplay — Xenon looked unlike any other game of 1988.
Its music was by David Whittaker; Bomb the Bass's 'Megablast' belonged to the sequel.
Xenon 2: Megablast used a version of Bomb the Bass's hit single 'Megablast (Hip Hop on Precinct 13)' — a rare licensed chart track in a 1989 game.
The Bitmap Brothers became one of Britain's most prestigious studios on the strength of Xenon's technical and aesthetic quality.
devStory: Xenon was developed by the Bitmap Brothers in 1988. The Bitmap Brothers were a British studio known for their visual and musical polish — Its sequel, Xenon 2, featured Bomb the Bass's 'Megablast', and both games had graphics that pushed the Amiga. Xenon established the Bitmap Brothers' reputation for style and technical excellence.

title: Speedball
description: Speedball (1988) is the Bitmap Brothers' violent future sport: two armoured teams fight to score in a steel arena, with coins to spend on upgrades.
longDescription: Speedball pits two teams of armoured players against each other in a closed metal arena, throwing a steel ball into the opposing goal by whatever means necessary — tackles, punches and all. Coins collected on the pitch buy upgrades and bribes between matches. Its invented sport and brutal tone drew in players who did not usually play sports games, and its sequel, Speedball 2: Brutal Deluxe, became one of the most admired Amiga games.
trivia: Speedball's rules were deliberately obscure — the sport felt plausibly real while being completely invented.
The sequel Speedball 2: Brutal Deluxe is regularly cited in "greatest Amiga games" lists alongside Sensible Soccer and Cannon Fodder.
The metal arena aesthetic was a departure from the Bitmap Brothers' usual polished style — more industrial, more brutal.
Speedball attracted an audience that rarely played sports games, bridging action gaming and sports through the science fiction setting.
devStory: Speedball was developed by the Bitmap Brothers in 1988. A violent futuristic sport played by armoured teams in a steel arena, Speedball featured heavy metal gameplay despite the studio's typically sleek aesthetic. The sequel Speedball 2: Brutal Deluxe (1990) is considered one of the finest sports games ever made for the Amiga.

title: Turrican
description: Manfred Trenz's run-and-gun for the Commodore 64, a technical showpiece of huge, explorable levels and heavy firepower that became one of Europe's best-loved home computer series.
longDescription:
Turrican was designed by Manfred Trenz, developed by Factor 5 and published by Rainbow Arts. Trenz created the concept and characters and programmed the Commodore 64 version himself; it was released in 1990 and converted to other systems afterwards.

The game combined run-and-gun shooting with large, open levels to explore, giving the player a powerful arm cannon, a rotating lightning beam and the ability to roll into an indestructible wheel. Its scale and speed on the C64 made it a showcase for the machine. Turrican II: The Final Fight followed in 1991 for the Commodore 64 and other platforms.
trivia: Turrican's world was enormous by 1989 standards — multiple large areas with hidden rooms and items rewarded thorough exploration.
Chris Hülsbeck's Amiga soundtrack used the platform's four-channel audio to create music that rivalled professional compositions.
The wheel transformation (rolling into a ball) and the line laser were direct Metroid references — Trenz cited it as a primary influence.
Factor 5, who ported and co-developed Turrican sequels, later became known for the Rogue Squadron Star Wars games on GameCube.
devStory: Turrican was designed by Manfred Trenz at Rainbow Arts in 1989 for the Commodore 64 and Amiga. The game combined the exploration of Metroid with the action of Contra, creating a huge, non-linear world of explosive platforming. Chris Hülsbeck's soundtrack — particularly for the Amiga version — is considered one of the finest in European gaming. Factor 5 ported the game and went on to develop the sequel.

title: Rick Dangerous
description: Rick Dangerous (1989) is Core Design's trap-filled platformer parodying Indiana Jones: learn every hidden hazard in the jungle, Egypt and a fortress.
longDescription: Rick Dangerous crash-lands in the South American jungle in 1945 and fights his way through a temple of the Goolu tribe, an Egyptian tomb, a castle fortress and a missile base. Nearly every screen hides a trap — spikes, falling blocks, darts — that kills instantly the first time, so progress comes from memorising them, helped by a pistol, dynamite and a stick for poking. Designed by Simon Phipps at Core Design, it was an early step towards the studio's later Tomb Raider.
trivia: Rick Dangerous required players to memorise trap locations through death — almost every hazard was invisible until triggered the first time.
The game was an explicit Indiana Jones parody, combining jungle temples, Egyptian tombs, and Nazi fortresses.
Core Design, Rick Dangerous's creators, went on to create Tomb Raider — Rick Dangerous was the studio's first adventure protagonist.
The humour of the death animations — Rick collapsing into a small pile — softened the relentless trial-and-error gameplay.
devStory: Rick Dangerous was designed by Simon Phipps at Core Design in 1989. An Indiana Jones parody, Rick Dangerous was known for its instant deaths from hidden traps — players had to memorise every lethal surprise through repeated death and retry. Core Design later made Tomb Raider, and Rick Dangerous was Lara Croft's spiritual predecessor in concept if not in tone.

title: Out of This World
description: Out of This World (1991), Another World in Europe, is Éric Chahi's cinematic action adventure: a scientist stranded on an alien planet fights to escape.
longDescription: A lab accident transports physicist Lester Chaykin to a hostile alien world. With no dialogue, no score and no on-screen gauges, the game tells its story entirely through animation and short cinematic scenes, as Lester escapes a prison with an alien companion and fights through caves and a city with a laser pistol that also makes shields. Éric Chahi created almost all of it himself, with vector-based graphics that gave it a striking film-like look.
trivia: Éric Chahi designed and programmed almost the entire game by himself over two years — one of the most ambitious solo development efforts in gaming history.
The game had no HUD, no score, and no health bar — it was designed to be experienced like a film rather than played like an arcade game.
The polygon-based graphics were hand-rotoscoped from filmed reference footage, giving characters movement that sprite animation couldn't achieve.
The alien world was never named or explained — players were dropped in without context, experiencing events through Lester's confusion.
Out of This World was selected by the Museum of Modern Art in New York as one of 14 games in its permanent collection.
devStory: Out of This World (Another World in Europe) was designed and programmed almost entirely by Éric Chahi at Delphine Software in 1991. Chahi used rotoscoped animation from filmed reference footage and developed a custom engine to render the game's striking polygon-based visuals. The game had no score, no health bar, and no HUD — it played like an interactive film. Chahi spent two years creating it alone, with music by Jean-François Freitas.

title: Gauntlet II
description: Gauntlet II (1986) is Atari's four-player dungeon sequel, adding 'It', acid puddles, reflective shots and shifting walls to the original.
longDescription: Gauntlet II keeps the original's Warrior, Valkyrie, Wizard and Elf, its monster generators and its constantly draining health, and adds new tricks: the 'It' monster, which makes the player it tags the target of every enemy, acid puddles, a dragon, walls that move or can be walked through, and power-ups such as reflective shots and invisibility. Any player can choose any hero, so four Wizards are possible. Designed by Ed Logg, it was as big a hit as the first game.
trivia: The "It" demon transferred a debilitating status effect to any player it touched — players avoided each other as frantically as they avoided enemies.
Gauntlet II introduced flying enemies that the original's pathfinding couldn't handle — they bypassed walls entirely.
The Supershot was a charged projectile that could clear entire rooms — holding the fire button for a few seconds was a skill in itself.
devStory: Gauntlet II was designed by Ed Logg at Atari Games in 1986. It expanded on the original with new enemy types including ghosts that could only be damaged briefly, IT enemies that transferred their status on touch, and the Supershot — a charge-up weapon. The game retained the four-player simultaneous format and the health-draining over time mechanic that made the original a revenue powerhouse.

title: Rygar
description: Rygar (1986) is Tecmo's side-scrolling action game in which a warrior fights with the diskarmor, a spiked shield on a chain.
longDescription: Rygar, a legendary warrior, battles through a mythic land with the diskarmor — a spinning, spiked shield flung out on a chain. The arcade game is a fast, straight-ahead side-scroller with power-ups that extend its reach and strength. The NES version that followed was a very different game, reworking the idea into a non-linear adventure with RPG-style growth and abilities that open new areas.
trivia: The arcade and NES versions of Rygar are essentially different games — the NES version added open-world exploration and RPG progression the arcade never had.
The diskarmor weapon — a spinning shield on a chain — was one of gaming's more exotic weapons, functioning as both attack and grapple.
Rygar on NES had no save system — the game had to be completed in a single session or abandoned.
The game's non-linear world and ability-gated areas make it a direct ancestor of the Metroidvania genre, despite predating the term.
devStory: Rygar was developed by Tecmo in 1986. The arcade version was a straightforward side-scrolling action game, while the NES version transformed it into an open-world adventure with RPG elements. The NES Rygar is considered one of the earliest "Metroidvania" style games — a largely non-linear world where new abilities unlocked previously inaccessible areas.

title: Ghosts 'n Goblins (NES)
description: The NES Ghosts 'n Goblins (1986) is Micronics' conversion of Capcom's arcade game, the first Famicom game on a 128 KB cartridge, which sold 1.64 million copies.
longDescription: As in the arcade original, the knight Arthur loses his armour to the first hit and his life to the second. Micronics programmed the conversion and Capcom published it, with music by the original composer, Ayako Mori.
trivia: It was the first Famicom game to use a 128 KB cartridge.
Famitsu gave it its Best Port award for 1986.
Computer Gaming World called it "an excellent example of what the [NES] can do".
devStory: It came out on the Famicom in Japan in June 1986 and on the NES in North America that November. A hidden credits screen confirms Ayako Mori as composer. It sold 1.64 million copies and later appeared on the Virtual Console and the NES Classic Edition.

title: Image Fight
description: Image Fight (1988) is Irem's demanding vertical shooter: a combat simulation where poor performance sends the pilot through penalty stages.
longDescription: Image Fight frames its vertical-scrolling missions as a training simulation. Players collect pods that attach to the ship and fire in different directions, and can switch the ship's speed. Five simulation stages test accuracy, and failing to destroy enough enemies sends the pilot to a punishing penalty stage before the real battle. From the studio behind R-Type, it is aimed at players who want a severe challenge.
trivia: Failing to achieve a minimum score in regular stages triggered mandatory penalty stages — a shame mechanic built into the game design.
Image Fight's difficulty was extreme even by Irem's standards — the studio that made R-Type made this game for players who wanted more punishment.
The game was set in a military near-future, with a training simulation framing that explained the penalty stage mechanic in-fiction.
Pod attachments mirrored R-Type's Force concept — Irem was developing a house style for shooter mechanics.
devStory: Image Fight was developed by Irem in 1988. The vertical-scrolling shooter was notable for its extreme difficulty and an unusual penalty system — playing poorly in the main stages forced players through "penalty stages" designed to be even harder. The game was designed for players who found other shooters too easy.

title: Twin Cobra
description: Twin Cobra (1987) is Toaplan's vertical helicopter shooter, the sequel to Tiger-Heli, with two-player co-op and dense enemy fire.
longDescription: Twin Cobra flies a gunship helicopter over land and sea, destroying tanks, ships and gun emplacements. Collectible colour-coded power-ups switch between weapon types and increase their strength, and bombs clear the screen in emergencies. Two players fly side by side. Its aggressive enemy fire and powerful weapons defined Toaplan's style, which went on to shape later shoot-'em-ups.
trivia: Twin Cobra's two-player mode had both helicopters sharing the screen in a genuinely co-operative format.
Toaplan's house style — developed through Twin Cobra and Truxton — influenced the "bullet hell" genre that Cave and RAIDEN perfected in the 1990s.
The helicopter setting was a refreshing alternative to the spacecraft-dominated shooter genre.
Toaplan closed in 1994, and its former staff went on to found studios including Cave, Takumi and Gazelle.
devStory: Twin Cobra was developed by Toaplan in 1987. The vertical-scrolling helicopter gunship game was one of Toaplan's most successful early titles. Toaplan became one of the most important shoot-em-up developers of the late 1980s, and Twin Cobra established their signature style: dense enemy formations, aggressive bullet patterns, and powerful weapons.

title: Truxton
description: Truxton (1988), Tatsujin in Japan, is Toaplan's vertical shooter with three switchable weapons and a devastating skull bomb.
longDescription: Truxton's ship switches among three weapon types — a spread shot, a powerful lightning beam and the Truxton beam — by collecting coloured power-ups, and its skull-shaped bomb wipes out almost everything on screen. Enemy formations are dense and relentless. The Japanese title Tatsujin means 'expert', a fair description of what it demands. Its Mega Drive conversion was one of the console's early showcase arcade ports.
trivia: Tatsujin means "master" or "expert" in Japanese — the name was a statement of the difficulty level Toaplan aimed for.
The Mega Drive port was one of the showcase titles demonstrating the console's superiority over the NES for arcade conversions.
Truxton's bomb was so powerful it was limited to three uses per life — the only mechanic preventing players from trivialising encounters.
Toaplan's colour palette and enemy design in Truxton pushed against the limitations of late-1980s arcade hardware.
devStory: Truxton (Tatsujin in Japan) was developed by Toaplan in 1988. The vertical-scrolling shooter featured a powerful screen-clearing bomb and intense enemy formations. The Mega Drive port was considered one of the finest early conversions for the console. Truxton represented Toaplan at the height of their creative power.

title: Mercs
description: Mercs (1989) is Capcom's three-player overhead run-and-gun, a follow-up to Commando, sending mercenaries to rescue a kidnapped president.
longDescription: Mercs sends a team of up to three mercenaries into a war zone to rescue a kidnapped former US president, fighting through jungles, rivers and bases in eight stages. Weapons can be upgraded, vehicles such as jeeps and boats can be commandeered, and a limited mega crash bomb clears the screen. It was released as Senjō no Ōkami II in Japan, the sequel to Commando, and was one of Capcom's last major overhead military shooters.
trivia: Mercs brought back Super Joe from Commando — one of gaming's earlier examples of sequel narrative continuity for a non-major character.
Three-player simultaneous play was supported in the arcade version, one of the earlier three-player overhead action games.
The shop system between missions let players purchase new weapons and equipment, adding RPG-lite progression.
Mercs was the last entry in Capcom's overhead military shooter lineage — the studio moved to Final Fight and Street Fighter II.
devStory: Mercs was developed by Capcom in 1989 as a sequel to Commando. Super Joe returned as the lead character, now heading a mercenary team. The overhead military shooter added a third player slot, varied missions, and a shop system for purchasing equipment between stages. It was one of Capcom's last major overhead run-and-gun games before the genre was largely replaced by beat-em-ups.

title: WrestleFest
description: WrestleFest (1991) is Technos Japan's WWF arcade wrestling game, with tag-team matches and a Royal Rumble for up to four players.
longDescription: Ten wrestlers, including Hulk Hogan, the Ultimate Warrior, Mr. Perfect and Earthquake, take part in two modes: Saturday Night's Main Event, a tag-team series ending in a title match against the Legion of Doom, and the Royal Rumble. Up to four can play, and extra credits buy energy.
trivia: Sinclair User named it Best Beat 'Em Up of 1991, jointly with Konami's Vendetta.
It was the highest-grossing arcade conversion kit of 1992 in the US.
devStory: Technōs Japan made it as the sequel to WWF Superstars, with more wrestlers and better graphics and sound. It came out in 1991 and ranked second on RePlay's arcade chart that October.

title: Galaxy Force II
description: Galaxy Force II (1988) is Sega's 3D space shooter, flying through planets and fortresses on Super Scaler hardware, some cabinets rotating the player.
longDescription: Galaxy Force II flies a starfighter into the screen across planet surfaces and into enemy fortresses, locking on to multiple targets and firing homing missiles while managing a draining energy supply. Sega's sprite-scaling hardware pushed large numbers of scaled objects to create a convincing sense of 3D speed. It was offered in a motion cabinet that could turn the seated player, one of the most elaborate machines of its time — and correspondingly rare in arcades.
trivia: The Galaxy Force II cabinet could rotate completely — full 360-degree motion in sync with the on-screen action.
The scaling hardware processed more sprites per frame than almost any other 1988 arcade game.
The game's cost and mechanical complexity made it rare in arcades — a paradox where the most impressive games were seen by the fewest players.
devStory: Galaxy Force II was developed by Sega in 1988. The third-person rail shooter used Sega's most advanced scaling hardware to render a vast three-dimensional tunnel at high speed. The motion-simulator cabinet version rotated 360 degrees. It was one of the most technically impressive arcade games of 1988, though its difficulty and the cabinet's mechanical complexity limited its commercial reach.

title: Thunder Blade
description: Thunder Blade (1987) is Sega's helicopter gunship shooter, alternating between overhead stages and behind-the-craft 3D flight.
longDescription: Thunder Blade pilots an attack helicopter against tanks, gunships and fortresses. Each stage begins viewed from above and then switches to a third-person view behind the helicopter as it weaves between skyscrapers and canyons. It used Sega's sprite-scaling hardware for its 3D sections, and a deluxe cabinet moved the seat with the flight stick. It was part of Sega's run of high-end arcade spectacles in the late 1980s.
trivia: Thunder Blade switched between overhead and third-person perspectives within the same game — a technical achievement in 1987.
The hydraulic joystick — rather than a full motion cabinet — was Sega's cost-reduced approach to simulated flight.
Both aircraft and ground enemies required different attack approaches, forcing players to switch mental models between phases.
Sega's Super Scaler hardware family — used across Space Harrier, Out Run, After Burner, and Thunder Blade — was the most capable sprite-scaling system of the era.
devStory: Thunder Blade was developed by Sega in 1987.
