description: Star Wars: Dark Forces (1995) is LucasArts' first-person shooter starring mercenary Kyle Katarn. Its Jedi engine added looking up and down, jumping and multi-floor levels.
longDescription: Kyle Katarn, a mercenary working for the Rebel Alliance, first recovers the Death Star plans and then uncovers the Empire's Dark Trooper Project, led by General Rom Mohc. The campaign ends with Katarn destroying Mohc's flagship, the Arc Hammer. The Jedi engine, built from scratch for the game, let the player look up and down, duck, jump and swim through levels with several floors.
trivia: Luke Skywalker was first planned as the hero; Kyle Katarn was created to give the team more freedom.
The Dark Troopers later appeared in The Mandalorian.
It shipped more than 300,000 copies before launch and debuted at number one on PC Data's chart.
devStory: Daron Stinnett directed the game, Ray Gresko led programming, Justin Chin wrote the story and worked on the art, and Clint Bajakian composed the music. Production began in September 1993, and it was released for MS-DOS on 8 March 1995. Jedi Knight: Dark Forces II followed in 1997.

title: Dungeon Keeper
description: Dungeon Keeper (1997) is Bullfrog's dungeon-management game, in which the player plays the villain, building a lair, recruiting monsters and fending off invading heroes. It was Peter Molyneux's last project at Bullfrog.
longDescription: The player builds and runs an underground dungeon, recruiting creatures and defending the lair against invading heroes, the last of whom is the Avatar. Imps dig the tunnels and mine the gold, and the player's Hand picks up, slaps and drops creatures, or possesses one. Up to four players can compete by modem or LAN.
trivia: Computer Gaming World called it "the most unique game in years".
The fan project KeeperFX, begun in 2010, fixes bugs and adds features.
devStory: Work began in November 1994 and took about two and a half years, with Peter Molyneux as designer and producer. Molyneux left Bullfrog in July 1997 to found Lionhead Studios, and the game was released at the end of June. It sold 700,000 copies worldwide by 2003, and Dungeon Keeper 2 followed in 1999.

title: Theme Hospital
description: Theme Hospital (1997) is Bullfrog's comic hospital-management game, in which the player treats patients with diseases such as Bloaty Head and King Complex. It sold more than 4 million copies.
longDescription: The player builds a hospital, hires doctors, nurses, handymen and receptionists, and researches new rooms and cures for a stream of patients suffering from invented diseases such as Bloaty Head, King Complex and Alien DNA. Critics praised the graphics and the humour, and a later patch added multiplayer for up to four players.
trivia: The original cover art was recalled because it used a green cross the developers had no right to use.
A Sega Saturn version, Sim Hospital, was cancelled.
Producer Mark Webley and artist Gary Carr later founded Two Point Studios, whose Two Point Hospital came out in 2018.
devStory: Mark Webley produced and designed the game, with art by Gary Carr and music by Russell Shaw and Adrian Moore. EA released it for MS-DOS and Windows on 28 March 1997, and Krisalis converted it to the PlayStation in 1998. CorsixTH is an open-source remake.

title: Duke Nukem 3D
description: Duke Nukem 3D (1996) is 3D Realms' first-person shooter set in an alien-invaded Los Angeles, known for its interactive levels, unusual weapons and Duke's one-liners. Its Build engine was written by Ken Silverman.
longDescription: Aliens have invaded an early 21st-century Earth, mostly Los Angeles, and turned the LAPD into "Pig Cops". The play resembles Doom, but much of the environment can be destroyed or used, and the non-linear levels hide air ducts and back routes. The arsenal includes a shrink ray and a freezethrower, and Duke can fly with a jet pack. Jon St. John voiced Duke's one-liners and pop-culture references.
trivia: Next Generation wrote that "Duke Nukem 3D has everything Doom doesn't."
Its sexual content and portrayal of women drew criticism, and it was restricted in Germany and banned in Brazil in 1999.
The source code was released under the GPL on 1 April 2003.
devStory: 3D Realms built the game on Ken Silverman's Build engine, with Greg Malone producing, Allen H. Blum III and Richard Gray designing, and Lee Jackson and Robert Prince composing. The shareware episode came out on 29 January 1996 and the full game on 19 April. It sold about 3.5 million copies.

title: Suikoden
description: Suikoden (1995) is Konami's PlayStation RPG, loosely based on the novel Water Margin, in which a general's son gathers the 108 Stars of Destiny to rebel against the Scarlet Moon Empire.
longDescription: The hero, son of a general of the Scarlet Moon Empire, joins a revolt against the corrupt state and sets out to gather the 108 Stars of Destiny. Up to 107 characters can be recruited, and more than 90 of them can fight. An abandoned castle becomes the Liberation Army's headquarters, and the player names it. Ordinary battles are turn-based with six-character parties, while one-on-one duels and large army battles use rock-paper-scissors systems.
trivia: Warren Spector cited it as an influence on Deus Ex.
GameFan named it RPG of the Year in its 1996 Megawards.
devStory: Yoshitaka Murayama directed the game and wrote the scenario, with Junko Kawano as designer and artist. Konami Computer Entertainment Tokyo developed it over roughly two years, and it was released in Japan on 15 December 1995 and North America a year later. Suikoden II followed in 1998.

title: Chrono Cross
description: Chrono Cross (1999) is Square's PlayStation RPG set in the world of Chrono Trigger, in which Serge moves between two parallel worlds — one where he drowned ten years before.
longDescription: Serge, a teenager in the El Nido archipelago, slips into a parallel dimension in which he drowned ten years earlier. With the thief Kid at his side and the shadowy Lynx against him, he looks for the cause of the split between the two worlds, a story centred on the Frozen Flame. There are no random encounters, and the player can flee from any fight. Battles use a stamina bar and an Element system of six opposing colours, 45 characters can be recruited, and New Game+ opens up twelve endings.
trivia: It is an indirect sequel to Chrono Trigger and draws on Radical Dreamers, a text adventure for the Satellaview.
Yasunori Mitsuda's "Scars of Time" topped Hardcore Gaming 101's 2009 poll of the best video game music.
It was never released in Europe.
devStory: Masato Kato directed and wrote the game, with Hiromichi Tanaka producing and Yasunori Mitsuda composing. It was released in Japan on 18 November 1999 and North America in August 2000, and it had sold about 1.5 million copies by 2003. The Radical Dreamers Edition remaster followed in 2022.

title: Tactics Ogre: Let Us Cling Together
description: Tactics Ogre (1995) is Yasumi Matsuno's Super Famicom tactical RPG, a dark political fantasy of ethnic conflict and civil war in the kingdom of Valeria, with branching paths and up to eight endings.
longDescription: Denim Powell is drawn into the ethnic conflicts of a civil war in the kingdom of Valeria, in what Matsuno called a "complex dark fantasy political tale". Battles are turn-based on a grid seen from a diagonal overhead view. The story splits into Law, Neutral and Chaos branches, and up to eight endings can be reached.
trivia: Denim's endings as king depend on a hidden algorithm, a version of Ogre Battle's Chaos Frame, which fans found by data mining in 2014.
Matsuno left Quest after finishing it and went on to make Final Fantasy Tactics (1997).
devStory: Yasumi Matsuno directed, wrote and designed the game, with character designs by Akihiko Yoshida and music by Hitoshi Sakimoto and Masaharu Iwata. A team of 15 to 16 people worked on it for two and a half years, and Quest released it in Japan on 6 October 1995. It sold more than 500,000 copies on the Super Famicom, and the PlayStation version reached North America in 1998.

sources.title: Tactics Ogre: Let Us Cling Together

title: Darkstalkers: The Night Warriors
description: Darkstalkers (1994) is Capcom's CPS II fighting game with a cast of classic monsters, which added air blocking and chain combos to the Street Fighter II system.
longDescription: Ten playable monsters, among them Demitri Maximoff, Morrigan Aensland, Felicia, Anakaris and Sasquatch, fight their way to the bosses Huitzil and Pyron. The game is built on the Street Fighter II system but adds air blocking, crouch walking and chain combos. Its Special meter drains over time unless the player spends it on a super move, and EX and ES moves are powered-up versions of special moves.
trivia: In Japan it is Vampire: The Night Warriors.
VideoGames named it the Best Arcade Game of 1994.
A 32X version was planned but never released.
devStory: Yoshiki Okamoto produced it, with Junichi Ohno designing and Akira Yasuda drawing. Capcom released it in Japanese arcades on 12 July 1994, and it sold about 24,000 arcade units. Psygnosis converted it to the PlayStation in 1996, and Night Warriors: Darkstalkers' Revenge followed in 1995.

title: Herzog Zwei
description: Herzog Zwei (1989) is Technosoft's Mega Drive strategy game, in which the player pilots a transforming mech that buys and airlifts units into battle. The makers of Dune II and Warcraft cite it as an influence.
longDescription: Each player pilots a transforming mech that buys ground units, airlifts them onto the battlefield and gives them orders such as patrolling or capturing a base. Nine permanent outposts are the only places that produce units. The game can be played against the computer or by two players.
trivia: Sega-16 called it "very probably the finest video game you've never played".
Game Informer gave it 9.75 out of 10 in 1999, its highest score for a Genesis game.
It is also considered a precursor of the MOBA genre.
devStory: Technosoft made it as the sequel to Herzog for the MSX and PC-8801, and Sega released it in Japan on 15 December 1989 and North America in March 1990. It sold poorly, partly because of weak marketing and its release early in the console's life.

title: Desert Strike: Return to the Gulf
description: Desert Strike (1992) is Mike Posehn's isometric helicopter shooter for the Mega Drive, in which a lone Apache flies four missions against an invading general. It was EA's best-selling game at the time.
longDescription: General Kilbaba invades a Persian Gulf emirate, and a single modified AH-64 Apache is sent to stop him across four missions. The isometric, scrolling levels ask the player to destroy weapons and installations, rescue hostages and capture personnel, while managing armour, fuel and ammunition. Its weapons trade quantity for power.
trivia: It began as Beirut Breakout, set in the Lebanese Civil War.
Critics called its Gulf War subject matter in poor taste.
Its sequels were Jungle Strike, Urban Strike, Soviet Strike and Nuclear Strike.
devStory: Mike Posehn led design and programming, with John Manley helping write it and Brian Schmidt and Rob Hubbard composing. Posehn built a momentum-based camera, and the vehicle sprites began as 3D models. EA released it in March 1992 and later converted it to the SNES, Amiga, Atari Lynx, MS-DOS and other systems.

sources.title: Desert Strike: Return to the Gulf

title: Rayman
description: Rayman (1995) is Michel Ancel's platform game, in which a limbless hero throws his fist to free the Electoons from Mr Dark. It became the best-selling PlayStation game of all time in the UK.
longDescription: Mr Dark steals the Great Protoon and defeats its guardian, Betilla the Fairy, and captures the Electoons. Rayman, whose hands float free of his body, crosses six worlds to free them, punching enemies with a "telescopic fist". Every level hides six Electoon cages, each world ends with a boss, and 100 Tings earn an extra life. Critics praised its animation, atmosphere and music, but often noted how hard it was, and GameSpot faulted its scarce save points.
trivia: Development moved from the Atari ST to a Super NES CD-ROM version, then to the Atari Jaguar; the cancelled Super NES version was rediscovered in 2016.
It was a PlayStation launch title in North America and Europe.
devStory: Michel Ancel created the character as a teenager and led the design. Ubi Soft released the game for the PlayStation in North America on 7 September 1995, followed by Jaguar, Saturn and MS-DOS versions. It had sold 900,000 copies by 1997 and reportedly more than 3 million in all.

title: Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee
description: Oddworld: Abe's Oddysee (1997) is a cinematic platformer in which Abe, a slave at a meat-packing plant, escapes and frees his fellow Mudokons using speech and possession instead of guns.
longDescription: Abe, a Mudokon slave at RuptureFarms, discovers that his species is about to become the factory's next meat product. He escapes and gains the power of the Shrykull to free his people, and rescuing at least 50 of the 99 Mudokons earns the good ending. Abe carries no firearms: he tiptoes, runs and crouches, throws meat, rocks and grenades, possesses Sligs to take control of them, and directs other Mudokons with GameSpeak commands. The game saves only at checkpoints.
trivia: In Japan it was retitled Abe a GoGo, and the Mudokons' hands were changed from four fingers to three.
A Sega Saturn version was announced but never released.
Just Add Water remade it in 2014 as Oddworld: New 'n' Tasty!
devStory: Lorne Lanning directed the game at Oddworld Inhabitants, which he co-founded with Sherry McKenna, who shaped the story and GameSpeak. GT Interactive released it for the PlayStation on 18 September 1997. It had sold 3.5 million copies by 2012.

title: Tenchu: Stealth Assassins
description: Tenchu: Stealth Assassins (1998) is Acquire's ninja game set in Sengoku-era Japan, which helped define the stealth genre alongside Metal Gear Solid and Thief.
longDescription: The ninja Rikimaru and the kunoichi Ayame serve Lord Gohda, and the player picks one of them for eleven open-ended missions. The aim is to stay unseen, slipping past guards or killing them quietly, with the Ki meter showing how alert nearby enemies are and how close they stand. The grappling hook is the only item kept between missions, and each mission is ranked from "Thug" to "Grand Master".
trivia: The Western release added two levels and alternate mission layouts, and was later released in Japan as Tenchu: Shinobi Gaisen.
It was Acquire's first project.
devStory: Takuma Endo directed it and wrote the scenario. Sony Music Entertainment Japan released it on 26 February 1998, and Activision published it in North America in September. It sold more than 1.4 million copies worldwide by 2003, and Tenchu 2 followed in 2000.

title: Syphon Filter
description: Syphon Filter (1999) is Eidetic's third-person stealth-action shooter, in which agents Gabe Logan and Lian Xing hunt a terrorist and his bioweapon.
longDescription: Agents Gabriel Logan and Lian Xing pursue the terrorist Erich Rhoemer and his group, Black Baton, who hold a bioweapon called Syphon Filter, and discover that their own agency director, Thomas Markinson, is Rhoemer's partner. The game mixes third-person shooting with stealth missions and some puzzles. Its display includes a radar, armour status and a "danger meter", and IGN counted at least thirty weapons and pieces of equipment.
trivia: It scored 90 on Metacritic and sold more than 900,000 copies.
It was followed by Syphon Filter 2 (2000), Syphon Filter 3 (2001) and three more games on the PS2 and PSP.
devStory: Richard Ham designed it at Eidetic, with John Garvin on art and writing and Chuck Doud composing. 989 Studios released it in North America on 16 February 1999.

title: Dino Crisis
description: Dino Crisis (1999) is Shinji Mikami's "panic horror" game, in which agent Regina fights dinosaurs on Ibis Island in real-time 3D environments rather than Resident Evil's pre-rendered backgrounds.
longDescription: Agent Regina and her team investigate Ibis Island, where Dr. Edward Kirk's secret project has pulled dinosaurs into the present through a rift in spacetime. Unlike Resident Evil, the game draws its environments in real-time 3D. Capcom marketed it as "panic horror", with faster, more intelligent dinosaurs as enemies. Locked doors open with D.D.K. codes, colour-coded emergency boxes hold supplies, Hemostats and Med Paks treat wounds, and "DANGER" moments call for quick button presses.
trivia: Critics often called it "Resident Evil with dinosaurs".
It sold more than 300,000 copies in its first week in Japan.
devStory: Shinji Mikami directed and produced it at Capcom Production Studio 4. It was released in Japan on 1 July 1999 and North America in September, and the PlayStation version sold about 2.4 million copies. Dino Crisis 2 followed in 2000.

title: Jumping Flash!
description: Jumping Flash! (1995) is a first-person PlayStation platformer starring Robbit, a mechanical rabbit that can jump three times in mid-air. Guinness World Records lists it as the first platform game in true 3D.
longDescription: The astrophysicist Baron Aloha hides the twelve jet pods that power the worlds of Crater Planet, and Robbit, a mechanical rabbit sent by Universal City Hall, must recover them. Robbit can jump up to three times in mid-air, and on the second and third jumps the camera tilts down so the player can judge the landing. Each world has three levels and a boss, for 18 main levels, and each level has a ten-minute limit.
trivia: It was developed as a technology demonstration for the PlayStation.
Some critics found it short and easy, but Next Generation ranked it 86th in its 1996 top 100 games.
devStory: Koji Tada directed the game at Exact and Ultra, and Sony released it in Japan on 28 April 1995. Jumping Flash! 2 followed in 1996 and Robbit Mon Dieu in 1999.

title: Klonoa: Door to Phantomile
description: Klonoa: Door to Phantomile (1997) is Namco's 2.5D platformer, in which Klonoa grabs enemies with a magic ring and throws them or uses them to jump higher, through the dream world of Phantomile.
longDescription: Ghadius sets out to turn the dream world of Phantomile into a world of nightmares and kidnaps the singer Lephise. Klonoa can run, jump and hover briefly, and with a ring inhabited by his companion Huepow he grabs enemies, then throws them or uses them as a springboard for a higher jump. The levels scroll from side to side through 3D scenery. The ending reveals that Huepow is a prince of the moon kingdom Cress, and Lephise's Song of Rebirth sends Klonoa home.
trivia: Klonoa won Best Character at the 1997 Japan Game Awards.
GameSpot called it "one of the best side-scrollers in years".
devStory: Hideo Yoshizawa directed the game, with Tsuyoshi Kobayashi as lead designer and Yoshihiko Arai designing the characters. Namco released it in Japan on 11 December 1997. Klonoa 2 followed on the PS2 in 2001, and Paon remade the original for the Wii in 2008.

title: Harvest Moon
description: Harvest Moon (1996) is Yasuhiro Wada's Super Famicom farming game, in which the player restores a run-down inherited farm. It is considered one of the first farm life sims.
longDescription: The player inherits a run-down farm from their grandfather and sets about restoring it. Each day brings chores: clearing land, planting and watering crops, selling the harvest, and caring for livestock, including milking cows. Between the work the player can attend festivals, befriend the villagers and forage. Electronic Gaming Monthly called it "an epic adventure in agriculture" that is "as fun as it is original".
trivia: The localised versions changed references to alcohol to "juice".
Later games in the series are released under the name Story of Seasons, because of a rights split over localisation.
devStory: Yasuhiro Wada directed and produced the game, developed by Amccus and published by Pack-In-Video in Japan on 9 August 1996. Natsume brought it to North America in 1997, and Nintendo released it in Europe in 1998.

title: Tales of Phantasia
description: Tales of Phantasia (1995) is the first game in the Tales series, a Super Famicom RPG with real-time battles and a sung opening theme on a 48-megabit cartridge.
longDescription: Cress Albane sets out for revenge after his hometown is destroyed, and the trail leads to the antagonist Dhaos. Cress travels through time to recruit allies from the past. Battles use the real-time Linear Motion Battle System on a 2D plane, with the player controlling Cress directly while the other party members follow passive or active settings.
trivia: It needed a 48-megabit cartridge to hold its voice clips and vocal opening theme.
The story grew from Yoshiharu Gotanda's unpublished novel Tale Phantasia.
Trouble during development led many staff to leave Wolf Team and form tri-Ace.
devStory: Eiji Kikuchi directed it at Wolf Team, with Yoshiharu Gotanda writing and programming, Kōsuke Fujishima designing the characters and Motoi Sakuraba and Shinji Tamura among the composers. Namco released it in Japan on 15 December 1995. The 1998 PlayStation version sold around 769,000 copies in Japan, and a Game Boy Advance version reached the West in 2006.

title: Revelations: Persona
description: Revelations: Persona (1996) is Atlus's first Persona game, in which high-school students in the town of Mikage-cho gain the power to summon Personas after playing a fortune-telling game.
longDescription: In 1996 a group of high-school students in Mikage-cho play a fortune-telling game and are drawn into supernatural events. Philemon grants them the power of Persona to fight demons and the SEBEC conspiracy. Battles take place on a grid, the party can talk to demons to provoke emotional reactions, and Igor fuses new Personas from spell cards in the Velvet Room. A second route, the Snow Queen quest, follows a separate story about a cursed mask.
trivia: The North American version changed names, hairstyles and ethnicities and cut the Snow Queen route; the 2009 PSP version restored it.
The Velvet Room was inspired by the Black Lodge in Twin Peaks.
devStory: Kouji Okada directed and produced the game, with Kazuma Kaneko designing the characters, Tadashi Satomi writing and Shoji Meguro composing. Atlus released it in Japan on 20 September 1996 and North America that December, and it sold 391,556 copies in Japan in its first year. Persona 2: Innocent Sin followed in 1999.

title: Puzzle Bobble
description: Puzzle Bobble (1994), known internationally as Bust-a-Move, is Taito's Bubble Bobble spin-off, in which the player fires coloured bubbles to make groups of three before the ceiling comes down.
longDescription: The player aims a launcher at the bottom of the screen and fires bubbles at the cluster above. Groups of three or more of the same colour burst, along with any bubbles hanging from them. The ceiling drops at intervals, and the arcade version has 30 levels. It uses the characters and themes of Bubble Bobble.
trivia: Its working title was Bubble Buster.
The Neo Geo version was Japan's second-highest-grossing arcade software of 1995, behind Virtua Fighter 2.
It inspired many clones, including Snood, Frozen Bubble and Bubble Shooter.
devStory: Kazuhiro Kinoshita and Seiichi Nakakuki designed it, and Taito released it in Japanese arcades in June 1994, with a Neo Geo MVS version that December. Conversions followed for the Super NES, Neo Geo CD and 3DO in 1995.

title: The Lost Vikings
description: The Lost Vikings (1993) is the puzzle-platformer from Silicon & Synapse, later Blizzard, in which the player switches between three Vikings with different abilities to escape an alien zoo.
longDescription: Tomator, emperor of the alien Croutonians, kidnaps three Vikings for an intergalactic zoo. They escape but are scattered across time. The player switches between them: Erik the Swift runs, jumps and smashes some walls with his helmet, Baleog the Fierce fights with sword and bow, and Olaf the Stout blocks with his shield, glides on it and serves as a platform. Each Viking has three hit points, and losing one makes the level impossible to finish. The game has 37 levels, or 42 on the Mega Drive.
trivia: It started out inspired by Lemmings, and the planned hundreds of tiny Vikings shrank to five and then three.
The Vikings later became playable heroes in Heroes of the Storm.
devStory: Silicon & Synapse developed the game and Interplay released it for the Super NES in April 1993, followed by Amiga and MS-DOS versions the same year. The Lost Vikings 2 followed in 1997.

title: Rock n' Roll Racing
description: Rock n' Roll Racing (1993) is Silicon & Synapse's isometric combat racer, set to licensed rock and heavy metal songs and called by announcer "Loudmouth Larry".
longDescription: Four racers drive four laps of isometric tracks scattered with mines, power-ups, oil, snow and lava, and up to two people can play. Destroying rival cars earns bonuses, and between races the money goes on upgrades, each of which can be raised up to seven times. The soundtrack uses licensed rock and heavy metal songs, and Larry "Supermouth" Huffman provides the commentary.
trivia: ZZ Top were the first choice for the music, but their fee was too high.
It began as RPMII, a sequel to RPM Racing.
Electronic Gaming Monthly named it the Best Driving Game of 1993.
devStory: Silicon & Synapse, later renamed Blizzard Entertainment, developed the game with extra work from Software Creations. Interplay released it for the Super NES on 4 June 1993, followed by a Mega Drive version in 1994.

title: Bosconian
description: Bosconian (1981) is Namco's multidirectional space shooter, in which the Starfighter fires forwards and backwards at once to destroy enemy bases, guided by radar and voice alerts.
longDescription: The Starfighter flies in eight directions with the screen centred on it, firing forwards and backwards at the same time. The goal is to destroy the green Bosco bases, each with six cannons around a core, while avoiding asteroids, mines and enemy ships. A radar display and spoken alerts help the player find the bases.
trivia: It inspired Sinistar (1983) and Time Pilot (1982).
It won the 1983 Arcade Award for Best Science Fiction/Fantasy Coin-Op Game.
devStory: Seiichi Sato and Shigeru Yokoyama designed it, Kazuo Kurosu programmed it and Nobuyuki Ohnogi composed the music. Sato had been asked to create swappable ROM boards, which became Galaga, Dig Dug and Bosconian. Namco released it in Japan on 20 November 1981, and it was the seventh highest-grossing arcade game in Japan that year.

title: Marathon
description: Marathon (1994) is Bungie's Macintosh first-person shooter set aboard a colony ship under alien attack, guided by three shipboard AIs. It was one of the earliest shooters with mouse-driven free look.
longDescription: In 2794 the colony ship UESC Marathon, bound for Tau Ceti, is attacked by aliens, and the player, a security officer, fights back under the guidance of the ship's AIs Leela, Durandal and Tycho, until Durandal goes "rampant" and turns against the crew. The player can aim up and down with the mouse, recharge stations stand in for power-up pickups, and pattern buffers serve as save points. Up to eight players can fight over a local network.
trivia: MacUser named it the best action game of 1995, ahead of Doom II.
Time included it in its 2012 list of the 100 best video games.
Bungie released the source code of Marathon 2 in 1999, which became the Aleph One engine.
devStory: Jason Jones programmed the game and designed it with Greg Kirkpatrick, Reginald Dujour and Alex Seropian. Bungie published it for the Macintosh on 21 December 1994, and it had sold more than 150,000 copies by October 1995. Marathon 2: Durandal followed in 1995 and Marathon Infinity in 1996.

title: Magic Carpet
description: Magic Carpet (1994) is Bullfrog's 3D action game, in which a wizard on a flying carpet collects mana and builds a castle to restore balance to each world.
longDescription: The player is a wizard on a flying carpet, gathering mana, building a castle and returning each world to "equilibrium". The carpet moves through three dimensions like a helicopter and climbs automatically over obstacles rather than crashing. Two spells can be ready at once, one in each hand, and stored mana lets the castle grow and stronger spells be cast. The box promised 50 worlds, but the game has 45, because five level numbers were skipped.
trivia: It supported anaglyph 3D, autostereogram effects and the VFX1 headset.
The Hidden Worlds expansion added 25 winter-themed levels in 1995.
devStory: Bullfrog developed it with Sean Cooper among the programmers and Russell Shaw composing. EA released it for MS-DOS in 1994, followed by Magic Carpet 2: The Netherworlds in 1995 and PlayStation and Saturn versions in 1996. Computer Gaming World gave it five stars out of five.

title: Heretic
description: Heretic (1994) is Raven Software's dark-fantasy shooter on a modified Doom engine, one of the first first-person games with an inventory and the ability to look up and down.
longDescription: The elf Corvus hunts D'Sparil, one of the three Serpent Riders who corrupted the seven kings of Parthoris, through the City of the Damned and Hell's Maw to D'Sparil's dome. Raven added an inventory of items, looking up and down and flying to the Doom engine. Health potions can be carried for later, the Tome of Power gives every weapon a stronger mode, and the Morph Ovum turns enemies into chickens.
trivia: John Carmack reportedly told the team to "do it like Doom, and add the fantasy flavor".
Computer Gaming World ranked being turned into a chicken third among the best ways to die in computer games.
Raven released the source code in 1999.
devStory: John Romero proposed a medieval game in the style of Doom, and Raven built it on a modified version of id's engine. The shareware version came out on 29 December 1994, and the retail Shadow of the Serpent Riders added two episodes in 1996. It sold more than 500,000 copies, and Hexen: Beyond Heretic followed.

title: I.Q.: Intelligent Qube
description: I.Q.: Intelligent Qube (1997) is a PlayStation puzzle game, known as Kurushi in Europe, in which the player clears rows of giant rolling cubes and is graded with an IQ score.
longDescription: The player runs about on a platform as rows of cubes roll towards them, marking a square and triggering it as a cube rolls over to capture it. Grey cubes should be captured, green advantage cubes clear a 3×3 area around them when triggered, and black forbidden cubes must be allowed to fall off the edge. Capturing a forbidden cube costs a row of the platform. At the end the score is turned into an IQ rating between 0 and 999.
trivia: Its designer, Masahiko Sato, was a professor at the Tokyo University of the Arts.
It won an Excellence Award for Interactive Art at the 1997 Japan Media Arts Festival.
devStory: Kenji Sawaguchi directed the game at G-Artists, with Masahiko Sato as designer and Takayuki Hattori composing. Sony released it in Japan on 31 January 1997, and it sold nearly 750,000 copies there by the end of the year. I.Q. Final followed on the PlayStation.

title: Ogre Battle: The March of the Black Queen
description: Ogre Battle (1993) is Yasumi Matsuno's real-time tactical RPG, in which a Liberation Army sends squads across a map to free towns from the Zeteginean Empire. Its 13 endings depend on the army's reputation.
longDescription: The player leads the Liberation Army against Empress Endora's Zeteginean Empire, which is influenced by the dark magic of the sage Rashidi. Squads of up to five fighters are sent across the map to liberate towns and temples, and the battles play out automatically according to the chosen tactics, with tarot cards played during combat. Each character has an alignment, and the revolution's reputation decides which of the 13 endings the player reaches. There are 25 main stages and four hidden ones.
trivia: The title comes from two songs by Queen, a band Matsuno liked.
The Japanese print run was doubled from 200,000 to 400,000 copies and still sold out soon after release.
devStory: Yasumi Matsuno directed and designed the game at Quest, pitching it as a real-time tactical rival to Dragon Quest and Final Fantasy. Masaharu Iwata, Hitoshi Sakimoto and Hayato Matsuo composed the music. It was released in Japan on 12 March 1993, and Enix America brought it to North America in May 1995 in a print run of about 25,000.

sources.title: Ogre Battle: The March of the Black Queen

title: Grandia
description: Grandia (1997) is Game Arts' Saturn RPG, in which young adventurer Justin searches for the lost civilisation of Angelou, with a battle system built around a turn-order bar.
longDescription: Justin, a young adventurer, sets out with his friends Sue and Feena to find the lost civilisation of Angelou, and runs up against General Baal and the Garlyle Forces, who are reviving the corrupting entity Gaia. The game puts 2D sprites on 3D maps with a camera the player can rotate. In battle a rotating IP bar sets the order of turns: attacking from behind earns a pre-emptive strike, and hitting an enemy while it prepares an attack cancels it. Weapon and magic skills improve with use, and the story ends with an epilogue set ten years later.
trivia: The game contains 20,000 frames of animation.
It was first planned for the Mega-CD before moving to the Saturn.
devStory: Takeshi Miyaji designed the game and Noriyuki Iwadare composed the music. It was released for the Saturn in Japan on 18 December 1997, selling 344,554 copies there. Sony brought the PlayStation version to North America in 1999, and Grandia II followed.

title: Bushido Blade
description: Bushido Blade (1997) is Lightweight's sword-fighting game with no health bar or time limit, in which most hits are fatal.
longDescription: Fights are one-on-one with swords and other weapons, with no health bar and no time limit, and most hits are fatal. The Body Damage System means a lesser wound can slow, disarm or cripple an opponent instead. There are eight weapons, six characters and three stances: high, neutral and low. In story mode dishonourable tactics can end the playthrough early, and Slash mode pits the player against 100 enemies in a row.
trivia: Its director wanted to capture the tension of a fight that could end with a single blow.
Some critics found the one-hit kills polarising.
devStory: Lightweight developed it, Square published it in Japan on 14 March 1997, and Sony released it in North America in October. It sold 387,937 copies in Japan in 1997, and Bushido Blade 2 followed a year later.

title: Space Channel 5
description: Space Channel 5 (1999) is Tetsuya Mizuguchi's Dreamcast rhythm game, in which reporter Ulala out-dances an alien invasion in a 1960s-styled future, with a cameo from Michael Jackson.
longDescription: The reporter Ulala covers an invasion by the alien Morolians in a science-fiction future styled after the 1960s. The player copies the moves of her opponents in time to the music, using six inputs. The invasion turns out to have been staged by Chief Blank to boost ratings. Michael Jackson appears as "Space Michael".
trivia: The main theme is "Mexican Flyer", written by Ken Woodman in 1966.
Deee-Lite's singer Kierin Kirby sued Sega in 2003 over Ulala's resemblance to her; she lost and was ordered to pay Sega's legal fees.
devStory: Tetsuya Mizuguchi produced it at Sega AM9, later United Game Artists, with Takashi Yuda directing and Naofumi Hataya and Kenichi Tokoi composing. Sega released it in Japan on 16 December 1999. Critics praised the music and art direction but found it short, and Space Channel 5: Part 2 followed in 2002.

title: ChuChu Rocket!
description: ChuChu Rocket! (1999) is Sonic Team's four-player puzzle game, in which players lay arrows to steer mice into their rockets and away from cats — the first Dreamcast game with online multiplayer.
longDescription: Players place arrows on the floor to steer ChuChus, mice, into their own rocket while keeping KapuKapus, cats, away from it. Modes include single-player puzzles, a puzzle editor, a 30-second challenge and competitive games for up to four players. Critics praised the multiplayer and the cute style, though network lag drew complaints.
trivia: Yuji Naka wanted to test the Dreamcast by moving about 100 sprites at once.
In Europe it was mailed free to Dreamarena subscribers.
Lessons from its online play helped Sonic Team build Phantasy Star Online.
devStory: Yuji Naka directed and produced the game at Sonic Team, and Sega released it in Japan on 11 November 1999 and North America in March 2000. A Game Boy Advance version in 2001 included 2,500 of the 17,000 puzzles players had made.

title: Seaman
description: Seaman (1999) is Yoot Saito's Dreamcast virtual pet, a creature with a human face that the player talks to through a microphone. Leonard Nimoy narrates the English version.
longDescription: The player raises a Seaman through five life stages — Mushroomer, Gillman, Podfish, Tadman and Frogman — talking to it through the Dreamcast microphone. It must be checked on at least once every real-time day or it may die. Leonard Nimoy narrates the English version, while in Japan Saito voiced the creature himself.
trivia: Saito modelled the Seaman's face on his own.
Testers' long sentences confused the creature, so Saito gave it the reply "You talk too long, I don't understand."
It was the third best-selling Dreamcast game in Japan.
devStory: Yoot Saito designed the game at Vivarium, and it was released in Japan on 29 July 1999, with Sega publishing it in North America in 2000. It sold 399,342 copies in Japan and won an Excellence Award at the 1999 Japan Media Arts Festival.

title: Vib-Ribbon
description: Vib-Ribbon (1999) is Masaya Matsuura's minimalist rhythm game, drawn in white vector lines, which builds its levels from any music CD the player puts in.
longDescription: Vibri, a rabbit, walks along a line of obstacles timed to the beat: blocks, loops, waves and pits, each matched to a button. Missing them degrades her into a frog and then an insect, and the game ends if she is hit too often in insect form. Because the whole game loads into the console's memory, players can swap in their own audio CDs, and the game generates levels from the tracks, harder for more intense music. The soundtrack is by the J-pop band Laugh and Peace.
trivia: It began as an advertisement for the Mercedes-Benz A-Class, until the car failed the moose test and Mercedes dropped the idea.
The Museum of Modern Art acquired it in 2012.
It never came out in North America on the PlayStation; it arrived there via PlayStation Network in 2014.
devStory: Masaya Matsuura led the game at NanaOn-Sha, and Sony released it in Japan on 9 December 1999, where it sold 100,000 copies in its first week. Two Japan-only follow-ups, Mojib-Ribbon and Vib-Ripple, came out on the PlayStation 2.

title: Shin Megami Tensei
description: Shin Megami Tensei (1992) is Atlus's Super Famicom RPG of a demon-overrun Tokyo, in which the player recruits demons by talking to them and fuses them into new ones, and the player's choices push them towards Law or Chaos.
longDescription: In a near-future Tokyo of "199X" a portal to the demon world opens and the United States orders a nuclear strike on the city; the story continues in the ruined Tokyo thirty years later. Exploration is in first person and battles are turn-based. Demons can be recruited through conversation and fused, two or three at a time, at the Cathedrals of Shadows. The player's choices move them along two axes, Light–Dark and Law–Chaos, which change how demons and factions respond.
trivia: It was not localised at the time, partly because of its religious content; the first official English release came on iOS in 2014.
Toby Fox cited it as an inspiration for Undertale, especially its dialogue system.
devStory: Atlus released it for the Super Famicom in Japan on 30 October 1992, directed by Yōsuke Niino with art by Kazuma Kaneko and music by Tsukasa Masuko. It was the third Megami Tensei game, a series that began with adaptations of Aya Nishitani's Digital Devil Story novels, and the first under the Shin name. Shin Megami Tensei II followed in 1994.

title: Star Ocean
description: Star Ocean (1996) is tri-Ace's Super Famicom RPG with real-time battles and voice clips packed onto the cartridge with the S-DD1 compression chip. It stayed in Japan until a 2008 remake.
longDescription: Roddick, Millie and Dorne look for a cure for a disease that turns people to stone, and learn it comes from Asmodeus, a demon king who died 300 years earlier. With Ronyx and Ilia of the Earth Federation starship Calnus, they travel back in time to find him. Battles run in real time, with the player controlling one character and the AI the others. "Private Actions" build relationships between characters that shape the endings, eight of ten possible recruits can join, and item creation can make gear better than anything in the shops.
trivia: Its voice clips during battle were rare on the Super Famicom.
Enix America had stopped publishing by the end of 1995, so the game never officially left Japan; fans made an English patch.
devStory: Joe Asanuma directed the game at tri-Ace, with Motoi Sakuraba composing, and Enix released it in Japan on 19 July 1996. The cartridge used the S-DD1 compression chip to hold about 48 megabits of data. It sold about 235,000 copies, and the PSP remake First Departure brought it to the West in 2008.

title: Phoenix
description: Phoenix (1980) is an arcade shooter of birds, hatching eggs and a mothership, and one of the first shooters to end with a boss battle.
longDescription: The player's ship slides left and right, dodging missiles and charging enemies, and can raise a force field that blocks attacks for a few seconds before it recharges. The first two stages bring formations of small phoenixes, the next two bring eggs that hatch into large ones, and the fifth is a fortress: the player has to shoot through its hull and a rotating shield band to hit the pilot inside. Then the cycle starts again, harder.
trivia: Its original developer is unknown because the credits were overwritten; Retro Gamer suggested Tehkan.
The arcade version plays "Romance de Amor" at the start and "Für Elise" when a level is cleared.
Atari sued Imagic over Demon Attack, which it considered too close to Phoenix, and settled in 1983.
devStory: Taito released Phoenix in Japan in December 1980 and Centuri in the US in January 1981, and it was Centuri's best-selling title by 1982. General Computer Corporation's Atari 2600 version, which had to cut over a third of the code to fit 8 KB, came out in 1983 and reportedly sold more than 600,000 copies.

title: Jumpman
description: Jumpman (1983) is Randy Glover's platform game for Epyx, in which Jumpman climbs ladders and ropes to defuse bombs planted around a base on Jupiter.
longDescription: Bombs have been planted across three buildings of a base on Jupiter, and Jumpman has to defuse them all, jumping and climbing ladders and ropes while avoiding falls and "smart" darts.
trivia: Compute! wrote that it "easily conquers that skepticism and establishes itself as a software classic".
Jumpman Junior, a 12-level cartridge version, was made for players without a disk drive.
devStory: Randy Glover designed the game, and Epyx, then still called Automated Simulations, released it on 26 February 1983 for the Atari 8-bit, followed by Commodore 64, Apple II and IBM PC versions. It sold about 40,000 copies on the Atari and C64 through 1987.

title: Spelunker
description: Spelunker (1983) is Tim Martin's cave-exploring platform game, whose famously fragile hero gave Japanese baseball a word for injury-prone players.
longDescription: The explorer sets off from the cave entrance to reach the treasure at the bottom, collecting dynamite, flares and keys on the way. His air supply runs down and must be refilled at points in the cave, bats drop deadly guano, and a ghost can carry him off to the shadow world unless he blasts it with air, which leaves him unable to move for a few seconds. Each cave has six levels, and the game repeats the layout across six caves of rising difficulty.
trivia: In Japan, "Speranker" is used for baseball players who are often injured, after the game's fragile hero.
The arcade version was the fourth most successful table arcade unit in Game Machine's February 1986 chart.
devStory: Tim Martin of MicroGraphicImage developed it for the Atari 8-bit computers in 1983, and Broderbund re-released the Commodore 64 version in 1984. Arcade and Famicom versions followed in Japan in 1985, and the NES version reached North America in 1987.

title: Renegade
description: Renegade (1986) is Yoshihisa Kishimoto's street-fighting game, called the first fully developed beat 'em up, which led directly to Double Dragon.
longDescription: A belt-scrolling brawler played with an eight-way joystick and three buttons, in which the player fights through street gangs. In the Western version he takes on four gangs to rescue his kidnapped girlfriend. For the West the game was restyled after the 1979 film The Warriors, and the Japanese delinquents and yakuza became generic street gangs.
trivia: In Japan it is Nekketsu Kōha Kunio-kun.
Kishimoto drew partly on his own high-school fights and on Bruce Lee's Enter the Dragon.
Ocean's home computer version topped the UK all-formats chart in September 1987.
devStory: Yoshihisa Kishimoto designed the game at Technos Japan, and it reached Japanese arcades in May 1986, with Taito publishing it in the West. The Famicom version, released in April 1987, sold around 400,000 copies, and the game became the basis for Double Dragon (1987).

title: Stunts
description: Stunts (1990), also known as 4D Sports Driving, is a 3D racing game of loops, jumps and corkscrews, with a track editor and replays that kept a fan community racing for decades.
longDescription: Players race a lap of a stunt track — loops, jumps, slalom roads and corkscrews — either against the clock or against one of six opponents, choosing from 11 cars with automatic or manual gears. A track editor lets players build new courses or change existing ones, and races can be saved and replayed from four camera views.
trivia: In Europe it was sold as 4D Sports Driving because Broderbund held the Stunts name.
Programmer Chris Taylor played the opponent Skid Vicious.
PC Gamer US ranked it the 22nd best computer game ever in 1994.
devStory: Distinctive Software made the game, drawing on the arcade game Hard Drivin', and Broderbund released it for MS-DOS in October 1990. Fans kept sharing replays for years, and a yearly World Stunts Meeting was held in the mid-2000s.

title: Powermonger
description: Powermonger (1990) is Bullfrog's real-time strategy game on a 3D landscape, in which a captain conquers towns, feeds an army and sends orders that travel slowly to distant commanders.
longDescription: The player wins by conquering most or all of the towns on a map and killing rival captains. Food is the most important resource, and orders to subordinate captains arrive after a delay that grows with their distance from the player's own captain. The map's terrain is three-dimensional, with people and objects drawn as sprites, and cutting down too many trees can change the weather.
trivia: It won Computer Gaming World's Strategy Game of the Year for 1991.
Advertisements quoted Peter Molyneux calling it "Better than Populous".
devStory: Peter Molyneux, Glenn Corpes and Kevin Donkin designed the game on an engine derived from Populous, and EA released it for the Amiga and Atari ST in October 1990. A World War I Edition expansion followed in 1991.

title: Front Mission
description: Front Mission (1995) is the first game in Square's mech tactics series, set on Huffman Island in 2090, where wanzers take damage part by part.
longDescription: On Huffman Island in 2090 the OCU and the USN fight over the territory in the Huffman Conflicts. The player commands mechs called wanzers, each built from four parts: a body, two arms and legs. Losing the body takes a wanzer out of the fight, while damage to arms or legs only weakens it. Weapons are divided into melee, short-range, long-range and support fire.
trivia: It was the first game Square had another developer make for it.
The original proposal was called "100 Mission".
It stayed in Japan until a Nintendo DS version reached North America in 2007.
devStory: Toshiro Tsuchida directed and wrote the game, Yoshitaka Amano provided artwork, and Yoko Shimomura and Noriko Matsueda composed the music. G-Craft developed it and Square released it in Japan on 24 February 1995. It sold more than 500,000 copies there.

title: Beyond Oasis
description: Beyond Oasis (1994), The Story of Thor in Japan and Europe, is Ancient's Mega Drive action-adventure, in which Prince Ali uses a gold armlet to summon four elemental spirits.
longDescription: Prince Ali finds a buried gold armlet that once summoned four spirits — Dytto of water, Efreet of fire, Shade of shadow and Bow of plants — and must stop the bearer of the evil silver armlet, who is using it to cause destruction again. Much like The Legend of Zelda, the game has Ali collect health and mana items, weapons such as swords, crossbows and bombs, many of which break after limited use, and the spirits themselves, found in shrines.
trivia: GameFan named it Action RPG of the Year in 1995.
A sequel, The Legend of Oasis, followed on the Saturn in 1996.
devStory: Yuzo Koshiro produced and scored the game at Ancient, with art by Ayano Koshiro. Sega released it in Japan on 9 December 1994 and in North America and Europe in March 1995.

title: Dynamite Headdy
description: Dynamite Headdy (1994) is Treasure's Mega Drive platform game starring a puppet who fights by throwing his own head, which can be swapped for 17 different powered-up heads.
longDescription: Headdy, a puppet, tries to stop the evil puppet king Dark Demon from turning the world's puppets into his minions. He attacks by throwing his detachable head, which can also grab hooks to pull him up to higher platforms. Seventeen power-up heads change his attacks and abilities, and falling into a pit does not kill him outright: he bounces back out and loses some health.
trivia: Sega of America asked for a harder North American version, about twice as difficult, and much of the dialogue was removed.
A Master System version, based on the Game Gear port, was released only in Brazil.
devStory: Development began in August 1993, after Gunstar Heroes, with Koichi Kimura leading. Sega released it in Japan on 5 August 1994 and North America that September. Critics praised its creativity, visuals and technical achievement.

title: Soul Edge
description: Soul Edge (1995), released abroad as Soul Blade, is Namco's weapon-based 3D fighting game and the first in the Soulcalibur series.
longDescription: In 1583 nine warriors hunt for Soul Edge, a cursed sword that feeds on the soul of whoever wields it. Every fighter carries a weapon, and a Weapon Gauge drains with each blocked blow; empty it, and the fighter is left to fight unarmed. Guard Impact lets players knock attacks back, and a ring out is possible only when an opponent is knocked out of the arena. The PlayStation version added the story mode Edge Master and five unlockable characters.
trivia: It was the first game made with motion capture using passive optical markers.
The PlayStation version's opening won a SIGGRAPH '97 award for best game video of 1996.
devStory: Project Soul developed the game on Namco's System 11 board, the hardware behind Tekken, and it reached Japanese arcades on 13 September 1995. The PlayStation version followed in December 1996 and was a UK bestseller. Soulcalibur followed in 1998.

title: Toki
description: Toki (1989) is TAD Corporation's arcade platform shooter, in which a tribesman turned into an ape spits energy balls to rescue Princess Miho from the witch doctor Vookimedlo.
longDescription: The witch doctor Vookimedlo turns the tribesman Toki into an ape and kidnaps Princess Miho. Toki crosses the island spitting energy balls at its creatures, against a timer on every stage and a boss at the end of each. Power-ups strengthen his spit, rabbit feet give bursts of agility, clocks add time, and a helmet protects him from attacks from above.
trivia: In Japan it is JuJu Densetsu.
Ocean's home computer versions won Best Coin-Op Conversion at the 1991 Golden Joystick Awards.
Microids released a remake in 2018.
devStory: TAD Corporation released the game in Japanese arcades on 8 December 1989, with Fabtek publishing it in North America in 1990. Ocean converted it to the Amiga, Atari ST and Commodore 64 in 1991, and Sega made a reworked Genesis version, Toki: Going Ape Spit.

title: Snow Bros.
description: Snow Bros. (1990) is Toaplan's arcade platform game, in which the snowman twins Nick and Tom bury enemies in snow and roll them into giant snowballs.
longDescription: Nick and Tom, snowman twins in blue and red overalls, fight through 50 stages to rescue the princesses Puripuri and Puchipuchi, with a boss on every tenth stage. They throw snow to bury enemies, then roll or kick the snowballs to take out others. Coloured potions boost speed, snow power, throwing distance or let the player fly, and a pumpkin head appears if players take too long.
trivia: It has been described as reminiscent of Bubble Bobble and Tumblepop.
The Mega Drive version added 20 levels.
devStory: Toaplan released it in Japanese arcades in April 1990, with Romstar distributing it in North America. Versions followed for the Game Boy, NES and Mega Drive, and Snow Bros. 2 (1994) was Toaplan's last arcade project.

title: Mega Man Legends
description: Mega Man Legends (1997) is Capcom's 3D action-adventure reinvention of Mega Man, in which Mega Man Volnutt explores ruins on a flooded Earth.
longDescription: On a flooded Earth, Diggers explore ancient ruins for refractors that produce energy. Mega Man Volnutt crash-lands on Kattelox Island, where the Bonne family of pirates are after a legendary treasure. Unlike the platforming of the original series, the game is set in 3D worlds, with ledge climbing and lock-on targeting. Refractor shards are sold for Zenny, the Buster's power depends on the parts equipped, and Roll can build new parts and special weapons.
trivia: It was shown at E3 1997 as Mega Man Neo.
Keiji Inafune said it did not sell well, arriving years before sandbox games became popular.
On the Nintendo 64 it was retitled Mega Man 64.
devStory: Producer Keiji Inafune wanted a Mega Man unlike the earlier games, mixing action, role-playing and adventure. Capcom released it in Japan on 18 December 1997 and North America in September 1998. A planned Mega Man Legends 3 was cancelled.

title: Alundra
description: Alundra (1997) is Matrix Software's puzzle-heavy action-adventure, a spiritual sequel to Landstalker, in which a dream-walking elf enters the nightmares killing a village's people.
longDescription: The elf Alundra, a silent hero who can enter people's dreams, is shipwrecked near the village of Inoa, whose people are being killed by nightmares. The source is the demon Melzas, disguised as a god. The game is played from above, with heavy puzzle-solving, real-time combat and platforming, and each dream level has a twist drawn from the dreamer's personality.
trivia: Its world contains more than 7,000 screens.
It was runner-up to Final Fantasy VII for RPG of the Year at Electronic Gaming Monthly and GamePro.
Working Designs sold over 100,000 copies in North America within a month.
devStory: Yasuhiro Ohori directed the game at Matrix Software, with music by Kōhei Tanaka. It began as an action RPG before the PlayStation launched and took three years to finish. Sony released it in Japan on 11 April 1997, and Working Designs brought it to North America in January 1998.

title: Lady Bug
description: Lady Bug (1981) is Universal's maze game in the style of Pac-Man, with twenty turnstile gates that the player swings to reshape the maze and shut out pursuing insects.
longDescription: Like Pac-Man, Lady Bug has the player clear a maze — of flowers, hearts and letters — while avoiding enemies, here insects. The twist is the twenty green turnstile gates, which swing as the player passes through them and change the layout of the maze. A timer runs around the maze border, releasing up to four insects, and from level 9 every level brings four different kinds of enemy.
trivia: Its ColecoVision version, a launch title for the console in 1982, was far more successful than the arcade original.
The ColecoVision version won its category at the 5th Arkie Awards.
devStory: Kazutoshi Ueda designed the game, and Universal released it in Japan in October 1981 and worldwide in December. Coleco's version added a "Vegetable Harvest" bonus level for completing the word SPECIAL, and an Intellivision version followed in 1983.

title: Pooyan
description: Pooyan (1982) is Konami's arcade shooter, designed by Tokuro Fujiwara, in which a mother pig in a lift shoots down the balloons of the wolves that kidnapped her piglets.
longDescription: Mama, a pig whose babies have been kidnapped by wolves, rides a lift up and down. One button fires arrows and throws meat. In the first round she shoots the balloons the wolves float down on; in the second the wolves try to push a boulder over the cliff edge. Mama loses a life if a rock hits her, a wolf eats her on the ladders or the boulder crushes her.
trivia: Metal Gear Solid: Peace Walker includes "Pooyan Missions".
A world record of 1,609,250 points was set on 16 December 1983.
devStory: Tokuro Fujiwara designed the game, and Konami released it in Japan in October 1982, with Stern Electronics distributing it in North America. Datasoft converted it to the Atari 8-bit and Commodore 64 in 1983, and versions for the Atari 2600, MSX and Famicom followed.

title: Circus Charlie
description: Circus Charlie (1984) is Konami's arcade game in which Charlie the clown performs six circus acts, from jumping a lion through flaming hoops to swinging between trapezes.
longDescription: Charlie the clown works through six circus acts. He rides a lion through flaming rings, walks a tightrope while jumping monkeys, bounces between trampolines past knife throwers and fire breathers, hops from ball to ball, rides a horse over trampolines and walls, and swings from trapeze to trapeze. After the sixth act the show starts again at a faster pace.
trivia: Its music is based on "American Patrol" and "The Blue Danube".
The Famicom and MSX versions drop the trampoline act.
Konami's Mikie hides a reference that makes Circus Charlie appear.
devStory: Konami released it in arcades in 1984, with Centuri distributing it in North America in March and the Japanese release following in April. An MSX version came out the same year, and a Famicom version in 1986.

title: Major Havoc
description: Major Havoc (1984) is Owen Rubin's vector arcade game for Atari, which runs a space shooter, a platform maze and a lunar-landing sequence back to back.
longDescription: Each round plays three segments in a row: a fixed shooter, a platform section and a lunar-lander sequence. A game of Breakout powers the warp system and can earn extra lives. Dedicated cabinets used a roller controller, while conversion kits for older vector games used the controls they came with, such as Tempest's spinner.
trivia: Some games name the enemy Vaxxian homeworld "Maynard", after the Massachusetts town where Digital Equipment Corporation, maker of the VAX, was based.
It inspired the MSX game Theseus and served as the basis for Silpheed.
devStory: Owen Rubin designed and programmed the game, with Mark Cerny designing and tuning some levels after joining about a year in. Atari released it in January 1984, followed by a conversion kit for machines such as Tempest in March. It was not a major commercial success in the West.

title: Cadash
description: Cadash (1990) is Taito's arcade action-RPG platformer, in which up to four players — fighter, mage, priestess and ninja — on linked cabinets level up while rescuing a kidnapped princess.
longDescription: The Balrog kidnaps Princess Salassa and carries her to Castle Cadash, where he plans a ritual to make himself invincible, and King Dilsarl promises his kingdom to whoever saves her. The game combines side-scrolling platforming with role-playing statistics, experience levels, gold and magic. Players choose a fighter, mage, priestess or ninja, and four players can join in by linking arcade cabinets. The five stages end in Castle Cadash itself.
trivia: Game Machine named it the most successful table arcade unit in its 1 May 1990 issue.
The Genesis version keeps only the fighter and the mage.
devStory: Hiroshi Tsujino directed and designed the game, and Taito released it in Japan in March 1990. Working Designs translated the TurboGrafx-16 version, which removed the arcade time limit, and a Genesis version followed in 1992.

title: The Ninja Warriors
description: The Ninja Warriors (1988) is Taito's side-scrolling beat 'em up played across three screens side by side, in which two androids fight to overthrow a dictator.
longDescription: In a dystopian 1993, President Banglar has declared martial law, and anarchist scientists led by Mulk build two androids, the red Kunoichi and the blue Ninja, to end his rule. The game scrolls across six levels on a cabinet of three joined screens, giving the effect of a single very wide picture. One button slashes with a kunai at close range, the other throws a limited supply of shuriken.
trivia: It was the eighth highest-grossing dedicated arcade game in Japan in 1988.
Natsume's 1994 Super NES game followed it, and new games in the series reached the Switch in 2019.
devStory: Taito released the game in arcades in early 1988, with Romstar distributing it in North America. It was converted to the Amiga, Atari ST, ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64 and Amstrad CPC, with Japan-only versions for the PC Engine and Mega-CD.

title: G-Police
description: G-Police (1997) is Psygnosis's combat flight game set in the domed cities of Jupiter's moon Callisto, where a pilot joins the police to investigate his sister's death.
longDescription: In 2097, on the colonised moon Callisto, Slater joins the G-Police to investigate the apparent suicide of his sister Elaine, which he believes was murder. The story grows from gang warfare into a conflict between the corporations Krakov and Nanosoft. The player flies a VTOL gunship — "a helicopter without the rotors" — through 35 missions, mostly inside urban domes, often scanning vehicles to tell criminals from civilians.
trivia: Peter Chung, creator of Æon Flux, animated its television advertisement.
The clothing company Diesel designed the police uniforms and appears in the game as an evil corporation.
GamePro called its short draw distance "one of the worst cases of draw-in since 32-bit gaming began".
devStory: A Psygnosis studio in Stroud developed the game, and it was released for the PlayStation in October 1997 and Windows in November. G-Police: Weapons of Justice followed in 1999.

title: Colony Wars
description: Colony Wars (1997) is Psygnosis's PlayStation space combat game, in which a pilot of the rebel League of Free Worlds fights the Earth Navy through a branching campaign with several endings.
longDescription: The rebel League of Free Worlds, led by the Father, fights the Earth Navy of the Tzar's empire for control of the Sol system's network of warpholes. The player flies one of seven League starfighters through missions grouped into acts of three, and the campaign branches according to how well each mission goes, leading to multiple endings.
trivia: The developers originally planned to let players choose between the League and the Earth Empire.
The mission tree was designed to hide mission failure.
Edge dismissed it as "little more than a 3D interpretation of Asteroids", while IGN gave it 9.3.
devStory: Mike Ellis designed the game and co-wrote it with Damon Fairclough, with music by Tim Wright. Psygnosis released it in November 1997, and it sold more than 150,000 copies in the US. Colony Wars: Vengeance followed in 1998 and Red Sun in 2000.

title: Um Jammer Lammy
description: Um Jammer Lammy (1999) is NanaOn-Sha's follow-up to PaRappa the Rapper, in which a shy guitarist plays her way through a day of mishaps to reach her band's first concert.
longDescription: Lammy, a shy left-handed guitarist who leads the band MilkCan, must reach her band's first concert on time despite a run of mishaps. She feels confident only with a guitar in her hands, real or imagined. As in PaRappa, the player trades call-and-response lines with a teacher, either following the prompts or freestyling, and ranks range from Awful up to Fever. Co-op and versus modes unlock after clearing levels, and PaRappa gets his own solo mode once Lammy's story is done.
trivia: An arcade version with a guitar controller, Um Jammer Lammy NOW!, was released in Japan.
GameRevolution called its story "the most obtuse, disjointed, drug-induced mess of a story that has ever been conceived, period."
devStory: Masaya Matsuura designed the game and composed its music, with art by Rodney Alan Greenblat. Sony released it in Japan on 18 March 1999 and North America in August. It won the Interactive Achievement Award for Outstanding Achievement in Original Music Composition.

title: Brave Fencer Musashi
description: Brave Fencer Musashi (1998) is Square's 3D action RPG, in which a young swordsman summoned to another world must stay rested — or fall asleep on his feet — while defending the Allucaneet Kingdom.
longDescription: Musashi, a young swordsman, is summoned to a parallel world to defend the Allucaneet Kingdom from the Thirstquencher Empire, and searches for the Five Scrolls that strengthen his sword Lumina. Combat is in real time in 3D, and the game runs on a day-night cycle: Musashi tires over time and must rest, or he may fall asleep. His second sword, Fusion, performs combos and absorbs Bincho energy.
trivia: In North America it came with a demo of Final Fantasy VIII.
Several reviewers compared it to The Legend of Zelda.
devStory: Yoichi Yoshimoto directed the game, Tetsuya Nomura designed the characters and Tsuyoshi Sekito composed the music. Square released it in Japan on 16 July 1998, where it sold about 648,803 copies that year, and in North America that November. Musashi: Samurai Legend followed on the PS2 in 2005.

title: Breath of Fire III
description: Breath of Fire III (1997) is Capcom's PlayStation RPG and the first in the series with 3D environments, in which Ryu, the last of the dragon Brood, learns why his people were wiped out.
longDescription: Ryu, the last of the Brood, searches for the truth about his people and comes up against Myria, the goddess who ordered the dragons' destruction. His companions include Nina, Rei, Teepo, Momo, Garr and Peco. Characters are 2D sprites in 3D environments, and battles are turn-based with a party of three. Ryu turns into dragons by combining chrysms, characters learn skills by becoming apprentices to Masters, and a Fairy Village can be built up to unlock items and mini-games.
trivia: It was the first Breath of Fire game with voice acting.
It sold at least 656,297 copies on the PlayStation.
devStory: Makoto Ikehara directed the game, and Capcom released it in Japan on 11 September 1997 and North America in May 1998. A PSP version followed in 2005.

title: Blackthorne
description: Blackthorne (1994) is Blizzard's cinematic platformer in the style of Another World and Flashback, in which Kyle returns to his home planet with a shotgun to overthrow the tyrant Sarlac.
longDescription: Kyle Vlaros was sent to Earth as a child. Twenty years later he returns to the planet Tuul to defeat the dark ruler Sarlac, avenge his father and reclaim the throne of Androth. He runs, climbs and hunts for keys through maze-like levels, fighting with an upgradable pump-action shotgun. He can fire backwards without turning round and press himself against the wall to let bullets pass. The game has 17 levels across four areas.
trivia: Early sprites were rotoscoped, using more than 1,000 frames.
Kyle is named after Kyle Reese in The Terminator.
Electronic Gaming Monthly made the Super NES version its Game of the Month.
devStory: Blizzard made the game, inspired by Another World and Flashback, and Interplay released it for the Super NES in September 1994 and MS-DOS that December. A 32X version, with a fifth area, followed in 1995.

title: Dead or Alive
description: Dead or Alive (1996) is Tecmo's 3D fighting game on Sega's Model 2 hardware, built around a hold button that catches attacking limbs, which helped the company back to profit.
longDescription: The game puts speed and counters first: in place of the usual guard, a hold button lets fighters catch an attacking limb, and the edges of the arena are danger zones laced with explosives. The fugitive ninja Kasumi enters the tournament to avenge her brother Hayate, crippled by their uncle Raidou, and the cast includes Ryu Hayabusa, Tina Armstrong and Zack. Critics praised the hold system and the graphics.
trivia: Tecmo was near bankruptcy and wanted a hit to rival Virtua Fighter.
The Saturn version topped the Japanese charts.
devStory: Tomonobu Itagaki directed it at Tecmo's in-house team, later Team Ninja, and it reached arcades on 26 November 1996, running on Sega Model 2 hardware. Its success helped Tecmo return to profit in 1996. Saturn and PlayStation versions followed in 1997 and 1998, and Dead or Alive 2 in 1999.

title: Smash TV
description: Smash TV (1990) is Eugene Jarvis's twin-stick arcade shooter set on a violent 1999 game show, where contestants gun down waves of enemies for cash and prizes.
longDescription: In a dystopian 1999, contestants on a television game show shoot their way through arenas full of enemies, collecting cash and prizes and fighting bosses, until they face the sadistic host himself. Like Jarvis's Robotron: 2084, it is played with two joysticks, one to move and one to shoot, and two players can play together. Collecting keys opens the bonus Pleasure Dome, which was added after players complained that the first release lacked it.
trivia: Its influences include RoboCop and The Running Man.
It won the AMOA's most innovative game award in 1990.
Total Carnage (1992), named after one of the host's catchphrases, shares much of its play but is not a sequel.
devStory: Eugene Jarvis designed the game and Mark Turmell programmed it at Williams, which released it in April 1990. Console versions were titled Super Smash TV, and Ocean made the home computer versions, one of which scored 97% in CRASH.

title: Rampart
description: Rampart (1990) is Atari Games' arcade castle game, in which players rebuild their walls with Tetris-like pieces between cannon battles — a precursor of tower defence.
longDescription: Play alternates between building and combat. In the building phase, players fit Tetris-like shapes into the gaps in their castle walls; in combat, they fire cannons at ships in the single-player game or at each other's walls in multiplayer. A player who fails to enclose at least one castle by the end of the building phase loses. The single-player game has six fixed levels, and it is played with a trackball.
trivia: Computer and Video Games gave the arcade version 93%.
Konami's Famicom version added seven training levels and three difficulty settings.
devStory: John Salwitz and Dave Ralston created the game, with music by Don Diekneite and Brad Fuller. Atari Games gave it a limited release in October 1990 and a wide one in February 1991, and it was converted to the NES, Super NES, Mega Drive, Master System, Lynx and many other systems.

title: Thrust
description: Thrust (1986) is Jeremy Smith's gravity game for the BBC Micro, in which a ship tows a heavy pod out of a planet's caves on a swinging tractor beam.
longDescription: The ship rotates and thrusts, and has to lift a pod out of the caves with its tractor beam and carry it into space. Gravity and inertia act on both ship and pod, so the pair can swing and spin out of control, and touching the cave walls is fatal. Turrets fire at the ship, fuel runs down, and the shield uses fuel and blocks firing. Shooting the planet's reactor enough times sends it critical, giving ten seconds to escape. After six levels the cycle repeats with reversed gravity, then invisible walls, then both.
trivia: Its play was heavily inspired by Atari's Gravitar.
Firebird's budget Commodore 64 version, at £1.99, topped the Gallup all-formats chart.
Hidden messages on the BBC Micro version include "Support Hotol" and "Physics is fun".
devStory: Jeremy Smith wrote the game for the BBC Micro, published by Superior Software, and later co-created Exile. It was converted to the Commodore 64, Spectrum, Amstrad CPC, Atari ST and other machines, and Thrust II followed in 1988.

title: Repton
description: Repton (1985) is Tim Tyler's BBC Micro puzzle game of diamonds and falling rocks, a calmer, more puzzle-minded cousin of Boulder Dash.
longDescription: Repton digs through an underground maze collecting every diamond before time runs out, including some locked in safes that open when he picks up a key. Falling rocks and monsters hatched from eggs are the dangers. There are 12 levels, and passwords let players skip ahead. Compared with Boulder Dash it is calmer and more ordered, with more emphasis on solving puzzles than on arcade improvisation.
trivia: Tyler was inspired by a review of Boulder Dash but had never played it.
Its theme tune is "Black and White Rag" by George Botsford.
devStory: Tim Tyler wrote the game for the BBC Micro and Acorn Electron, and Superior Software released it in the summer of 1985. Repton 2 followed that November and Repton 3, with a map editor, in 1986. The series sold about 125,000 copies by 1990.

title: Mercenary
description: Mercenary (1985) is Paul Woakes's open-ended 3D vector adventure, in which a stranded pilot plays two warring factions against each other to earn a way off the planet Targ.
longDescription: The player crash-lands on the planet Targ, which is in the middle of a civil war between the Palyars and the Mechanoids. Working for either side — or both — earns money towards a way home, and there are several different ways to escape. Tasks can be tackled in any order, and the player is guided by Benson, a "9th generation PC", whose messages scroll across the screen.
trivia: Zzap!64 gave it 97% and a Gold Medal.
It was also released as Mercenary: Escape from Targ.
devStory: Paul Woakes and Bruce Jordan designed the game, and Novagen released it in 1985 for the Atari 8-bit and Commodore 64, with versions for the Spectrum, Amstrad CPC, Atari ST and Amiga. An expansion, The Second City, followed in 1986, and the sequel Damocles in 1990.

title: Driller
description: Driller (1987) is Incentive Software's first-person 3D puzzle game, the first built on the Freescape engine, in which a probe must place eighteen drilling rigs to stop a moon from exploding.
longDescription: The moon Mitral is filling with gas and will explode, destroying the colony on Evath, unless eighteen drilling rigs are placed to release it. The player guides the probe "Last Hope" through eighteen regions in first person, working out where the rigs should go from clues in the landscape and by trial and error, and disabling or avoiding security systems. The probe cannot fly, so driving off a platform strands it on the surface.
trivia: In the US it was called Space Station Oblivion.
Orson Scott Card called its story a "thinly veiled excuse" for the 3D graphics, but still praised the game.
devStory: Chris and Ian Andrew of Major Developments designed the game, and Incentive released it in 1987, with versions for the ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, Amiga, Atari ST and MS-DOS. CRASH gave it 97%. The Freescape engine, offering filled-polygon 3D and free looking, went on to power Dark Side, Total Eclipse and Castle Master.

title: Carrier Command
description: Carrier Command (1988) is Realtime Games' filled-polygon strategy game, in which a robotic aircraft carrier and its aircraft and amphibious tanks race an enemy carrier to claim 64 islands.
longDescription: Two robotic carriers are sent to colonise an archipelago of sixty-four islands, and terrorists seize the more advanced one. From the ACC Epsilon the player commands up to four Manta aircraft and four Walrus amphibious vehicles at a time, claiming neutral islands by dropping command units and capturing enemy ones with virus pods. Vehicles that stray too far from the carrier lose contact and are destroyed, and the game is lost if the carrier's superstructure is wrecked.
trivia: The Games Machine ranked it the number one game of 1988 and gave the Atari ST version 98%.
The team wrote it in 68000 assembly because C was too slow for 3D on 8 MHz machines; Ian Oliver recalled they "slept under our desks".
Bohemia Interactive remade it in 2012 as Carrier Command: Gaea Mission.
devStory: Ian Oliver and Graeme Baird developed the game at Realtime Games in Leeds, and Rainbird released it for the Atari ST and Amiga in 1988, with other versions through 1989. Battle Command followed, and Hostile Waters (2001) was inspired by it.

title: Laser Squad
description: Laser Squad (1988) is Julian Gollop's turn-based tactics game for the ZX Spectrum, with action points, line of sight and hidden enemies — the direct ancestor of X-COM.
longDescription: Players spend limited credits on weapons and armour, deploy their squad and take turns moving, shooting and picking up objects with action points. Different shot types trade accuracy against cost, line of sight decides who can see whom, and in one-player games enemy movements stay hidden. Units can panic if their morale breaks. Each mission has a turn limit, and a player wins by reaching 100 victory points across scenarios such as "The Assassins" and "Moonbase Assault".
trivia: A demo of Laser Squad 2 became the starting point for UFO: Enemy Unknown, published by MicroProse.
Computer and Video Games gave it 97%.
devStory: Julian Gollop led the game at Target Games, later Mythos Games, and Blade Software released it for the ZX Spectrum in 1988, followed by versions for the Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, Amiga, Atari ST and MS-DOS. Laser Squad Nemesis revived the name in 2002.

title: Zarch
description: Zarch (1987) is David Braben's solid-3D shooter for the Acorn Archimedes, in which a mouse-controlled lander stops alien Seeders spreading a virus across the landscape.
longDescription: The player flies a lander controlled by the mouse: a downward thruster lifts it, and tilting it moves it across the landscape. Enemy Seeders spread a virus over the ground, and the lander has to shoot them down before it takes over, refuelling at the launchpad and using limited smart missiles and bombs.
trivia: It began as Lander, a demo bundled with Archimedes computers.
ACE gave it 979, its highest score at the time, under the headline "SOLID 3D - the future of games?"
Amiga Power ranked its port, Virus, fifth on its 1991 list of the best games of all time.
devStory: David Braben wrote the game as a launch title for the Archimedes, and Superior Software released it in 1987. Firebird published versions for the Amiga, Atari ST, MS-DOS and ZX Spectrum as Virus in 1988, and Frontier Developments made Virus 2000 in 1998.

title: Midwinter
