description: Midwinter (1989) is Mike Singleton's frozen-world strategy RPG, in which the player recruits 32 islanders, each with their own history, to resist an invading general across a vast 3D island.
longDescription: In 2099 a meteorite strike has plunged the world into an ice age. On the island of Midwinter, 160,000 square miles of polygon landscape, John Stark, commander of the Free Villages Peace Force, must recruit allies and stop General Masters by destroying his headquarters at Shining Hollow. The game's 32 recruits each have personal histories that decide who else they can win over, and each gets two hours of game time before the clock moves on. They travel by ski, snowmobile, cable car and hang glider.
trivia: Recruits can be injured but not killed.
Eurogamer called it "a priceless transitional specimen in the fossil record of gaming".
devStory: Mike Singleton designed the game at Maelstrom Games, and MicroProse released it on its Rainbird label for the Atari ST and MS-DOS, followed by the Amiga. Zzap gave the Amiga version 97%, and Midwinter II: Flames of Freedom followed in 1991.

title: The Legend of the Mystical Ninja
description: The Legend of the Mystical Ninja (1991) is Konami's Super Famicom adventure, the first Ganbare Goemon game released in the West, mixing town exploration, side-scrolling action and minigames.
longDescription: Goemon and Ebisumaru — Kid Ying and Dr. Yang in the West — work through stages that each begin with a town, full of shops, minigames and places to learn new abilities, and end with a side-scrolling section and a boss. Two players can play together, and can ride piggyback with one moving and the other attacking. One of the minigames recreates the first level of Gradius.
trivia: Electronic Gaming Monthly said it "didn't catch on too much in the U.S." but was popular in Japan, where it sold 521,205 copies.
IGN ranked it 32nd among the top 100 SNES games.
devStory: Konami released the game in Japan on 19 July 1991 as Ganbare Goemon: Yuki-hime Kyūshutsu Emaki, in North America in February 1992 and in Europe in 1994.

sources.title: The Legend of the Mystical Ninja

title: Super Cobra
description: Super Cobra (1981) is Konami's follow-up to Scramble, a scrolling shooter in which a fuel-hungry helicopter fights through caverns to a base and carries off its loot.
longDescription: The player flies a helicopter through caverns, using a laser and bombs against defences, tanks and UFOs. Fuel drains steadily and is topped up by destroying fuel tanks. After ten levels the helicopter reaches a base, which it must get through safely to carry off the loot.
trivia: It runs on the same arcade hardware as Scramble.
Stern built 12,337 cabinets in the US by October 1981, its third best-selling arcade game after Berzerk and Scramble.
devStory: Konami released Super Cobra in August 1981, with Stern distributing it in North America. Parker Brothers converted it to the Atari 2600, Atari 5200, ColecoVision, Intellivision and other systems, and the 2600 version won a Certificate of Merit at the 1983 Arkie Awards.

title: Tutankham
description: Tutankham (1982) is Konami's scrolling maze shooter set in the tomb of Tutankhamun, where the explorer's laser fires only left and right.
longDescription: An explorer works through the scrolling tomb of Tutankhamun collecting keys and treasures. The laser fires only left and right, and each level or life brings one screen-clearing flash bomb. Only one key can be carried at a time, so players have to backtrack, and the laser stops working when the timer runs out. The tomb is guarded by asps, vultures, parrots, bats, dragons and curses.
trivia: It appeared in a January 1983 LIFE photograph of six video game record holders.
Gauntlet and Time Bandit drew on its maze-shooter design.
devStory: H. Tanigaki designed the game, and Konami released it in 1982, with Stern distributing it in North America. It topped the Play Meter charts in October 1982, and Parker Brothers brought it to the Atari 2600, ColecoVision and Intellivision in 1983.

title: Moon Cresta
description: Moon Cresta (1980) is a fixed shooter in which the player docks the three stages of a rocket together in mid-game, gaining firepower but becoming a bigger target.
longDescription: The player starts with a single-laser ship. Docking with the second and third stages of the rocket adds more lasers, up to five in all, but makes the combined ship a larger target, and a misaligned docking destroys the stage. The game ends when all three stages are lost.
trivia: Centuri released it in North America as Eagle, adding an eagle-shaped enemy.
It was the fourth highest-earning arcade game of 1980 in Japan.
devStory: Jorudan developed the game, with Shigeki Fujiwara as designer, and Nichibutsu released it in Japan on 15 February 1980, with Gremlin/Sega distributing it in North America. Incentive Software published several home versions, and the series continued with Terra Cresta (1985).

title: Atic Atac
description: Atic Atac (1983) is Ultimate Play the Game's castle maze for the ZX Spectrum, in which a wizard, knight or serf hunts for the three pieces of the Golden Key of ACG.
longDescription: The player is trapped in a castle of several floors and must find the three pieces of the Golden Key of ACG to escape. There are three characters to choose from — Wizard, Knight or Serf — each with a different weapon, a different grip on the floor and a secret passage only they can use. Health drains as the player moves and is restored by eating food, while poisonous fungi drain it on contact.
trivia: Computer and Video Games called it "the best yet from Ultimate".
It was a major inspiration for the TV show Knightmare.
It was included in Rare Replay in 2015.
devStory: Tim Stamper wrote the game and Chris Stamper designed the graphics, and Ultimate released it for the ZX Spectrum in 1983. It entered the charts at number 5 in November 1983 and reached number 1. A BBC Micro version followed in 1985.

title: Hyper Sports
description: Hyper Sports (1984) is Konami's sequel to Track & Field, with seven new events from swimming and skeet shooting to weightlifting and pole vault.
longDescription: Like Track & Field, the game uses two run buttons and an action button for each player, with each event needing its own timing. The seven events are swimming, skeet shooting, long horse, archery, triple jump, weightlifting and pole vault.
trivia: In Japan it was Hyper Olympic '84, officially licensed for the 1984 Summer Olympics.
It became the number-one arcade game in the UK.
The home versions topped the UK all-formats chart in July and August 1985.
devStory: Konami released the game in Japan on 12 May 1984, with Centuri publishing it in North America. Home versions followed for the ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, BBC Micro and MSX, several of them without the pole vault.

title: Zero Wing
description: Zero Wing (1989) is Toaplan's side-scrolling shooter, whose badly translated Mega Drive intro gave the internet "All your base are belong to us".
longDescription: In 2101, Trent seeks revenge on the space pirates CATS, who have broken a peace treaty, flying the ZIG fighter through eight levels, each ending in a boss. The Seizer Beam grabs enemies to use as shields or to fling at others, and three weapons — Red Cannon, Blue Laser and Green Homing — can be switched and upgraded.
trivia: The Mega Drive version's English translation was done in-house; its intro was rediscovered in 1999 and became the "All your base are belong to us" meme.
The project began as a training exercise for new Toaplan staff and reused the Hellfire engine.
It was Toaplan's last side-scrolling shooter.
devStory: Toshiaki Ōta led development, and Namco published the arcade game in Japan in October 1989. Sega released the Mega Drive version in 1991, which Computer and Video Games scored 93%.

title: Batsugun
description: Batsugun (1993) is Toaplan's vertical shooter, regarded by many as the first "manic" or bullet hell shooter, in which ships level up their guns with experience.
longDescription: Players choose one of three ships — Sky Mirage, Dragon's Whisper or Judgement Flasher — and fly five levels. Alongside the usual "P" power-ups and "B" bombs, the main gun gains experience separately from the score and levels up twice; once it is maxed out, further experience adds bombs instead. Extra lives come every million points, with gold medals and hidden bonus spots for higher scores.
trivia: A Special Version, with a smaller hitbox, a shield and extra loops, was shown at the 1994 AOU Show but never officially released.
Toaplan closed in March 1994, before a planned sequel came out.
It influenced Cho Ren Sha 68K and Eschatos.
devStory: Junya Inoue and Takeshi Kawamoto designed the game, and Toaplan released it on 7 December 1993. It won two Gamest awards. Banpresto published a Saturn version in Japan in 1996 that included both the original and the Special Version.

title: Tiger-Heli
description: Tiger-Heli (1985) is Toaplan's first shoot 'em up, a vertical helicopter shooter whose screen-clearing bomb became a staple of the genre.
longDescription: The player flies a Tiger attack helicopter whose missiles hit both air and ground targets, while bombs destroy enemies and their bullets within range. Shooting certain bunkers releases extra bombs or small helper helicopters: red ones fire to the sides, grey ones forwards. After four stages the game loops back to the second stage at a higher difficulty.
trivia: Game Machine listed it as the most popular arcade game in its 1 October 1985 issue.
The NES version reportedly sold more than a million copies in North America.
devStory: Masahiro Yuge, Tatsuya Uemura and Yuichirō Nozawa programmed the game, with music by Yuge and Uemura. Taito released it in October 1985, and Micronics converted it to the NES, which Acclaim published in North America in 1987. Twin Cobra followed in 1987.

title: Bump 'n' Jump
description: Bump 'n' Jump (1982) is Data East's vehicular combat game, in which the player's car bumps rivals off the road and leaps over water and obstacles.
longDescription: The player drives to the end of each course, knocking enemy cars into the sides of the road or jumping on top of them, and leaping over obstacles such as water. Trucks can only be jumped on and sometimes drop debris. A jump needs at least 100 mph, and the seasons change from level to level. Finishing a level without wrecking any vehicles earns a 50,000-point bonus.
trivia: In Japan it is Burnin' Rubber.
Next Generation ranked it 65th in its 1996 top 100 games.
devStory: Data East released the game in Japan in November 1982, with Bally Midway distributing it in North America in 1983. Versions followed for the Intellivision, Atari 2600 and ColecoVision, and for the Famicom as Buggy Popper, which reached the NES under its original name in 1988.

title: Front Line
description: Front Line (1982) is Taito's overhead war game, one of the first run-and-guns, in which a lone soldier fights through infantry and tanks to lob a grenade into the enemy fort.
longDescription: A lone soldier advances on foot against enemy infantry, then takes over tanks to fight enemy armour, and must finish by throwing a grenade over the brick barricade of the enemy fort. A rotary dial aims and fires his gun, and a button throws grenades and gets in and out of tanks. The light tank is nimble but fragile, while the heavy tank's cannon can take one hit from a light tank. Each time the fort falls, the stage repeats with faster and deadlier troops.
trivia: It was runner-up for Coin-Op Game of the Year at the 1983 Arcade Awards, behind Pole Position.
It was the basis for SNK's TNK III, which in turn fed into Ikari Warriors.
devStory: Tetsuya Sasaki designed the game, and Taito released it on 10 November 1982. It was the seventh highest-grossing arcade game of 1982 in Japan, and it preceded Capcom's Commando (1985) as an overhead run-and-gun.

title: Xybots
description: Xybots (1987) is Ed Logg's split-screen 3D maze shooter for Atari Games, which began life as a sequel to Gauntlet.
longDescription: Major Rock Hardy and Captain Ace Gunn fight their way through a 3D maze of robots called Xybots, alone or together. The lower half of the screen shows the action and the upper half each player's status and a map of the level. Coins dropped by defeated Xybots buy energy, armour, speed, firepower and maps in shops between levels, and some levels end with a large boss Xybot.
trivia: It was first conceived as Gauntlet III: Catacombs, until Atari's marketing department wanted a different name.
Its joystick rotated the player, which the article cites as one reason for its limited sales.
GamesTM called it "ahead of its time".
devStory: Ed Logg designed and programmed the game with Bob Flanagan, and Atari Games released it in November 1987. Logg recalled in 2005 that it was not a financial success. Home versions followed in 1989 and a Lynx version in 1991.

title: Pit-Fighter
description: Pit-Fighter (1990) is Atari Games' street-fighting game built from digitised footage of live actors, in which up to three players brawl through 15 matches in front of a rowdy crowd.
longDescription: Three fighters — Buzz, Ty and Kato — take on opponents such as Southside Jim, Heavy Metal and Mad Miles across 15 matches, with up to three players at once. Every third fight is a Grudge Match, and the last is the Championship against the Masked Warrior. The crowd joins in, attacking fighters, dropping weapons and shoving players back into the fight, and a power pill briefly boosts strength. Pressing all three buttons triggers a super move.
trivia: Its fighters were digitised from live actors filmed against a bluescreen, making it the second fighting game with digitised sprites.
It topped the RePlay chart for upright cabinets in October 1990.
devStory: Gary Stark and Mark Stephen Pierce designed the game, and Atari Games released it in August 1990, selling 5,500 arcade units in the US. Tengen published home versions from 1991, and a planned Pit Fighter II was never released.

title: Kula World
description: Kula World (1998), released as Roll Away in North America, is a PlayStation puzzle-platformer in which a beach ball rolls over floating structures where gravity follows it round every edge.
longDescription: The player rolls a beach ball across floating structures, collecting keys to unlock the exit along with coins and jewels. Gravity turns with the ball as it rolls over edges, so walls become floors. One fruit hidden in each stage unlocks bonus levels in which every cube must be activated. Falling off, hitting spikes or running out of time costs points, and the game ends if the score drops below zero.
trivia: It was Game Design Sweden's only video game.
Playable demos came on the Demo One disc packed with European PlayStations in 1998.
Academic studies later used it to examine gamification in corporate training.
devStory: Game Design Sweden developed it, and Sony released it in Europe on 10 July 1998, with Psygnosis publishing it in North America as Roll Away. IGN gave it 8.9 out of 10.

title: Uniracers
description: Uniracers (1994) is DMA Design's Super NES racing game for riderless unicycles, in which stunts mid-race give a burst of speed.
longDescription: Players race riderless unicycles around 2D tracks. Stunts speed the unicycle up on race tracks and score points on stunt tracks, while wiping out loses all the speed built up. There are nine tours of five tracks, ending in a race against the Anti-Uni, whose collisions reverse the controls and turn the track invisible. Two players can race split-screen, and a league mode takes up to eight.
trivia: Mike Dailly says Pixar sued over the unicycle's resemblance to Red's Dream, limiting it to an initial run of 300,000; no record of such a lawsuit has been found.
The developers practised riding real unicycles in their offices.
In Europe it was called Unirally.
devStory: DMA Design developed the game under the working title "1x1", and Nintendo released it in North America on 5 December 1994. Nintendo Power ranked it the eighth best Super NES game of 1994.

title: Cool Spot
description: Cool Spot (1993) is Virgin Games' platformer starring Spot, the 7 Up mascot, who rescues his caged friends by collecting spots. It sold a million copies.
longDescription: Spot jumps, throws soda bubbles at enemies and climbs by jumping against surfaces. In each level he has to collect a set number of spots to free a caged Spot, and each level has a time limit. His health is shown by a Spot face that sags as he takes damage. Flagpoles act as checkpoints, and hidden letters spelling 7 Up's slogan "UNCOLA" earn continues.
trivia: It came out at a time when other brand mascots, such as Chester Cheetah and the Noid, were also getting their own games.
The sequel, Spot Goes to Hollywood, followed in 1995.
devStory: David Bishop and Bill Anderson designed the game, David Perry programmed it and Tommy Tallarico composed the music. Virgin released it for the Genesis in April 1993, followed by Super NES, Master System, Amiga and Game Boy versions.

title: Tobal No. 1
description: Tobal No. 1 (1996) is DreamFactory's 60-frames-per-second fighting game for Square, with characters by Akira Toriyama and a dungeon-crawling Quest Mode — and a demo of Final Fantasy VII in every box.
longDescription: The game runs at up to 60 frames per second, and Akira Toriyama designed all of its characters. Alongside the fighting modes, its Quest Mode mixes fighting with 3D dungeon exploration, though progress there cannot be saved. Clearing the 30-floor Udan's Dungeon unlocks the secret fighter Toriyama Robo.
trivia: Every copy included a playable demo of Final Fantasy VII and previews of Final Fantasy Tactics, Bushido Blade and SaGa Frontier.
It sold 752,000 copies in Japan in 1996, the ninth best-selling home game there that year.
devStory: Seiichi Ishii helped design its mechanics at DreamFactory, and Square released it in Japan on 2 August 1996, with Sony distributing it abroad. Tobal 2 followed in 1997 but stayed in Japan.

title: The Tower of Druaga
description: The Tower of Druaga (1984) is Masanobu Endō's arcade maze game, in which the knight Gilgamesh climbs 60 floors to rescue Ki, uncovering treasures hidden behind deliberately obscure conditions.
longDescription: The knight Gilgamesh climbs 60 floors of a tower to rescue the maiden Ki from Druaga, an eight-armed, four-legged demon who means to enslave mankind with the Blue Crystal Rod. Each floor holds a key that opens the door to the next, guarded by slimes, knights, wizards, ghosts that pass through walls and dragons. Every floor also hides a treasure, such as a pickaxe, speed boots or a candle, revealed by a secret task like defeating certain enemies or entering a joystick code — and some are needed to finish the game. A time limit releases indestructible Will-o-Wisps.
trivia: Endō described it as a "fantasy Pac-Man"; the 60 floors were inspired by Sunshine 60, then Asia's tallest building.
It is credited with influencing Ys, Hydlide, Dragon Slayer and The Legend of Zelda, and with getting players to share tips and guidebooks.
Eurogamer called the 2009 Wii release "diabolically obtuse".
devStory: Masanobu Endō, creator of Xevious, designed the game after buying Dungeons & Dragons on a trip to North America, and Junko Ozawa composed the music. Namco released it in Japan in June 1984 on Mappy hardware, and it began the Babylonian Castle Saga, continued by The Return of Ishtar (1986).

title: Dragon Buster
description: Dragon Buster (1985) is Namco's side-scrolling action RPG, in which the swordsman Clovis fights his way to a dragon — the earliest game with a double jump, and one of the first with a health meter.
longDescription: Clovis, a swordsman trained by a monk, sets out to slay a dragon and rescue Princess Celia, the daughter of King Lawrence. Between rounds of side-scrolling platform action, the player picks a route across an overworld map of caves, towers, boneyards, mountains and ruins. Clovis's vitality is shown on screen, recovers by 25% after each level and ends the game when it runs out.
trivia: It is described as the earliest game with a double jump.
Dragon Valor on the PlayStation was both a remake and a sequel.
devStory: Namco released the game in Japan in January 1985, with music by Yuriko Keino, and it placed third in Game Machine's chart of table arcade units that March. Tose made the Famicom version, and Dragon Buster II followed in Japan.

title: Baraduke
description: Baraduke (1985) is Namco's run-and-gun through 48 floors, whose ending revealed its space-suited hero as a woman a year before Metroid.
longDescription: A space-suited fighter — Kissy for player one, Takky for player two — works through eight worlds of five floors and a boss floor each, 48 in all. Destroying the Octy enemies opens the pipe to the next floor, and rescuing the one-eyed Paccets earns points and a chance at an extra shield in bonus games. The bosses include the Blue Worm, the Turning Eye and, in the last world, the Octy King.
trivia: In North America it was released as Alien Sector.
Kissy later appeared in Mr. Driller and Namco × Capcom.
devStory: Yukio Takahashi designed the game, and Namco released it in Japan in May 1985. Baraduke II followed in Japan in 1988.

title: Metro-Cross
description: Metro-Cross (1985) is Namco's obstacle-course race against the clock, in which a runner dodges pitfalls and tyres, rides skateboards and kicks drink cans across 32 rounds.
longDescription: Runner sprints automatically through 32 timed rounds while the player steers him and controls his speed. Slip zones, pitfalls and crackers appear early, followed by giant tyres, walls, cubes, mice and chess pieces. Springboards launch him forward, skateboards speed him up and make him immune to slip zones, and drink cans can be kicked for up to 5,000 points or jumped on to pause the timer. Time left over becomes bonus points, every fourth round runs on the time saved from the three before it, and running out of time electrocutes him.
trivia: Its European and Australian Xbox 360 release was renamed Retro-Cross.
A Metro-Cross theme appeared as downloadable content in Pac-Man 99.
devStory: Tatsuro Okamoto designed the game and Nobuyuki Ohnogi composed the music. Namco released it in Japan in May 1985, and home versions followed for the Famicom, Commodore 64, ZX Spectrum, Amstrad CPC and Atari ST.

title: Gaplus
description: Gaplus (1984) is Namco's sequel to Galaga and the third Galaxian game, in which the player's ship can also move up the screen and capture enemies with a tractor beam.
longDescription: The player fights waves of diving enemies through levels called Parsecs, and, unlike in Galaga, the ship can move up and down as well as sideways. Some enemies drop power-ups: a tractor beam that captures enemies, a large drill, and effects that slow enemies or cancel their shots. Collecting parts builds a new ship for an extra life. In the Challenging Stages, the player juggles enemies by hitting them as many times as possible.
trivia: North American operators could convert it with a kit that renamed it Galaga 3.
It was the most successful table arcade unit in Japan in May 1984, according to Game Machine.
devStory: Namco released the game in Japan in April 1984, with Bally Midway distributing it in North America that September. It was the only game besides Phozon to run on Namco's Phozon hardware.

title: The Legend of Valkyrie
description: The Legend of Valkyrie (1989) is Namco's top-down action-adventure for one or two players, in which the warrior Valkyrie helps defeat the warlord Kamooz. Gamest readers voted it the best arcade game of all time.
longDescription: Kurino Xandra searches for the Golden Seed to save his people's dying fields, joined by Sabina and Zuul and later by the warrior Valkyrie, who helps him defeat the warlord Kamooz at the Northern Spring. Players fight enemies with projectile attacks, collect gold, and buy spells and weapons in shops, through eight areas that each end in a boss, against a timer.
trivia: Development began as a four-player, Gauntlet-style game with several Valkyries, before those ideas were dropped.
One designer used the pseudonym "Koakuman" ("little devil"), which North American versions mistranslated as "Quarkman".
Its first fully English release came in Namco Museum Vol. 5 in 1997.
devStory: Hiroshi Fujii led the design, with music by Hiroyuki Kawada, and Namco released it in Japanese arcades in April 1989 as a follow-up to the Famicom game Valkyrie no Bōken (1986). A PC Engine version with new stages followed in 1990.

title: The Hobbit
description: The Hobbit (1982) is Beam Software's illustrated text adventure based on Tolkien's novel, whose characters acted on their own in real time — "Thorin sits down and starts singing about gold."
longDescription: The game follows Tolkien's 1937 novel, with illustrations for many of its locations. Its "Inglish" parser understood more complex sentences than most adventures of the time. The game runs in real time, so leaving it idle lets events happen, and other characters act independently: Gandalf wanders around some fifty locations. One of its lines, "Thorin sits down and starts singing about gold", has entered popular culture.
trivia: Every copy came with a copy of Tolkien's novel.
It won the 1983 Golden Joystick Award for best strategy game.
CRL released a parody, The Boggit, in 1986.
devStory: Veronika Megler and Philip Mitchell designed the game at Beam Software, and Melbourne House released it for the ZX Spectrum in December 1982. It sold more than 100,000 copies in its first two years and more than 500,000 in Europe.

title: Saboteur!
description: Saboteur! (1985) is Clive Townsend's stealth action game, in which a ninja breaks into a warehouse, steals a disk listing rebel leaders and escapes by helicopter.
longDescription: An anonymous ninja infiltrates a warehouse to steal a floppy disk listing rebel leaders, then escapes through rooms, dark tunnels and a secret command centre to a helicopter. He can crouch, climb, run, punch and drop-kick, starts with a single shuriken and can pick up bricks and pipes as weapons. Guards, guard dogs and automatic guns stand in his way, his energy drains from falls and attacks, and a time limit runs throughout. The difficulty level sets the number of guards, the time limit and how many security doors are locked.
trivia: It reused routines and ideas from Townsend's cancelled game Death Pit.
Crash called it "one of the better releases on the Spectrum this year".
devStory: Clive Townsend designed and programmed the game, and Durell released it in 1985 for the ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC and Commodore 16. Saboteur II: Avenging Angel followed in 1987.

title: The Way of the Exploding Fist
description: The Way of the Exploding Fist (1985) is Beam Software's karate game for the Commodore 64, scored with yin-yang points instead of energy bars — the UK's best-selling computer game of 1985.
longDescription: Two karateka fight one-on-one under the eye of a wise old master. Instead of an energy bar, bouts are scored with yin-yang symbols: a half symbol for a committed technique and a full one for a decisive blow, with two full points winning. The fighter has 18 moves on the joystick or keys. After several stages a bull charges in a bonus round and has to be knocked out with a single blow.
trivia: It was one of the first games to borrow heavily from Data East's Karate Champ.
The Commodore 64 version uses more than 600 sprite images.
It won Game of the Year at the Golden Joystick Awards.
devStory: Gregg Barnett, Bruce Bayley, David Johnston and Neil Brennan designed the game at Beam Software, and Melbourne House released it in June 1985. It topped the UK charts in September and October and sold 500,000 copies across Europe.

sources.title: The Way of the Exploding Fist

title: IK+
description: IK+ (1987), International Karate +, is Archer Maclean's three-way karate game on a beach, with bonus rounds of deflecting bouncing balls and a Rob Hubbard score.
longDescription: Three karateka fight at once on a beach, each trying to be first to six points, with one or two human players and the computer controlling the rest. Every two rounds a bonus game has players deflecting bouncing balls or, in some versions, kicking away bombs. The Amiga version hides background antics — a Pac-Man, a descending spider, a U-boat periscope — and a key combination that makes all three fighters' trousers fall down.
trivia: Rob Hubbard wrote the music for the 8-bit versions and David Lowe for the Atari ST and Amiga.
The Atari ST version took six months to make; the Amiga version took seven days.
Zzap!64 gave the Commodore 64 version 97%.
devStory: Archer Maclean designed the game at System 3 as a successor to International Karate (1985), and it was released in October 1987 for the Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC and ZX Spectrum, with Atari ST and Amiga versions in 1988. Activision published it in the US as Chop N' Drop.

title: Barbarian: The Ultimate Warrior
description: Barbarian: The Ultimate Warrior (1987) is Palace Software's sword-fighting game, notorious for its decapitations and for a box cover photographed with Page 3 model Maria Whittaker.
longDescription: Two barbarians fight with swords, each with 12 life points shown as six circles — but a well-timed blow to the neck takes the opponent's head off instantly. In the story mode the player fights eight barbarians to reach the wizard Drax and rescue Princess Mariana.
trivia: The box used photographs of Michael Van Wijk and Maria Whittaker rather than painted art, and UK complaints focused on the packaging more than the violence.
Germany banned the game for its violence; a version with green blood was later allowed.
In North America Epyx released it as Death Sword.
devStory: Steve Brown designed the game, Stanley Schembri programmed it and Richard Joseph composed the music. Palace released it in 1987 for the Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC and ZX Spectrum, and it topped the all-format charts. Barbarian II: The Dungeon of Drax followed in 1988.

title: Nebulus
description: Nebulus (1987) is John M. Phillips's platform game, in which Pogo climbs rotating towers in the sea — the tower turns around him as he moves, giving a striking 3D effect.
longDescription: Pogo has to climb and destroy eight cylindrical towers standing in the sea. As he walks, the tower rotates rather than the character moving across the screen, creating a 3D effect. Enemies can knock him off ledges, and falling into the sea is fatal. Between towers, a submarine bonus stage lets him shoot fish.
trivia: In the US it was released as Tower Toppler.
It won Best Original Game at the Golden Joystick Awards.
The Commodore 64 version earned 97% and a Zzap!64 Gold Medal.
devStory: John M. Phillips designed the game, and Hewson released it in 1987 for the Commodore 64, ZX Spectrum, Amstrad CPC, Amiga and Atari ST. Bits Studios later made Game Boy and NES versions, and Nebulus 2 followed on the Amiga.

title: Dizzy – The Ultimate Cartoon Adventure
description: Dizzy (1987) is the Oliver Twins' first Dizzy game for Codemasters, in which the somersaulting egg gathers four ingredients for a potion to defeat the wizard Zaks.
longDescription: Dizzy searches the fairy-tale land of Katmandu for four items to put in a cauldron and brew a potion that will defeat the evil wizard Zaks. He can carry only one item at a time, many hazards kill on contact, and he starts with just three lives, which makes the game hard. It relies less on inventory puzzles than the later games in the series.
trivia: His name comes from the somersaults he does when he jumps.
He was first conceived as a face with hands and feet; the egg came about after fans assumed he was one.
Eurogamer included it in its 2017 list of 10 games that defined the ZX Spectrum.
devStory: The Oliver Twins wrote the game, keeping the character simple because their Panda Sprites software distorted complex rotating sprites. Codemasters released it in 1987 for the ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64 and Amstrad CPC, starting the Dizzy series.

title: Spellbound
description: Spellbound (1985) is David Jones's Magic Knight adventure for Mastertronic, played through a pull-down "Windimation" menu, in which the knight rescues a wizard trapped by his own spell.
longDescription: The wizard Gimbal is trapped by his own "white-out" spell, gone wrong during a rice-pudding experiment. Magic Knight must free him and return everyone to their proper time and place. Commands are chosen from drop-down menus called "Windimation", and the puzzles mostly involve using or giving objects to the right characters and casting spells. The other characters grow hungry and fall asleep, and Magic Knight has to look after them, all within a 48-hour time limit.
trivia: Rob Hubbard wrote the music.
Crime Busters (1986) was withdrawn after a dispute over its reported use of Spellbound's code.
devStory: David Jones designed and programmed the game as the second Magic Knight adventure, after Finders Keepers, and Mastertronic released it on its M.A.D. label in 1985 for the ZX Spectrum and Amstrad CPC. Knight Tyme followed in 1986 and Stormbringer in 1987.

title: Vulgus
description: Vulgus (1984) is Capcom's first arcade game, a vertical shooter designed by Tokuro Fujiwara, which introduced the Yashichi later used as a power-up across Capcom's games.
longDescription: The player shoots down waves of enemies with an unlimited main gun and a limited supply of bombs, picking up "Pow" icons to restock. There are no separate levels: the game loops with rising difficulty until the last life is lost. One enemy, the Yashichi, later returned as a power-up in other Capcom games.
trivia: Capcom later gave the game away as freeware.
An NES follow-up, Titan Warriors, originally called Neo Vulgus, was never released.
devStory: Tokuro Fujiwara designed the game and Ayako Mori composed the music. Capcom released it in Japan in May 1984, with SNK publishing it abroad, and it was among Japan's most popular arcade games that June.

title: SonSon
description: SonSon (1984) is Capcom's auto-scrolling arcade game loosely based on Journey to the West, starring a monkey boy patterned after Sun Wukong, with a pig partner for a second player.
longDescription: The screen scrolls on its own across six rows of platforms, and the player fires energy blasts from a fighting staff while dodging enemies, which cost a life on contact. Fruit earns points, and a cloud grants extra lives and brief invincibility. The hero is a monkey boy modelled on Sun Wukong, and a second player can join as TonTon, based on Zhu Bajie.
trivia: Marvel vs. Capcom 2 includes a character called SonSon, the original hero's granddaughter.
Its PC Engine sequel, SonSon II, was heavily based on Black Tiger.
devStory: Yoshiki Okamoto directed the game and drew its art, Hirokazu Fujinaka programmed it, and Ayako Mori and Tamayo Kawamoto composed the music. Capcom released it in July 1984, and Micronics made a Famicom version in 1986.

title: Exed Exes
description: Exed Exes (1985), Savage Bees in North America, is Capcom's insect-themed vertical shooter for one or two players, in which destroyed enemies can be turned into collectable fruit.
longDescription: One or two players fly up a vertically scrolling screen against insect- and skull-themed enemies. One reviewer singled out the way enemies can be turned into collectable fruit as the game's greatest attraction.
trivia: Its full Japanese title is Super Floating Fortress Exed Exes.
Its character Colonel Issue cameos in Project X Zone 2.
devStory: Yoshiki Okamoto directed it, Takashi Aoki programmed it and Tamayo Kawamoto composed the music. Capcom released it in Japan in February 1985, licensing it to Memetron in North America, and Micronics made a Famicom version that December.

title: Gun.Smoke
description: Gun.Smoke (1985) is Yoshiki Okamoto's Wild West shooter, in which bounty hunter Billie Bob walks up the screen firing left, right and centre with three buttons.
longDescription: In place of a spaceship, the player controls Billie Bob, a bounty hunter in the Wild West, walking up a vertically scrolling screen. Three buttons fire left, right and straight ahead, and pick-ups include a horse, boots, bullets, a rifle and a Yashichi for an extra life.
trivia: The NES version has a new story, set in Hicksville against the Wingates gang, and different music.
The Amstrad CPC version was called Desperado – Gun.Smoke.
devStory: Yoshiki Okamoto directed and designed the game, Takashi Aoki programmed it and Ayako Mori composed the music. Capcom released it in Japan on 23 October 1985, and it was the second most successful table arcade unit in Game Machine's January 1986 chart. The NES version followed in 1988.

title: Trojan
description: Trojan (1986) is Takashi Nishiyama's post-apocalyptic sword-and-shield game for Capcom, whose NES version added Capcom's first attempt at a one-on-one fighting mode.
longDescription: After a nuclear war, warlord spirits possess the survivors and rule under Achilles, and the warrior Trojan rebels against him, fighting through pirates and gladiators. One button swings his sword and the other raises his shield to block, but magic balls can knock both away and leave him fighting bare-handed. Each of the six stages has a sub-boss and an end boss, and the true ending appears only on a second playthrough.
trivia: It is considered a spiritual successor to Kung-Fu Master.
Computer and Video Games called it a worthy successor to Ghosts 'n Goblins.
In Japan it is Tatakai no Banka.
devStory: Takashi Nishiyama directed and designed the game, and it reached arcades in March 1986, with Romstar releasing it in North America. The NES version, released that December in Japan, added power-ups, hidden rooms, an extra boss and a two-player versus mode.

title: Legendary Wings
description: Legendary Wings (1986) is Capcom's two-player shooter, in which winged warriors fly overhead stages and then fight on foot in side-scrolling sections to destroy the supercomputer Dark.
longDescription: In the future the alien supercomputer Dark turns against humanity, and two young warriors are given wings by the god Ares to destroy it. Each stage starts as an overhead flying section and continues as a side-scrolling section on foot, ending with a boss, and optional "Danger" and "Lucky" areas appear along the way. Power-ups raise the warriors' firepower through five levels.
trivia: Its heroine, Michelle Heart, later appeared in Marvel vs. Capcom: Clash of Super Heroes.
Hardcore Gaming 101 called the arcade version "remarkably average" but rated the NES version one of the better shooters on the console.
devStory: Takashi Nishiyama directed the game, with Tamayo Kawamoto composing the music. Capcom released it in November 1986, and the NES version, with longer levels and different bosses, reached North America in 1988.

title: Side Arms
description: Side Arms (1986) is Capcom's horizontal shooter, in which two Mobilsuit pilots fire left and right with separate buttons and can merge their suits into one eight-way-firing machine.
longDescription: The alien Bozon empire attacks Earth, and Lt. Henry and Sgt. Sanders fight back in Mobilsuits, alone or together. The eight-way joystick moves the suit, separate buttons fire left and right, and a third switches between weapons such as a shotgun and a mega bazooka. Collecting α and β power-ups merges a suit with its ally to fire in eight directions.
trivia: Its full title is Hyper Dyne Side Arms.
Capcom made the PC Engine version, but NEC Avenue published it to avoid offending Nintendo, according to composer Takashi Tateishi.
devStory: Capcom released the game in Japan on 6 November 1986, and it was the ninth most successful table arcade unit in Game Machine's February 1987 chart. The PC Engine version followed in 1989, and Probe Software made European home computer versions.

title: 1943: The Battle of Midway
description: 1943: The Battle of Midway (1987) is Capcom's follow-up to 1942, in which a P-38 Lightning flies 16 stages to sink the battleship Yamato, with a fuel meter in place of lives.
longDescription: The player flies a P-38 Lightning through 16 stages to defeat the battleship Yamato. Instead of several lives there is a single large fuel meter. Shooting down formations of red planes releases power-ups, and there are six weapons and three special attacks.
trivia: Okamoto said it drew protests from Japanese right-wing groups, who saw it as an insult to the war dead at Yasukuni Shrine.
The NES version renamed its warships and battlefields with fictional names.
An alternate arcade version, 1943 Kai, was released in Japan.
devStory: Yoshiki Okamoto produced the game, Noritaka Funamizu designed it and Kumi Yamaga composed the music. Capcom released it in Japan in June 1987, and it was the second highest-grossing table arcade game in Japan that year. The NES version followed exactly a year later.

title: Black Tiger
description: Black Tiger (1987) is Capcom's platform game, in which a barbarian hunts three demonic dragons, freeing wise men and spending Zenny coins on better weapons and armour.
longDescription: Three evil dragons bring darkness and destruction to a kingdom, and a barbarian sets out to slay them across eight levels that scroll in eight directions. Rescued wise men hand out rewards, mostly Zenny coins, which buy weapon and armour upgrades, keys for treasure chests and anti-poison potions. The Japanese version, Black Dragon, is harder, with falling rocks and higher prices.
trivia: It was one of ten games in a $2,000,000 deal between U.S. Gold and Japanese coin-op makers.
Its planned release around October 1986 slipped because of "programming placement difficulties".
devStory: Yoshiki Okamoto produced the game, Masayuki Akahori programmed it and Tamayo Kawamoto composed the music. Capcom released it on 1 August 1987, and U.S. Gold brought it to the Amiga, Atari ST, Amstrad CPC and ZX Spectrum in 1989.

title: Forgotten Worlds
description: Forgotten Worlds (1988) is the first game on Capcom's CP System board, a two-player shooter in which supersoldiers aim in sixteen directions with a rotating roll switch.
longDescription: In the 29th century the evil god Bios has left Earth a wasteland, the Dust World, and two nameless supersoldiers are created to defeat him and eight other evil gods across nine stages. A rotating "roll switch" aims in sixteen directions, and pressing it rapidly triggers a "megacrush" attack that costs vitality. A satellite module gives backup fire, and Zenny collected along the way buys upgrades in shops.
trivia: Its working title was Lost Worlds.
It took two years to make, on a budget cited as about $5,000,000.
It won Best Graphics at the 1988 Gamest Awards.
devStory: Capcom released it in Japan on 13 May 1988 as the first title on its CP System hardware. Sega made a Genesis version in 1989 with seven of the nine stages, and U.S. Gold released European home computer versions.

title: U.N. Squadron
description: U.N. Squadron (1989), Area 88 in Japan, is Capcom's mercenary jet shooter based on the manga, in which pilots buy weapons between missions and fly on an energy bar instead of lives.
longDescription: Three mercenary pilots — Shin Kazama, Mickey Simon and Greg Gates — fight a terrorist group called Project 4. Unlike Capcom's 1942 and 1943, the game scrolls sideways. Each pilot has an energy bar that drains with damage instead of a stock of lives, and money earned from destroyed enemies buys weapons in a shop before each mission.
trivia: The North American release dropped all references to the Area 88 manga.
Entertainment Weekly gave the Super NES version an A.
Its spiritual successor is Carrier Air Wing.
devStory: Capcom released the arcade game in August 1989, and it topped the RePlay chart for conversion kits in North America in February 1990. The Super NES version, which let each pilot choose between several planes, followed in 1991.

title: Captain Commando
description: Captain Commando (1991) is Capcom's four-player beat 'em up starring its former American mascot, with a mummy-like alien, a ninja and a baby in a robot as his companions.
longDescription: In the Metro City of 2026, Captain Commando and his three Commando Companions fight crime and the alien Scumocide. The captain fights with energy gloves; Mack the Knife is a mummy-like alien with knives; Ginzu is a ninja, the only one who throws shuriken; and Baby Head is a genius infant in a robot. Following Final Fight's formula, up to four players fight through nine stages, and they can climb into robots that punch, burn or freeze enemies.
trivia: The character began as a fictional spokesman in Capcom USA's console games before Akira Yasuda redesigned him.
Captain Commando became a playable character in Marvel vs. Capcom (1998).
The Super NES version cut the robots and the four-player mode.
devStory: Yoshiki Okamoto produced the game, Akira Yasuda and Junichi Ohno designed it and Masaki Izutani composed the music. Capcom released it in North America in September 1991 as its 17th CP System game, and it sold about 15,000 arcade units.

title: Knights of the Round
description: Knights of the Round (1991) is Capcom's Arthurian beat 'em up, in which Arthur, Lancelot and Perceval level up as they fight to overthrow the evil king Garibaldi.
longDescription: Arthur pulls Excalibur from the stone, and Merlin sends him with Lancelot and Perceval to overthrow the evil king Garibaldi and unite Britain. Seven stages each end in a boss. Players block by pressing attack and pushing away just as an enemy strikes, which also grants a moment of invincibility, and can ride horses to trample enemies. Arthur is balanced and strongest on horseback, Lancelot is the fastest, and Perceval the strongest.
trivia: Game Machine listed it as the most popular arcade game in Japan for two weeks in early 1992.
The Super NES version sold only 5,225 copies in Japan, according to Famitsu.
devStory: Capcom released the game in North America on 27 November 1991, with music by Isao Abe, and the Super NES version followed in 1994.

title: Cadillacs and Dinosaurs
description: Cadillacs and Dinosaurs (1993) is Capcom's three-player beat 'em up based on the comic Xenozoic Tales, in which four heroes fight poachers hunting dinosaurs in the 26th century.
longDescription: In the 26th century Jack, Hannah, Mustapha and Mess fight the Black Marketeers, a gang hunting dinosaurs, whose mastermind is Dr. Simon Fessenden. Up to three players fight through eight stages using guns, thrown objects and melee weapons, and two or more players together can launch a team attack. A defeated player gets a 20-second countdown to continue, with a villain holding a gun to their head.
trivia: It was made to tie in with the animated series Cadillacs and Dinosaurs, which aired the same year.
A version for the Capcom Power System Changer was previewed but never released.
Go Play listed it among the best CPS1 games "you're unlikely to ever play on a Capcom compilation".
devStory: Capcom released the game in April 1993 on its CP System Dash board. Computer and Video Games gave it 89/100, and it was among Japan's most popular arcade games that June.

title: Akalabeth: World of Doom
description: Akalabeth (1980) is the Apple II role-playing game Richard Garriott wrote as a Houston teenager, often counted as the first Ultima and nicknamed "Ultima 0".
longDescription: Lord British sends the player to kill ten monsters, each harder than the last. Most of the game takes place in underground dungeons drawn in first-person wireframe, with an overhead map of the world above. Each world is generated from a "lucky number" the player types in at the start.
trivia: The name comes from Tolkien's Akallabêth, although the game does not follow Tolkien's story.
Garriott claims about 30,000 copies sold at $5 each to him; historian Jimmy Maher thinks the real figure was nearer 10,000.
devStory: Garriott began it as a school project on a PDP-11 under the working title DND, then finished it in Applesoft BASIC on an Apple II his father bought. Staff at a ComputerLand where he showed it suggested selling it, and he packed copies in Ziploc bags with photocopied instructions before California Pacific picked it up.

title: Freeway
description: Freeway (1981) is David Crane's Activision game about getting chickens across a ten-lane highway, alone or against a second player, in two minutes and sixteen seconds.
longDescription: Each chicken that reaches the far side scores a point. On difficulty A a chicken that is hit goes back to the kerb; on B it is only pushed back a lane. The game's freeways are based on Chicago's Lake Shore Drive, New York's Long Island Expressway and San Francisco's Bayshore Freeway.
trivia: Reviewers compared it with Frogger, but Crane said the two were made independently at about the same time.
It received an Honorable Mention for Most Innovative Game at the 1982 Arcade Awards.
devStory: Crane said he based the play on Space Race (1973), and his first version had two men racing up the screen. Activision CEO Jim Levy suggested chickens instead, for the old joke and a marketing idea involving a chicken costume.

title: Gridrunner
description: Gridrunner (1982) is Jeff Minter's fast Centipede-style shooter, written in about a week for the unexpanded VIC-20, which topped the US computer game chart in April 1983.
longDescription: The player's ship moves freely at the foot of a grid and fires upwards at enemies, while zappers on the grid's edges send out pulses that must be dodged. There are twenty waves. Versions followed for the Commodore 64, Atari 8-bit computers, ZX Spectrum, PET and Dragon 32.
trivia: The name came from posters for Blade Runner.
Its sequel, Matrix: Gridrunner 2, was sold in the US as Attack of the Mutant Camels, a title Minter had already used for a different game.
devStory: Minter wrote it in roughly a week, taking Atari's Centipede as a starting point but making it faster. Llamasoft published it, with HESware, Quicksilva and Salamander handling other releases. It was remade and sequelled for decades, up to Gridrunner Revolution (2009) and a 2012 iOS version.

title: Raiders of the Lost Ark
description: Raiders of the Lost Ark (1982) is Howard Scott Warshaw's Atari 2600 adventure based on the film, played with two joysticks: one moves Indiana Jones and the other manages his inventory.
longDescription: Set in Cairo in 1936, the game sends Indy through the Temple of the Ancients, across a mesa and into the Map Room, with stops at a Thieves Den and a Black Market. The Ark is finally dug up inside the mesa after a parachute jump. The second controller selects and drops items, so Indy can carry more than one thing at a time.
trivia: Warshaw opposed Atari's decision to print hints in the manual.
Bruce Chadwick wrote that it sold under a million copies by February 1983, below Atari's hopes.
devStory: Warshaw volunteered when Atari offered the licence and started work in mid-1981 after meeting Steven Spielberg. It fitted on an 8 KB cartridge, with Indy animated by Jerome Domurat. Warshaw's next licensed game for Atari, released a month later, was E.T.

sources.title: Raiders of the Lost Ark (video game)

title: E.T. the Extra-Terrestrial
description: E.T. (1982) is Howard Scott Warshaw's Atari 2600 film tie-in, made in just over five weeks, whose returned and buried cartridges became a symbol of the 1983 video game crash.
longDescription: E.T. must find three pieces of an interplanetary telephone hidden in pits across six areas, then reach a landing zone before time runs out. Reese's Pieces restore his energy, and he has three lives. Critics attacked the gameplay, the visuals and how often E.T. falls into pits; it is regularly listed among the worst games ever made.
trivia: Unsold cartridges were reportedly buried in a landfill at Alamogordo, New Mexico; diggers found E.T. cartridges there in April 2014.
It sold about 2.6 million copies by the end of 1982, but Atari's Ray Kassar later said about 3.5 million of the 4 million made came back.
devStory: The licence reportedly cost $20–25 million, and negotiations ended in late July 1982, leaving Warshaw just over five weeks to finish the game for the holiday season. He designed and programmed it, with art by himself and Jerome Domurat.

title: Attack of the Mutant Camels
description: Attack of the Mutant Camels (1983) is Jeff Minter's Commodore 64 shooter in which a small jet must bring down giant yellow camels before they reach its base.
longDescription: The camels march across a scrolling landscape spitting fireballs, and if one reaches the base the game is over. Clearing a wave leads to a "hyperspace" stage of dodging fast missiles, then a slightly harder herd. The set-up follows Atari's 1982 The Empire Strikes Back, with camels standing in for the AT-AT walkers.
trivia: It was shown in the Smithsonian's "The Art of Video Games" exhibition in 2011.
Its sequel was Revenge of the Mutant Camels (1984).
devStory: Minter designed it for Llamasoft on the Commodore 64 and Atari 8-bit computers. Commodore User called it skilfully designed, and Home Computing Weekly praised the sound and graphics but thought it perhaps a little too difficult. The source for an unreleased Konix version was published on GitHub in 2012.

title: F-15 Strike Eagle
description: F-15 Strike Eagle (1984) is Sid Meier's combat flight simulator for MicroProse, which sold more than 1.5 million copies across home computers, consoles and an arcade version.
longDescription: The player picks a theatre — Libya, the Persian Gulf or Vietnam — and starts already airborne in an F-15 armed with missiles, bombs, drop tanks, flares and chaff. The task is to bomb a primary and a secondary target while fighting off enemy fighters, and the mission ends with a crash, a shoot-down or a return to base.
trivia: It was MicroProse's best-selling Commodore game as of late 1987.
Computer Gaming World readers voted it Action Game of the Year in 1985.
devStory: Sid Meier designed it, and it appeared first on Atari 8-bit computers in 1984, followed by Apple II, Commodore 64, PC and Atari ST versions. A 1991 arcade version ran on the TMS34010 graphics processor, and NES, Game Boy and Game Gear ports followed. Sales passed 250,000 by March 1987 and a million by 1989.

title: NARC
description: NARC (1988) is Eugene Jarvis's Williams run and gun about arresting or shooting drug dealers, the first arcade game on Texas Instruments' TMS34010 processor and one of the first "ultra-violent" games.
longDescription: Max Force and Hit Man arrest or shoot drug users and dealers on the way to Mr. Big, head of the K.R.A.K. organisation. Arrests are counted at the end of each level and score more than kills. Its enemies were played by costumed actors whose movements were recorded on a treadmill.
trivia: The NES version, made by Rare and sold as anti-drug, removed the blood and renamed K.R.A.K. to K.W.A.K.
The Pixies recorded Brian L. Schmidt's main theme as a B-side in 1990.
devStory: Jarvis designed it and programmed it with George N. Petro and Todd Allen. The TMS34010 was too slow for what he wanted, so Williams engineer Mark Loffredo built a custom blitter chip. The same digitising technique was later used in Mortal Kombat and NBA Jam.

title: The Colonel's Bequest
description: The Colonel's Bequest (1989) is Roberta Williams's Sierra murder mystery, in which student Laura Bow investigates on a decaying sugar plantation island off Louisiana in 1925.
longDescription: Laura gathers clues about the other characters' backgrounds and relationships while the clock advances a quarter-hour at a time, one act per hour. There is no visible score, and the game can be finished without solving a single puzzle; at the end a screen hints at everything that was missed. The ending depends on what Laura does in the attic.
trivia: It was one of Sierra's last games with a text parser, along with King's Quest IV.
Its sequel, The Dagger of Amon Ra (1992), takes Laura to New York as a reporter.
devStory: Roberta Williams wrote it and directed it with Chris Iden, with Jacqueline Austin as designer and Ken Williams producing. It ran on Sierra's SCI0 engine in 16-colour EGA, with support for AdLib, Sound Blaster and Roland MT-32 music. Amiga and Atari ST versions followed in 1990.

title: Railroad Tycoon
description: Sid Meier's Railroad Tycoon (1990) is the MicroProse business simulation, designed by Meier and Bruce Shelley, in which the player builds and runs a railway company for a century.
longDescription: Players lay track, build stations and buy and schedule trains in one of four regions, with the books closed every two years. Supply and demand, a stock market and rival railway companies shape the economy, which comes in Simple and Complex models.
trivia: It was based on Avalon Hill's 1986 board game 1830: The Game of Railroads and Robber Barons.
Computer Gaming World named it Game of the Year for 1990 and added it to its Hall of Fame in 1992.
devStory: Meier and Shelley designed it at MicroProse's MPS Labs, with music by Jeff Briggs. It came out for MS-DOS, Amiga, Mac, Atari ST, FM Towns and PC-98, and planned SNES and Mega Drive ports were never released. Sales passed 400,000 by September 1997, and the DOS version became freeware in 2006.

title: SimCity 2000
description: SimCity 2000 (1993) is Maxis's sequel to SimCity, designed by Will Wright and Fred Haslam, which moved the city into a near-isometric view with hills, underground pipes and subways.
longDescription: Land now has height, and a separate underground view holds water pipes, subways and road tunnels. New buildings include schools, hospitals, prisons, libraries, museums and futuristic arcologies, with nine kinds of power plant. Players set separate taxes for each zone type, pass city ordinances and read pre-written newspaper articles.
trivia: Build 300 or more Launch Arcologies in 2051 or later and they leave the city for space.
The Museum of Modern Art acquired it in December 2012.
devStory: Haslam was asked to make the sequel in December 1990, and Wright joined when Haslam struggled with the isometric style. Wright contributed arcologies, the underground view and small-scale simulations; Haslam contributed the newspaper, free-size zoning and bonds. It sold about 4.23 million copies and was ported to the Saturn, SNES, PlayStation and N64.

title: D
description: D (1995) is Kenji Eno's full-motion video horror game for the 3DO, played in a single two-hour sitting with no saves and no pause, which sold about a million copies in Japan.
longDescription: Laura Harris goes to a Los Angeles hospital after her father, Dr. Richter Harris, has gone on a killing spree, and finds the building has become a medieval castle. Pre-rendered video shows her moving through it. The game ends after two hours of real time, and the ending depends on what the player has done.
trivia: Eno reportedly submitted a clean version, then swapped in the disturbing one on the flight to the US.
GameFan named it 3DO Game of the Year for 1995.
devStory: Eno directed and wrote it at Warp over about a year, rendering the video on Amiga 4000 computers, and added violence and cannibalism when the first plot seemed dull. Saturn and PlayStation versions followed. When Sony made far fewer PlayStation copies than the roughly 100,000 pre-ordered, Eno said his later games would be on Sega platforms.

title: Phantasmagoria
description: Phantasmagoria (1995) is Roberta Williams's seven-disc horror adventure, filmed with 25 actors and Sierra's first game to sell a million copies.
longDescription: Victoria Morsell plays the heroine, Adrienne Delaney, and Robert Miano plays Zoltan "Carno" Carnovasch. The actors were filmed in front of a blue screen and set into more than 1,000 rendered 3D backgrounds. A password-protected option blurs the violence.
trivia: Australia refused to classify it, effectively banning it, and the retailer CompUSA would not stock it.
The script ran to about 550 pages, around four times a typical Hollywood screenplay.
devStory: Williams designed and co-wrote it, and Sierra built a $1.5 million studio in Oakhurst, California, to film about 600 scenes over four months. The budget grew from $800,000 to about $4.5 million. It took about $12 million in its first weekend and was the ninth best-selling game of 1995.

title: Enemy Zero
description: Enemy Zero (1996) is Kenji Eno's Sega Saturn horror game set on a space station full of invisible creatures, which the player can only track by sound.
longDescription: Laura Lewis wakes from cryogenic sleep aboard the research station AKI to find the crew being killed. Video-based puzzle exploration alternates with real-time first-person sections in which the enemies cannot be seen; the pitch of a tone tells the player how close they are and from which direction. Guns must be charged before every shot, and overcharging resets them.
trivia: Michael Nyman composed the music after Eno persuaded him at a meeting in Kobe.
Fumito Ueda worked on it as an animator.
devStory: It was planned for the PlayStation, but after his dispute with Sony, Eno announced at the 1996 PlayStation Expo that it would be a Saturn exclusive. Development took about nine months. Sega took over publishing in the West after Acclaim withdrew, and a Windows version followed in 1998.

title: Speed Race
description: Speed Race (1974) is Tomohiro Nishikado's Taito driving game on a vertically scrolling road, sold in America by Midway as Wheels and Racer.
longDescription: The player steers with a wheel and controls speed with an accelerator, scoring by passing other cars without hitting them. Points rise with speed, and a run lasts 90 seconds. Its vertical scrolling influenced later games.
trivia: Wheels and Wheels II together sold 10,000 cabinets in the US, which Ralph Baer's figures make the best-selling arcade game of 1975.
Its success in Japan helped make 100 yen per play the standard arcade price.
devStory: Nishikado designed it at Taito, which released it in Japan in November 1974. Midway brought it to North America in 1975 as Racer and Wheels. A follow-up, Speed Race DX, became Japan's highest-grossing arcade video game of 1977.

title: Gee Bee
description: Gee Bee (1978) is Toru Iwatani's cross between Breakout and pinball for Namco, described as the first video game Namco designed in-house.
longDescription: A rotary dial moves the paddles that knock the ball into walls of bricks, pop bumpers worth 10 points and spinners that slow it down. Lighting every letter of the NAMCO rollover targets (Gremlin's logo in North America) raises the score multiplier.
trivia: Iwatani had wanted to make pinball machines, and a video game with pinball elements was the compromise.
It was followed in 1979 by Bomb Bee and Cutie Q.
devStory: Iwatani designed it with help from programmer Shigeichi Ishimura. It sold about 10,000 units and was Japan's eighth highest-earning arcade game of 1978, but fell short of Namco's hopes, partly because of Space Invaders. Gremlin released it in North America in January 1979.

title: The Portopia Serial Murder Case
description: The Portopia Serial Murder Case (1983) is Yuji Horii's detective adventure for Enix, a game Hideo Kojima named among his biggest influences, whose menu interface Horii reused in Dragon Quest.
longDescription: A bank president, Kouzou Yamakawa, is found dead in a locked room, apparently by his own hand, and the police send a detective known as "Boss" to investigate with his assistant Yasu. Play is nonlinear, with branching dialogue and red herrings, and the ending depends on whom the player accuses. The Japanese press called it "a game without game over".
trivia: The 1985 Famicom version, the console's first adventure game, swapped the typed parser for a menu of fourteen commands and sold 700,000 copies.
Nintendo's Famicom Detective Club series was inspired by it.
devStory: Horii developed, designed and wrote it in BASIC, and Enix released it on the NEC PC-6001 in June 1983 before versions for the PC-8801, FM-7, MSX, Sharp X1 and Famicom. The Famicom version added a magnifying glass for finding clues and a 3D maze.

title: Libble Rabble
description: Libble Rabble (1983) is the Namco twin-stick puzzle game begun by Toru Iwatani, in which two arrows joined by a line wrap it round poles to fence in creatures.
longDescription: The player steers Libble (red) and Rabble (blue) at the same time. The line between them wraps around poles to enclose Mushlins and enemies, while a timer runs around the edge of the screen. A life is lost if an enemy touches an arrow or time runs out, and uncovering treasure chests leads to a bonus stage.
trivia: The 1994 Super Famicom version came with a D-pad cover to mimic the twin-stick controls.
Retro Gamer later called it an underappreciated puzzle classic, comparing it favourably with Qix.
devStory: Iwatani started the design and produced the game; Seiichi Sato took over design partway through and added the treasure chests. Kazuo Kurosu programmed it and Nobuyuki Ohnogi composed the music. It ran on Namco's System 16 Universal board.

title: Snatcher
description: Snatcher (1988) is Hideo Kojima's cyberpunk adventure for Konami, in which an amnesiac agent hunts the robots replacing people in Neo Kobe City.
longDescription: Humanoid robots called Snatchers are killing people and taking their places. The player is Gillian Seed, an amnesiac American who joins the anti-Snatcher agency JUNKER. Play runs through text menus such as look and investigate, with mostly still images, simple puzzles and a few shooting sections.
trivia: Kojima planned five acts but had to cut the story to two because of memory limits, so the original ends on a cliffhanger.
Its first working title was Junker.
devStory: Kojima wrote and designed it, drawing on Blade Runner, Akira, The Terminator and Invasion of the Body Snatchers. It sold poorly but gained a cult following. The 1992 PC Engine CD version added a third act, and the English Sega CD version of 1994–95 was a commercial failure in North America.

title: Sweet Home
description: Sweet Home (1989) is Tokuro Fujiwara's Famicom horror role-playing game, loosely based on the film of the same name, and the main inspiration for Resident Evil.
longDescription: Five characters explore alone or in groups of two or three. Each carries an item the others need to finish — a camera, lighter, medical kit, lockpick or vacuum cleaner — and items can be dropped and picked up. A character who dies is gone for good, and the five endings depend on how many survive.
trivia: Capcom no longer held the Sweet Home licence when it made Resident Evil, so it created a new setting.
It was released only in Japan, on 15 December 1989.
devStory: Fujiwara directed it. Juzo Itami, who produced the film, also produced the game, and the film's director, Kiyoshi Kurosawa, supervised it. The game's plot departs from the film's.

title: Monkey Island 2: LeChuck's Revenge
description: Monkey Island 2 (1991) is Ron Gilbert's sequel to The Secret of Monkey Island, the first LucasArts game with the iMUSE adaptive music system, remembered for its divisive ending.
longDescription: Guybrush Threepwood hunts for the treasure of Big Whoop while the zombie pirate LeChuck hunts him. Players could pick the full game or a "Lite" mode with many puzzles removed. The ending, in which LeChuck is revealed as Guybrush's brother Chuckie, was meant as a deliberately provocative metaphor and split players.
trivia: Gilbert said five scenes were cut to fit the game on floppy disks.
iMUSE was co-designed by Michael Land and Peter McConnell.
devStory: Gilbert directed and designed it, writing with Tim Schafer and Dave Grossman. Work began shortly after the first game's October 1990 release and took about a year. It came out in December 1991 on six floppy disks; the Amiga version followed in 1992 on eleven. It was a critical success but a commercial disappointment.

title: Policenauts
description: Policenauts (1994) is Hideo Kojima's Japan-only adventure game, written and directed by him over about four years, with occasional shooting sections.
longDescription: Play is point-and-click, with dialogue choices and some first-person shooting; the Saturn version supports a light gun. The original PC-98 release used pixel art and animated stills, while the 3DO, PlayStation and Saturn versions added cel animation and full-motion video.
trivia: It was first called Beyond, and Konami renamed it after a trademark problem.
An English Saturn version was advertised in North America in 1996 but cancelled; fans translated it in 2009 and 2016.
devStory: Kojima began writing it in 1990; the project stalled and was revived in 1992. It came out on the NEC PC-9821 in July 1994, followed by the 3DO in 1995 and PlayStation and Saturn in 1996. Critics praised its presentation and writing, while some found it slow.

title: Tokimeki Memorial
description: Tokimeki Memorial (1994) is Konami's high-school dating sim, which sold over a million copies and popularised the genre in Japan; Koji Igarashi wrote its scenario.
longDescription: The player is a freshman at Kirameki High School, dividing time between study, exercise, clubs, appearance and dates. Girls who feel neglected turn into "bombs" and gossip, lowering every love meter, so players learn to date in rotation. The game avoids the sexual content common in the genre.
trivia: Igarashi had help with the writing from his then-girlfriend, later his wife, while he was playing Castlevania: Rondo of Blood.
The series grew to more than fifty games, counting remakes and spin-offs.
devStory: Yoshiaki Nagata directed it and Igarashi wrote the scenario. It launched on the PC Engine Super CD-ROM² in May 1994 and was ported to PlayStation, Super Famicom, Saturn, Windows and Game Boy Color, all in Japan. It had sold 1.1 million copies by 1996.

title: The Last Express
description: The Last Express (1997) is Jordan Mechner's real-time adventure aboard the Orient Express in July 1914, drawn in rotoscoped Art Nouveau style.
longDescription: The player explores the train in first person as the clock runs at six times real speed, and can rewind or fast-forward from the pause menu. Around thirty passengers follow their own scripted agendas, and there are several endings. The characters were filmed against bluescreen, rotoscoped and coloured by hand.
trivia: It went out of print within a year of release.
Producer Mark Netter later called it "a total commercial failure".
devStory: Mechner designed and directed it at Smoking Car Productions over five years, for about $5–6 million. Critics praised its atmosphere, story, music and visuals, but it had sold about 100,000 copies by 2000, not enough to break even. Later editions reached iOS, Android and Steam.

title: Tomba!
description: Tomba! (1997) is the PlayStation platform adventure from Whoopee Camp, the studio Tokuro Fujiwara founded after leaving Capcom, built around 130 optional quests called events.
longDescription: Tomba bites enemies' backs and throws them, and also fights with flails and boomerangs. Play is mostly side-on, with some isometric areas and walls that let him climb between foreground and background. Completing events earns Adventure Points.
trivia: It was released in Europe as Tombi!
It did not sell well enough for Sony's Greatest Hits range, but was the third best-selling PSOne Classic in its 2012 North American launch month.
devStory: Fujiwara directed, produced and led the design, with music by Harumi Fujita. Critics praised its controls, visuals and variety. A sequel, Tomba! 2 (1999), sold less, and Whoopee Camp disbanded after it.

title: Resident Evil 2
description: Resident Evil 2 (1998) is Capcom's two-disc sequel directed by Hideki Kamiya, in which rookie cop Leon Kennedy and student Claire Redfield escape a zombie-filled Raccoon City.
longDescription: Set two months after the first game, it gives Leon and Claire separate scenarios, linked by the "Zapping System", for four playthroughs in all. It keeps the series' tank controls and fixed camera angles.
trivia: The PlayStation version sold 4.96 million copies, the series' best-selling release on a single platform.
Next Generation called it "the must-own title of the year".
devStory: Work began in early 1996 with a team of 45 to 50. An earlier version, known as Resident Evil 1.5, was scrapped when 60–80% complete and the game was redesigned. Kamiya directed, Shinji Mikami produced and Noboru Sugimura wrote it. It sold over 6 million copies across all platforms.

title: Super Smash Bros.
description: Super Smash Bros. (1999) is Masahiro Sakurai's Nintendo 64 crossover fighter, in which twelve Nintendo characters try to knock each other off the stage rather than drain a health bar.
longDescription: Every hit raises a fighter's damage percentage, and the higher it climbs, the farther attacks send them. Up to four players fight across nine stages. Eight characters are available from the start and four more can be unlocked.
trivia: Satoru Iwata suggested the "Bros." in the title.
Marth, King Dedede, Bowser and Mewtwo were planned but cut.
devStory: Sakurai pitched it to Iwata as Dragon King: The Fighting Game and built a prototype in September 1997 without telling Nintendo, showing it at the end of the year. Nintendo approved it, and HAL developed it. It sold over five million copies by 2001.

title: Omega Boost
description: Omega Boost (1999) is Polyphony Digital's first game and its only non-racing title, a PlayStation mecha shooter produced by Kazunori Yamauchi with mecha designs by Shoji Kawamori.
longDescription: The player's mech fights fixed waves of enemies across nine levels. Leveling up unlocks the Viper Boost ability, and using it adds "Pixy" to the player's final ranking title.
trivia: Some reviewers thought nine levels made it too short.
Next Generation gave it 2 out of 5, calling it "competent, but totally uninspired".
devStory: Yasushi Taki and Zaika Tei directed it, and Yuji Yasuhara, who had worked on Panzer Dragoon Zwei, designed and programmed it. It came out in Japan in April 1999 and worldwide that September, averaging 73% on GameRankings.

title: Dragster
description: Dragster (1980) is David Crane's drag-racing game, one of Activision's first releases, and the subject of one of gaming's best-known disputed world records.
longDescription: Two cars race a short strip against each other or the clock, and the lowest time wins. Players shift through up to four gears, and shifting during the countdown disqualifies them. Crane called it a homage to Kee Games' 1977 arcade game Drag Race, squeezed onto a four-way joystick and one button instead of a wheel, pedal and gear lever.
trivia: Todd Rogers's 1982 time of 5.51 seconds stood until 2018, when an analysis of the game's code showed 5.57 was the best possible; Twin Galaxies and Guinness removed his records.
Video magazine called it the least of Activision's early releases and its controls clumsy.
devStory: Crane designed and programmed it for Activision's first line-up. It sold over 500,000 copies, more than half of Activision's first-year revenue.

title: Doomdark's Revenge
description: Doomdark's Revenge (1984) is Mike Singleton's sequel to The Lords of Midnight, a larger and busier war-and-adventure game in which the lords of the Icemark act on their own.
longDescription: Luxor's Moonring lets the player see through the eyes of allied characters and move them each day. Five peoples — Fey, Barbarians, Dwarfs, Giants and Icelords — can be won over or fought, and lords travel and react without waiting to be recruited, while Shareth tries to win them to her side. Victory ranges from rescuing Morkin to destroying Shareth; the computer only needs Luxor dead.
trivia: Amstrad Action gave it 95% and a Mastergame award.
Your Sinclair readers voted it the 71st best game of all time in 1993.
devStory: Singleton followed The Lords of Midnight with the same mechanics and far more characters and places, including an underground tunnel world. Beyond Software released it on the ZX Spectrum in 1984, with Amstrad CPC and Commodore 64 versions in 1986. It was a commercial hit.

title: Gribbly's Day Out
description: Gribbly's Day Out (1985) is Andrew Braybrook's Commodore 64 game for Hewson, in which Gribbly Grobbly hops and floats about rescuing the little gribblets.
longDescription: Gribbly hops and levitates around each level, blowing bubbles to defend himself, and carries stranded gribblets to safety. The enemies change through several forms, from seed pods to Topsies, chrysalises, Stompers and Fliers. When only one gribblet is left, the energy web fails and Seon is set free.
trivia: Braybrook wrote it in about three months.
An Acorn Archimedes version, Gribbly's Day Out on the Arc, followed in 1992.
devStory: Braybrook designed and programmed it, and Hewson Consultants published it in 1985, later reissuing a revised version on its Rack-It budget label.

title: Heart of Africa
description: Heart of Africa (1985) is Danielle Bunten Berry's follow-up to The Seven Cities of Gold, an exploration game set in 1890 in search of a lost pharaoh's tomb.
longDescription: The player lands from a steamer north of Cairo in January 1890 and sets out to find the Lost Tomb of Pharaoh Ahnk Ahnk. Along the way they trade for supplies, keep a diary, consult the map and leave caches. The tomb's location changes with every game.
trivia: Unlike Seven Cities of Gold, it has only one map, as Compute! pointed out.
Ahoy! thought it too easy, since the tomb could be found by accident.
devStory: Bunten Berry designed it at Ozark Softscape in the style of The Seven Cities of Gold, and Electronic Arts published it for the Commodore 64. Computer Gaming World praised its graphics and side quests.

title: Dragon Quest III
description: Dragon Quest III (1988) is Yuji Horii's Famicom role-playing game, released in North America as Dragon Warrior III, which sold about 1.1 million copies in Japan on its first day.
longDescription: The Hero, child of the warrior Ortega, sets out to defeat the archfiend Baramos, though Zoma proves to be the real villain. Party members are hired at a tavern from several classes and can change class at level 20. A day and night cycle controls when some people, items and quests can be found. It is a prequel to the first two games.
trivia: About 300 students were arrested for truancy while skipping school to buy it; Enix later chose to release its games at weekends, though no law required it.
It was the best-selling game of 1988 in Japan, with 3.8 million copies.
devStory: Chunsoft developed it with Koichi Nakamura directing, Horii designing and writing, Akira Toriyama drawing and Koichi Sugiyama composing. It won Famitsu's 1988 Game of the Year. The NES version reached North America in 1992, after 16-bit consoles had arrived, and sold poorly.

title: War in Middle Earth
description: War in Middle Earth (1988) is a real-time Tolkien strategy game, designed by Mike Singleton with Alan Clark and Robert Clardy, that runs armies and individual characters at once.
longDescription: Armies move and fight on the world map while individual characters travel the same map. Battles of up to about 100 units can be watched at ground level, while larger ones show only numbers. On the ground, characters pick up objects and talk to figures such as Radagast and Tom Bombadil.
trivia: Computer Gaming World praised its faithfulness to the books but found little real strategy in it.
