Compute! faulted only its "anticlimactic ending".
devStory: Synergistic Software built it on its World Builders engine, and Virgin Mastertronic released it on the Melbourne House label for computers from the ZX Spectrum and Commodore 64 to the Amiga, Atari ST, Apple IIGS and MS-DOS.

title: A Boy and His Blob: Trouble on Blobolonia
description: A Boy and His Blob (1989) is David Crane's NES puzzle-platformer, in which a boy who cannot jump feeds jelly beans to his blob friend Blobert to turn him into tools.
longDescription: The boy can only walk left and right, so progress depends on Blobert, who changes shape with each of 14 jelly bean flavours: licorice makes a ladder, apple a jack and punch a hole. A whistle turns him back. The pair travel through caves and subways under Earth on the way to Blobolonia, whose emperor lets his people eat nothing but sweets.
trivia: It won Best of Show at CES 1989 and a 1990 Parents' Choice Award.
Imagineering finished it in about six weeks, when NES games usually took six to eight months.
devStory: Crane was chief programmer and designer, with Garry Kitchen co-designing, at Absolute Entertainment's in-house studio Imagineering. Reviews were mixed. A 2009 Wii reimagining by WayForward was made without Crane.

sources.title: A Boy and His Blob: Trouble on Blobolonia

title: Welltris
description: Welltris (1989) is an official entry in the Tetris series, designed by Alexey Pajitnov and Andrei Snegov, in which flat pieces drop down the four walls of a well seen from above.
longDescription: Pieces slide down the walls and, on reaching the 8×8 floor, keep sliding until they hit an edge or another piece. Full horizontal or vertical lines clear. A piece left partly on a wall freezes that wall for a while, and the game ends when all four are frozen.
trivia: MacUser called it "highly addictive".
Macworld complained about its learning curve and how fast the pieces eventually fall.
devStory: Pajitnov and Snegov designed it, and Spectrum HoloByte in North America and Infogrames in Europe published it. The MS-DOS version came first in 1989, followed by Mac, Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, ZX Spectrum, arcade and PC-98 versions.

title: Ultima VI: The False Prophet
description: Ultima VI (1990) is Richard Garriott's role-playing game that put all of Britannia on one seamless map and turned a war against invading gargoyles into a search for peace.
longDescription: The Avatar is rescued from a sacrificial altar by Shamino, Dupre and Iolo and sets out to retake the shrines the gargoyles have seized. Later the story shows the war from the gargoyles' side. Towns sit on one 1024×1024 tile map instead of separate maps, dungeons are seen from above rather than in first person, and commands are reduced to ten icons for the mouse.
trivia: It sold fewer than 100,000 copies in the United States in 1990.
Computer Gaming World added it to its Hall of Fame in 1992.
devStory: Garriott designed it and produced it with Warren Spector at Origin. It supported VGA, a mouse and sound cards for music, though sound effects still came through the PC speaker. It ended the "Age of Enlightenment" trilogy and was ported to computers from the Commodore 64 to the X68000 and to the Super NES.

title: Metal Gear 2: Solid Snake
description: Metal Gear 2: Solid Snake (1990) is Hideo Kojima's Japan-only MSX2 sequel, whose radar, hearing guards and crawling set the pattern for Metal Gear Solid.
longDescription: In 1999 Snake infiltrates Zanzibar Land to rescue Dr. Kio Marv and destroy Metal Gear D. Guards now patrol across screens, see farther and hear gunshots and footsteps. Snake can crawl into tight spaces, and a radar shows nearby enemies until an alert switches it off. He finds that Big Boss survived the first game and must face him and Gray Fox.
trivia: Kojima made it in response to Snake's Revenge, the NES sequel Konami was making for Western markets.
It had no official English release until Metal Gear Solid 3: Subsistence in 2006.
devStory: Kojima designed and wrote it, and Konami released it on the MSX2 in Japan in July 1990. It topped MSX Magazine's best-seller list that October. Jeremy Parish later called Metal Gear Solid "basically a high-spec remake of Metal Gear 2".

title: Commander Keen in Invasion of the Vorticons
description: Commander Keen (1990) is the shareware platformer by the team that became id Software, whose smooth scrolling on the PC came from John Carmack's adaptive tile refresh.
longDescription: Eight-year-old genius Billy Blaze becomes Commander Keen to recover stolen ship parts, stop a Vorticon invasion of Earth and defeat the Grand Intellect. The game came in three episodes — Marooned on Mars, The Earth Explodes and Keen Must Die!, distributed as shareware.
trivia: It began after the team recreated the first level of Super Mario Bros. 3 on the PC; Nintendo turned down the demo.
Apogee had been taking about $7,000 a month; Keen brought in over $60,000 a month by June 1991.
devStory: Tom Hall designed it and John Carmack and John Romero programmed it, working as Ideas from the Deep. Apogee's Scott Miller commissioned an original game after seeing the Mario demo. The royalties let the team leave Softdisk and found id Software on 1 February 1991.

sources.title: Commander Keen in Invasion of the Vorticons

title: Fire and Ice
description: Fire and Ice (1992) is Andrew Braybrook's Graftgold platformer starring Cool Coyote, who freezes monsters with his shots and defeats them to collect the pieces of each level's key.
longDescription: Cool Coyote must find and unlock each level's exit, which needs key pieces carried by monsters. Shooting a monster freezes it, and touching it while frozen defeats it. The 1994 CD32 version added detailed backgrounds, 256 on-screen colours and several layers of parallax scrolling.
trivia: A finished Mega Drive version was never released.
Amiga magazines scored it 90% and above, including 92% from Amiga Mania.
devStory: Braybrook designed it with Phillip Williams, with music by Jason Page, and Renegade published it on the Amiga and Atari ST. MS-DOS, CD32, RISC OS and Master System versions followed between 1993 and 1996.

title: Prince of Persia 2: The Shadow and the Flame
description: Prince of Persia 2 (1993) is Jordan Mechner's sequel, with bigger fights, richer scenery and a 75-minute limit, ending on a cliffhanger that was never resolved.
longDescription: Eleven days after the first game, Jaffar takes the throne disguised as the Prince and puts a death spell on the Princess. The Prince's journey takes him to an island and the ruins of Basra, where he learns of his royal birth, separates his shadow from his body and claims a magic flame. Lives are unlimited, but time lost cannot be won back except by reloading a save.
trivia: Computer Gaming World named it Action Game of the Year in 1994.
Mechner said the planned sequel to resolve its cliffhanger never came.
devStory: Mechner designed it but, unlike the original, did not program it. Broderbund released it for MS-DOS in May 1993, and it had sold 750,000 copies by 2000. A 1996 Super NES port by Titus left out several levels, including the last.

sources.title: Prince of Persia 2: The Shadow and the Flame

title: Ultima Online
description: Ultima Online (1997) is Origin's online role-playing world, produced by Richard Garriott, with skills instead of levels, player housing and open player-versus-player combat.
longDescription: Characters improve skills rather than gaining levels or classes, build and keep houses, and craft goods for an economy run by players. At launch any player could attack any other; the 2000 Renaissance expansion split the world into Trammel, where fighting was by consent, and Felucca, where it was not.
trivia: During the 1997 beta, a player called Rainz killed Lord British, Garriott's own character, with a fire field spell because his invulnerability had not been reset after a crash.
It reached about 100,000 subscribers within six months and peaked at around 250,000 in 2003.
devStory: Garriott produced it, Starr Long directed and Raph Koster led the design, aiming to give players as much freedom as possible. It launched on 24 September 1997 and won Online Game of the Year at the first Interactive Achievement Awards.

title: Roc'n Rope
description: Roc'n Rope (1983) is Tokuro Fujiwara's Konami arcade game, described as the first "wire action" game, in which an archaeologist fires a harpoon rope to climb towards a phoenix.
longDescription: The archaeologist carries a flashlight and a harpoon gun. He climbs rocky ledges by firing ropes, stuns dinosaurs and red-haired cavemen with the light, or waits until they get caught on a rope and fall. Phoenix feathers and eggs make him briefly invulnerable.
trivia: It became the basis for Capcom's Bionic Commando (1987); Fujiwara later worked at Capcom.
Coleco made Atari 2600 and ColecoVision versions in 1984.
devStory: Fujiwara designed it at Konami, which released it in Japan in March 1983 and worldwide in April, with Interlogic publishing in North America. It is counted among Konami's early arcade hits alongside Scramble, Frogger and Yie Ar Kung-Fu.

title: Mikie
description: Mikie (1984) is Konami's school maze game, in which a student dodges staff while collecting hearts that spell out a letter from his girlfriend, to chiptune versions of Beatles songs.
longDescription: Mikie runs through classrooms and other parts of the school picking up hearts while staff chase him. He can head-butt them or slam doors in their faces. A later revision, High School Graffiti Mikie, toned it down: Mikie shouts to stun enemies instead, and they speed up after each loop.
trivia: In Japan it was set in an office and titled Shinnyū Shain Tōru-kun, because of concerns about school violence.
Its music includes versions of "A Hard Day's Night" and "Twist and Shout".
devStory: Konami released it in Japan in September 1984, with Centuri publishing in North America. Imagine Software ported it to the ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64, Amstrad CPC, BBC Micro and Electron, and Crash gave it a Smash award.

title: TwinBee
description: TwinBee (1985) is Konami's two-player "cute 'em up", in which bells shot out of clouds change colour to give different power-ups.
longDescription: Player one flies TwinBee and player two WinBee, with separate buttons for air shots and ground bombs. Shooting a bell changes its colour: yellow for points, white for a twin cannon, blue for speed, green for copies of the ship and red for a barrier. Lose both arms and an ambulance comes to repair them, but only once; the two ships can also line up for stronger attacks.
trivia: It was the first game on Konami's Bubble System arcade hardware.
It did not come out outside Japan until 2007, on a Nintendo DS compilation.
devStory: Konami released it in arcades in February 1985, followed by Famicom and MSX versions in 1986, with music by Shigeru Fukutake and Yoshinori Sasaki. It is credited with Sega's Fantasy Zone as an early cute 'em up and began the TwinBee series.

title: Konami's Ping Pong
description: Konami's Ping Pong (1985) is an arcade table tennis game, described as the first to play like the real sport, with players shown as floating hands.
longDescription: Games go to 11 points with a two-point lead needed, capped at 14–14 when the next point wins, and matches are best of three. The table is seen from an isometric angle, and the player can play forehand, backhand, lob and smash. Hitting from the far side is harder, so the single player always stands on the near side.
trivia: The penguin from Antarctic Adventure, later known as Penta, appears on the title screen and in the crowd.
Nintendo published it on the Famicom Disk System in 1987 as Smash Ping Pong.
devStory: Konami released it in Japan in May 1985, with an MSX version the same year. Imagine Software brought it to the ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64 and Amstrad CPC in 1986 as Ping Pong, and Crash gave it a Smash award.

title: Shao-lin's Road
description: Shao-lin's Road (1985) is Konami's arcade beat 'em up, released in North America as Kicker and sold in Europe as a follow-up to Yie Ar Kung-Fu.
longDescription: With a four-way joystick and two buttons, the player must defeat a set number of enemies on each step before a boss appears. Green-clad enemies can drop a meteor hammer, fireballs or an orbiting ball.
trivia: Taito's The Legend of Kage (1985) was influenced by it.
It was a commercial success in European arcades.
devStory: Konami released it in Japan in April 1985 and in North America that August. Commodore 64 and ZX Spectrum versions followed in 1986 and an Amstrad CPC version in 1987.

title: Haunted Castle
description: Haunted Castle (1987) is Konami's arcade Castlevania, in which Simon Belmont faces Dracula to rescue his wife Selena, with a difficulty Time Extension called brutal.
longDescription: Six linear stages each end with a boss, among them Medusa, Frankenstein's monster and Dracula. Simon's whip can be upgraded to a spiked morning star and then a sword, and hearts power one sub-weapon at a time: bombs, boomerangs, a stopwatch, crosses or torches. Several board versions exist, with Version M the hardest.
trivia: It was the second arcade Castlevania after VS. Castlevania, and the first not ported from a console.
M2 remade it as Haunted Castle Revisited for the 2024 Castlevania Dominus Collection.
devStory: Masaaki Kukino designed it, and Konami released it in December 1987 in the West and in February 1988 in Japan, where it was called Akumajō Dracula. Time Extension ranked it last among the Castlevania games.

title: Thunder Cross
description: Thunder Cross (1988) is Konami's horizontal shooter, in which the Thunder fighter lines up to four option pods and switches between Vulcan, Laser and ricocheting Boomerang shots.
longDescription: The seven stages each end with a boss. Up to four options can be collected; they line up vertically and fire on command. After the seventh stage the game loops into a harder version, so it must be beaten twice.
trivia: Its sequel, Thunder Cross II, came out in 1991.
Space Manbow (1989) is sometimes considered a spin-off because of their similarities.
devStory: Konami released it in Japan in October 1988 and abroad in 1989. Game Machine ranked it the second most successful table arcade unit in its December 1988 issue. Hamster later re-released it on PlayStation 4 and Switch.

title: Parodius! From Myth to Laughter
description: Parodius (1990) is Konami's comic send-up of Gradius, flown as Vic Viper, an octopus, TwinBee or Pentarou to remixes of classical music.
longDescription: It plays like Gradius, but each of the four characters — Vic Viper, Octopus, TwinBee and Pentarou — has its own weapon set, and TwinBee's bells give one-off effects such as clearing the screen. The ten arcade stages range from a pirate planet to a pinball planet, with jokes including a neon "Viva Core" boss and a moai stage.
trivia: The soundtrack remixes works by Strauss, Tchaikovsky, Beethoven and Rossini.
Super Play described the SNES version as "Gradius on hallucinogens".
devStory: It followed the lesser-known MSX game Parodius (1988). Released in arcades in February 1990, it was one of Japan's five highest-grossing arcade games that year and won Gamest's Best Shooting Game award. Versions followed for the Famicom, Game Boy, PC Engine, SNES, PlayStation and Saturn.

title: The Simpsons
description: The Simpsons (1991) is Konami's four-player arcade beat 'em up, in which the family chase Smithers after he kidnaps Maggie.
longDescription: Smithers steals a diamond for Mr. Burns, it ends up in Maggie's mouth, and he takes her too. Homer punches and kicks, Marge swings a vacuum cleaner, Bart uses his skateboard and Lisa her jump rope across eight stages to the nuclear plant, ending with Smithers and then Burns in a battle suit.
trivia: The Japanese version supports only two players.
It mixes first-season recordings with new lines from Dan Castellaneta, Julie Kavner, Nancy Cartwright and Yeardley Smith.
devStory: Konami released it in North American arcades in March 1991. It was one of the three best-selling arcade machines of the year and won an AAMA Platinum award. Novotrade ported it to the Commodore 64 and MS-DOS, and it came to Xbox Live Arcade and PlayStation Network in 2012.

title: Vendetta
description: Vendetta (1991) is Konami's street-gang beat 'em up, known in Japan as Crime Fighters 2, in which four Cobras fight the Dead End Gang to rescue Kate.
longDescription: Blood, Hawk, Boomer and Sledge fight through waves of enemies with separate punch and kick buttons, picking up shotguns, bats, knives and bottles. Hitting enemies while they are down was new to the genre. After the last boss, the earlier bosses return together, and then the game loops at a higher difficulty.
trivia: Outside Asia, an enemy's sexual grabbing attacks were cut, most heavily in the US.
Sinclair User named it Best Beat 'Em Up of 1991, jointly with WWF WrestleFest.
devStory: Satoru Okamoto directed it, with music by Michiru Yamane and Hideaki Shikama. Released in July 1991 in Japan, it was the top-grossing new video game on RePlay's chart that September. Hamster re-released it in 2021.

title: X-Men
description: X-Men (1992) is Konami's arcade beat 'em up for up to six players, whose deluxe cabinet joined two screens into one wide display.
longDescription: Cyclops, Colossus, Wolverine, Storm, Nightcrawler and Dazzler fight to stop Magneto. Each has a mutant power that hits many enemies at once but costs three health points. The character designs come from the 1989 TV pilot Pryde of the X-Men.
trivia: Its script is remembered for lines such as "Welcome to die!"
At MAGFest, crowds have taken to imitating Colossus's roar.
devStory: Konami released it in North America in March 1992. It was one of the five highest-grossing dedicated arcade games in the US that year and topped RePlay's deluxe cabinet chart from May to October. Backbone Entertainment ported it to PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360 in 2010.

title: Asterix
description: Asterix (1992) is Konami's two-player arcade beat 'em up based on the French comics, in which Asterix and Obelix fight side by side.
longDescription: Besides punches, kicks and claps, each hero has a charged spinning-arm attack, released once his face turns red, which is the only way to beat the strongest bosses. Downed enemies can be picked up: Asterix whirls them overhead and Obelix slams them into the ground. Dogmatix sometimes brings a Magic Potion or a roast boar for brief invincibility.
trivia: The first level ends with a bonus chariot race.
Game Zone gave it 4 out of 5 in May 1992.
devStory: Masaaki Kukino, who had designed Haunted Castle, directed it, with Hitoshi Akamatsu and Yuko Ito programming. It ran on a 68000 with a Z80 for sound.

title: Lethal Enforcers
description: Lethal Enforcers (1992) is Konami's light gun game built from digitised photographs, whose realistic violence drew attention in the 1993 US Senate hearings that helped prompt the ESRB.
longDescription: The player starts with a .38 revolver and can pick up a .357 Magnum, shotgun, assault rifle or grenade launcher. Each of the six stages ends with a boss, and shooting civilians or fellow officers lowers the player's rank.
trivia: Home versions came with the Konami Justifier, a revolver-shaped light gun that some toy stores pulled from sale.
The Genesis version was among the first games rated MA-17.
devStory: Konami released it in North American arcades in September 1992, and it became one of the five highest-grossing dedicated arcade games of 1993 in the US. Genesis, Sega CD and SNES versions followed, and a sequel, Lethal Enforcers II: Gun Fighters. It helped popularise digitised sprites in light gun games until Virtua Cop moved the genre to polygons.

title: Sparkster: Rocket Knight Adventures 2
description: Sparkster (1994) is Konami's Genesis sequel to Rocket Knight Adventures, in which Sparkster sets out to rescue Princess Cherry from Axel Gear and King Gedol.
longDescription: The sword now attacks only at close range, maximum health drops from eight hearts to five, and the rocket pack charges itself and adds a screw attack. A slot machine hands out power-ups or bombs. Six stages each end with a boss, and seven hidden Keys to the Seal unlock a golden form needed for the true ending.
trivia: A separate SNES game, also called Sparkster, came out the same year but does not continue this story.
Akira Yamaoka and Michiru Yamane composed the music.
devStory: Yasushi Takano directed it, with Shiori Satoh and Noboru Shirasu designing. Reviews were positive but less enthusiastic than for the first game; GamePro called it "a good progression from the original" but noted slowdown in later levels.

title: Congo Bongo
description: Congo Bongo (1983) is Sega's isometric platform game, in which a safari hunter climbs after Bongo, a gorilla who set fire to his tent.
longDescription: Four single-screen stages — Steep Peak, Snake Lake, Rhino Ridge and Lazy Lagoon — loop at higher difficulty once completed. Its fixed isometric view resembles Sega's Zaxxon, while critics compared its structure to Donkey Kong.
trivia: Ikegami Tsushinki, credited with its development, had earlier done programming work on Donkey Kong.
A planned sequel was abandoned in the early-1980s market downturn.
devStory: Sega released it in Japan in February 1983, with Sega/Gremlin handling North America. Ports reached a dozen home systems, from the Atari 2600 and ColecoVision to the Commodore 64 and MSX; the ColecoVision, Atari 5200 and Intellivision versions won a 1984 Arkie Award for audio-visual effects.

title: Flicky
description: Flicky (1984) is Sega's arcade game about a flightless blue bird leading yellow Chirps to the exit while cats and lizards try to scatter them.
longDescription: Flicky must lead the Chirps to an exit while cat and lizard enemies try to scatter them. Throwable items defeat enemies, and bonus rounds involve catching falling Chirps in a net. After 48 stages the game loops at higher difficulty.
trivia: It began as a maze game inspired by Namco's Mappy and was called "Busty", then "Flippy".
Flicky became a Sega mascot and appears in Sonic games, notably Sonic 3D Blast.
devStory: Yoji Ishii designed it over about a year, with art by Yoshiki Kawasaki. Bally Midway released it in the US, and versions followed for the SG-1000, Japanese home computers and, in 1991, the Mega Drive.

title: Enduro Racer
description: Enduro Racer (1986) is Yu Suzuki's dirt-bike racer for Sega, the off-road counterpart to Hang-On, with a full-size bike cabinet.
longDescription: Five stages of hills, turns, logs and boulders are raced against a timer. Players steer with handlebars that work the throttle and brake, pull up for wheelies and jump logs, and lose time restarting after a crash.
trivia: Its ZX Spectrum version reached No. 2 in the UK chart in August 1987.
The Japanese Master System version has ten levels; other regions got about half, on a smaller cartridge.
devStory: Suzuki designed it on an engine and board similar to Hang-On's, with music by Hiroshi Kawaguchi. It came in a stand-up version with handlebars and a full-size bike cabinet. Activision handled the home computer versions, which got mixed reviews.

title: Super Hang-On
description: Super Hang-On (1987) is Yu Suzuki's sequel to Hang-On, a motorbike racer across four continents with a turbo button and a choice of music.
longDescription: Courses run through Africa (6 stages), Asia (10), the Americas (14) and Europe (18). At 280 km/h the turbo kicks in, pushing top speed to 324 km/h. As in Out Run, the player picks one of four songs before setting off.
trivia: The Mega Drive version added a mode for recruiting sponsors and buying bike upgrades, saved by password.
Sinclair User gave the ZX Spectrum version 10/10 and its SU Classic award.
devStory: Suzuki designed it at Sega R&D1, keeping the sit-on motorbike cabinet of the original. It was Japan's second-highest-grossing upright arcade game of 1987, behind Out Run, and was ported to home computers in 1987 and the Mega Drive in 1989.

title: Alien Syndrome
description: Alien Syndrome (1987) is Sega's two-player shooter in which Ricky and Mary rescue hostages from alien-infested ships before a time bomb goes off.
longDescription: The players move through levels that scroll in eight directions, freeing hostages against the clock and then facing a guardian at the end. After seven levels the game loops with more aggressive aliens and less time.
trivia: Critics praised its horror atmosphere and sound.
A sequel came out on the Game Gear, and a new Alien Syndrome followed on PSP and Wii in 2007.
devStory: Sega R&D1 made it for Sega's System 16 boards, with music by Tohru Nakabayashi. It was a commercial success, and versions followed on the Master System, NES, home computers and Game Gear, handled by several different companies.

title: Power Drift
description: Power Drift (1988) is Yu Suzuki's kart racer for Sega, built entirely from scaling sprites on a cabinet that tilted and shook, recognised by Guinness as the first kart racing game.
longDescription: Players must finish third or better to go on. There are five courses of five tracks, four laps each. Winning every race on a course unlocks an extra stage flown in After Burner II's F-14 or ridden on Super Hang-On's motorbike.
trivia: Sinclair User called it "the single most spectacular game ever to arrive in an arcade".
Its ZX Spectrum version knocked RoboCop off the top of the UK chart in 1989.
devStory: Suzuki directed, produced and designed it on the Sega Y Board, which could rotate and scale both sprites and background, with music by Hiroshi Kawaguchi. The sit-down cabinet sat on a hydraulic platform. Activision's 1989 computer versions lacked that motion, and Mega Drive, 32X and Sega CD versions were cancelled.

title: Shadow Dancer
description: Shadow Dancer (1989) is Sega's arcade sequel to Shinobi, in which the ninja fights alongside a dog he can set on enemies.
longDescription: It plays much like Shinobi. Crouching and attacking sends the dog at an enemy, but if the enemy fights back too long the dog shrinks to a pup until the next time bomb is collected or the stage ends. Four missions each end with a boss, with a bonus game between them.
trivia: It was the first game made for Sega's System 18 board.
Shadow Dancer: The Secret of Shinobi on the Genesis is a loose adaptation, not a port.
devStory: Motoshige Hokoyama directed it, and it reached North American arcades in May 1989. U.S. Gold released computer versions in Europe in 1991. Critics praised its graphics and music, though some thought it derivative, and it sold about 300,000 copies.

title: The Revenge of Shinobi
description: The Revenge of Shinobi (1989) is Sega's Genesis ninja game scored by Yuzo Koshiro, whose enemies looked so like Spider-Man, Batman and Godzilla that it went through several revisions.
longDescription: Joe Musashi crosses eight districts, each with two platforming scenes and a boss. A somersault lets him throw eight shuriken at once in mid-air. There are four difficulty levels and two endings, depending on whether he saves his bride.
trivia: Spider-Man was licensed only in some versions, and later re-releases replaced him with a recoloured character.
In Japan it was called The Super Shinobi.
devStory: Noriyoshi Ohba directed it. Koshiro's score was a turning point in his career, and Ohba later asked him to compose Streets of Rage. Dragon gave it five stars, though it found the final boss too hard.

sources.title: The Revenge of Shinobi (1989 video game)

title: Phantasy Star II
description: Phantasy Star II (1989) is Sega's science-fantasy role-playing game for the Mega Drive, on a 6-megabit cartridge described as the largest console game of its time.
longDescription: Rolf leads a party of up to four, drawn from eight characters, through turn-based, menu-driven battles. Exploration is seen from above and battles in a third-person view. Its story includes the death of Nei, mortally wounded fighting Neifirst at Climacontrol.
trivia: Dragon called it "one of the best role-playing games yet to be released for any video game system".
It was remade for the PlayStation 2 in Japan as Phantasy Star Generation 2 in 2005.
devStory: Chieko Aoki directed and wrote it, with Yuji Naka producing and programming, Rieko Kodama on art and music by Tokuhiko Uwabo. It came out in Japan in March 1989 and in North America a year later.

title: Bonanza Bros.
description: Bonanza Bros. (1990) is Sega's split-screen stealth game, in which brothers Robo and Mobo sneak past guards to grab loot and escape by blimp.
longDescription: In buildings from a bank and a casino to a mint and an art gallery, the brothers avoid guards, collect the loot against a time limit and climb to a blimp on the roof. Two players can work together, and the screen is always split in two.
trivia: In Japan the brothers are thieves; in the West a police chief recruits them to test security.
Several reviewers found it too easy.
devStory: Sega released it on its System 24 board in June 1990, followed by a Mega Drive version in 1991 and conversions for the Master System, PC Engine CD and home computers, the last published by U.S. Gold. Critics praised its graphics, originality and humour.

title: Kid Chameleon
description: Kid Chameleon (1992) is Sega Technical Institute's Genesis platformer of more than 100 levels, in which masks turn the hero into forms with different powers — with no way to save.
longDescription: Each level ends at a flag, and teleporters can jump the player elsewhere or skip ahead. Masks change the hero's form, each with its own abilities and hit points, and diamonds power special moves. There is no password or save system.
trivia: MegaTech thought it lacked challenge.
Mega ranked it 35th among its top Mega Drive games of all time.
devStory: Graeme Bayless directed it at Sega Technical Institute, and it came out in North America in March 1992. It later appeared on the Sega Genesis Collection and the Virtual Console, and was adapted in Sonic the Comic.

title: Sonic CD
description: Sonic CD (1993) is the Sega CD's best-selling game, in which Sonic travels between the past, present and future of each stage, and the debut of Amy Rose and Metal Sonic.
longDescription: Sonic can travel back and forward in time within each stage, and turning stages into "good futures" — or collecting all seven Time Stones — leads to the best ending. Amy Rose and Metal Sonic made their first appearances here.
trivia: Sega of America delayed the North American release two months to replace the house- and techno-influenced Japanese score with a new one by Spencer Nilsen and others.
Electronic Gaming Monthly named it the best Sega CD game of 1993.
devStory: Naoto Ohshima directed it. It came out in Japan in September 1993 and sold over 1.5 million copies. Christian Whitehead's 2011 remake brought it to modern platforms, and it was later included in Sonic Origins.

title: Virtua Striker
description: Virtua Striker (1994) is Sega AM2's arcade football game on the Model 2 board, the first football game with 3D computer graphics.
longDescription: Three buttons handle passes and tackles, long balls and crosses, and shots, which can be charged or tapped for headers and volleys. Teams play in fixed formations through a knockout tournament, with two-minute matches settled by sudden death and penalties.
trivia: A hidden team, FC Sega, made up of the developers, could be unlocked with a code.
Next Generation gave it four stars for its controls and texture-mapped visuals.
devStory: Sega advertised it as "the first three-dimensional computer graphic soccer game". Game Machine ranked it the most successful dedicated arcade game of July 1995. Sequels followed in 1997, 2001 and 2004.

title: Panzer Dragoon II Zwei
description: Panzer Dragoon II Zwei (1996) is Team Andromeda's Saturn rail shooter, in which the rider's dragon evolves through several forms depending on the player's scores.
longDescription: Lundi fires his gun while the dragon locks on with lasers, and a Berserk attack, charged by shooting down enemies, hits everything on screen. Levels 2 to 4 branch into different routes. The dragon evolves through six forms, with a seventh for the final boss, and finishing the game opens the Pandora's Box extras menu.
trivia: A system called ADEC adjusted enemy behaviour to how well the player was doing.
Electronic Gaming Monthly ranked it 90th in its 1997 list of the best games of all time.
devStory: Tomohiro Kondo directed it with a team of 15 to 20, reusing the first game's engine; development took under a year from mid-1995. Yayoi Wachi composed the music, much of it played on the Saturn's own sound hardware. Sega Saturn Magazine gave it 95%.

title: Athena
description: Athena (1986) is SNK's platformer about a princess who falls into Emperor Dante's world with nothing, described as one of the first games with a playable female lead.
longDescription: Athena starts without weapons or armour and takes them from defeated enemies; tools such as a hammer break stone blocks to reveal hidden gear. Eight worlds each end with an oversized boss, and the game has light role-playing elements.
trivia: Athena later appears in SNK fighting games, as a secret character or helping her descendant Athena Asamiya.
Your Sinclair gave the Spectrum version a Megagame award.
devStory: Koji Obata designed it, and SNK released it in Japanese arcades in July 1986. Micronics made the 1987 Famicom/NES version, and Ocean released Spectrum and Commodore 64 versions under its Imagine label.

title: Kiki Kaikai
description: Kiki Kaikai (1986) is Taito's overhead shooter set in feudal Japan, in which the shrine maiden Sayo-chan fights yokai with paper charms and a purification rod.
longDescription: Sayo throws o-fuda in eight directions or swings her rod at close range, and slips of paper left by defeated enemies power up both attacks. Each level ends with a boss. Its mythological setting was unusual for a genre then full of science fiction.
trivia: Taito later licensed it to Natsume, which made Pocky & Rocky (1992).
Hisayoshi Ogura's music gives Japanese folk tunes a chiptune sound.
devStory: Taito released it in Japan in October 1986, and it was one of Japan's ten highest-grossing table arcade games of 1987. Versions followed on the MSX2, Famicom Disk System and PC Engine. Later reviewers were harsher, with GameSpot calling it one of Taito's sleepier titles.

title: Heavy Barrel
description: Heavy Barrel (1987) is Data East's overhead run and gun with rotary joysticks, in which players collect six pieces to build a superweapon.
longDescription: Terrorists hold a nuclear missile site, and the players fight into its underground complex to kill their leader. Keys open crates holding power-ups or pieces of the Heavy Barrel. Assembled, it destroys almost anything in one shot for 30 seconds, and there are enough pieces to build it three times; in two-player games, whoever picks up the sixth piece gets it.
trivia: A Commodore 64 version was contracted but never finished because its developer closed.
It was included in Data East Arcade Classics on the Wii in 2010.
devStory: Data East released it in arcades in 1987 with eight-way rotary joysticks. Quicksilver Software made Apple II and MS-DOS versions in 1989, and Data East made the NES version in 1990.

title: Psycho Soldier
description: Psycho Soldier (1987) is SNK's distant sequel to Athena and the first appearance of Athena Asamiya, who with Sie Kensou was among the first game characters to have a theme song.
longDescription: Athena and Kensou use Psycho Energy to make spheres that orbit them for defence or can be launched at enemies. A green egg-like item turns them into a Psycho Creature — a phoenix for Athena, a green dragon for Kensou. Two can play together.
trivia: Athena Asamiya is a descendant of the heroine of Athena (1986).
Your Sinclair liked the Spectrum version's movement but not its monochrome graphics.
devStory: SNK released it in Japan in March 1987. Ocean's Imagine label published ZX Spectrum, Commodore 64 and Amstrad CPC versions the same year.

title: The NewZealand Story
description: The NewZealand Story (1988) is Taito's platformer about Tiki the kiwi rescuing his girlfriend and friends from a leopard seal, inspired by a Taito programmer's holiday in New Zealand.
longDescription: Tiki dies in one hit and can ride balloons, blimps, UFOs and other flying vehicles. Four zones of four rounds each end with a boss.
trivia: Home computer boxes call the villain a walrus, but the arcade credits say leopard seal.
The NES version was released in North America as Kiwi Kraze.
devStory: Taito released it in 1988, with music by Yasuko Yamada and Yasuhisa Watanabe. Ocean published home computer versions in Europe in 1989, and it was bundled with the Amiga 500 Batman Pack. Amiga Power ranked it 19th among the best games of all time.

title: Vigilante
description: Vigilante (1988) is Irem's side-scrolling beat 'em up, a spiritual sequel to Kung-Fu Master moved to an American setting.
longDescription: Across five stages the player fights Skinheads with punches and kicks and can pick up nunchaku, losing them if hit.
trivia: It began as a Kung-Fu Master sequel, Beyond Kung-Fu: Return of the Master, which was tested in 1987 and shelved.
The TurboGrafx-16 version is the closest to the arcade.
devStory: Irem released it in 1988, with Data East handling North America. Ports followed on the Master System, home computers through U.S. Gold, and the TurboGrafx-16.

title: Chase H.Q.
description: Chase H.Q. (1988) is Taito's police driving game, in which the player catches fleeing criminals and rams their cars until they stop.
longDescription: Officer Tony Gibson and partner Raymond Broady drive a black Porsche 928. Each of the five levels gives 60 to 70 seconds to reach the criminal, with forks in the road where the wrong turn costs time. Nancy at Chase HQ radios in at the start of each level.
trivia: Nancy's radio frequencies are mostly in the 2-metre amateur radio band.
Ocean's home computer versions topped the UK chart at Christmas 1989.
devStory: Taito released it in Japan in September 1988, and it was Japan's highest-grossing dedicated arcade game of 1989. Ocean converted it to home computers, and Taito made versions for the Famicom, Game Boy, Master System, TurboGrafx-16 and Game Gear.

title: Midnight Resistance
description: Midnight Resistance (1989) is Data East's Contra-like run and gun, aimed in eight directions with a rotating joystick, in which brothers fight to rescue their family from King Crimson.
longDescription: Up to two players fight through nine stages. Keys collected along the way unlock weapons and power-ups in a storeroom between stages. The rotating joystick was borrowed from Ikari Warriors.
trivia: Crash ranked the ZX Spectrum version 10th among the best Spectrum games.
The Genesis version, one player only, was on the Sega Genesis Mini 2.
devStory: Data East released it in arcades in 1989 and on the Mega Drive in 1991. Special FX made home computer versions for Ocean, and the Spectrum one scored 93% in Crash.

title: Joe & Mac
description: Joe & Mac (1991), also called Caveman Ninja, is Data East's two-player prehistoric platformer in which two cavemen rescue women kidnapped by a rival tribe.
longDescription: Joe and Mac fight with boomerangs, fire and stone wheels. Their health drains steadily except during boss fights.
trivia: A sequel, Joe & Mac 2: Lost in the Tropics, followed.
Microids released a remake, New Joe & Mac – Caveman Ninja, in 2022.
devStory: Data East released it in arcades in early 1991 and on the Super NES that December. Other studios made the NES, Game Boy and Genesis versions. Critics praised the graphics and sound but criticised the controls.

title: Metal Black
description: Metal Black (1991) is Taito's horizontal shooter that began as a third Darius game, with no extra weapons or bombs, only a beam powered by collecting Newalone molecules.
longDescription: Rogue pilot John Ford flies the Black Fly against the alien Nemesis. The ship has no extra weapons or bombs; collecting Newalone molecules raises its beam level, and at high levels the beam can clash with a boss's own in a "beam duel". There are two endings.
trivia: It was developed as "Darius Part 22" and reworked as an original game because its tone was considered too dark.
Its beam system inspired G.rev's Border Down.
devStory: Takatsuna Senba designed it, with music by Yasuhisa Watanabe, on Taito's F1 System board. It received mixed reviews and a Japan-only Saturn version in 1996.

title: Undercover Cops
description: Undercover Cops (1992) is Irem's Final Fight-inspired beat 'em up, set in New York in 2043, whose team later went on to form Nazca and make Metal Slug.
longDescription: Zan Takahara, Matt Gables and Rosa Felmonde are "city sweepers" fighting mole creatures, mutants and Dr. Crayborn. Objects lying around can be picked up as weapons. The Japanese arcade version has more moves than the world version.
trivia: The 1995 Super Famicom version has no two-player mode; its American release was cancelled until Retro-Bit published it in 2021.
It spawned a manga and a Game Boy spin-off.
devStory: Irem released it in arcades in 1992, and it ranked sixth among Japan's table arcade units that August. Varie made the Super Famicom version.

title: In the Hunt
description: In the Hunt (1993) is Irem's submarine shooter, whose designers went on to found Nazca and create Metal Slug.
longDescription: The player steers the submarine Granvia freely, as the screen does not scroll by itself. Forward missiles destroy most enemies in one hit, and missiles fired upward bring down helicopters and planes. Some enemies drop a machine gun, a wave cannon or a spread shot, and there are several endings.
trivia: Its Japanese title, Kaitei Daisensō, means Undersea War.
A Super NES version was playable at CES 1994 but never released.
devStory: Kazuma Kujo designed it, with art by Akio Oyabu, on Irem's M-92 board. Reviewers have compared it to Metal Slug and R-Type. PlayStation and Saturn versions came in 1995–96, and it has a cult following in Japan.

title: Fighting Vipers
description: Fighting Vipers (1995) is Sega AM2's 3D fighting game on the Virtua Fighter 2 engine, with armour that breaks off and walled arenas instead of ring-outs.
longDescription: Guard, punch and kick buttons drive combo-heavy fights. Armour can be knocked off, after which the fighter takes more damage, and the walls of the arena allow wall attacks. The nine fighters — among them Bahn, Candy, Raxel and Picky — have a Western, freeform style.
trivia: The Saturn version added Pepsiman as a guest fighter, in Japan only.
Sonic the Fighters started when a programmer put Sonic and Tails into this game.
devStory: Sega AM2 released it on the Model 2 board in November 1995. It was very popular in Japan but less so in North America, and the 1996 Saturn version added training and playback modes. Fighters Megamix and Fighting Vipers 2 followed.

title: Virtual On: Cyber Troopers
description: Virtual On (1996) is Sega AM3's twin-stick mech battle game, in which two Virtuaroids fight one-on-one.
longDescription: Each Virtuaroid carries three weapons — left, right and centre — and is piloted with two joysticks. It mixes action, shooting and fighting in head-to-head duels.
trivia: The Saturn version supported online play through the NetLink.
A twin-stick controller was made for the Saturn and PC versions.
devStory: Sega AM3 built it on the Model 2 board, and it reached Japanese arcades around the start of 1996. Game Machine named it the most successful dedicated arcade game of that March, though it was not popular in US arcades. Saturn and Windows versions followed.

title: Zak McKracken and the Alien Mindbenders
description: Zak McKracken (1988) is Lucasfilm Games' second SCUMM adventure, in which a tabloid writer and three allies stop aliens from dumbing down humanity with a 60 Hz hum.
longDescription: In 1997, tabloid writer Zak, a freelance scientist and two Yale students take on the Caponians, aliens who run a telephone company and use it to lower human intelligence. The heroes must rebuild the Skolarian Device, whose parts are scattered across Earth and Mars. Critics noted its many mazes.
trivia: Players had to enter copy-protection codes every time they flew out of the US.
New Age writer David Spangler consulted on the game's materials.
devStory: David Fox led the project and co-designed it with Matthew Alan Kane, on the SCUMM engine first used for Maniac Mansion. It came out for the Commodore 64 and MS-DOS in October 1988, with Amiga and Atari ST versions in 1989. Fox said it was more popular in Germany and Europe than in the US.

sources.title: Zak McKracken and the Alien Mindbenders

title: Xenon 2: Megablast
description: Xenon 2: Megablast (1989) is the Bitmap Brothers' vertical shooter, named after and scored to Bomb the Bass's "Megablast", with a shop the player can visit twice per level.
longDescription: Across five levels the player destroys five bombs planted by the Xenites. Twice per level the player can visit Crispin's Swop Shop to trade cash.
trivia: David Whittaker arranged Bomb the Bass's "Megablast (Hip Hop on Precinct 13)" as the main theme.
An Atari Jaguar version came out in 2016.
devStory: Mike Montgomery, Steve Kelly and Eric Matthews designed it, with programming by The Assembly Line and graphics by Mark Coleman. Image Works released it for the Amiga and Atari ST in September 1989. Computer and Video Games gave the Amiga version 96%, and ST Format named it the best shoot 'em up of 1990.

title: Stunt Car Racer
description: Stunt Car Racer (1989) is Geoff Crammond's racer on elevated tracks with no barriers and gaps to jump, Your Sinclair's game of 1989.
longDescription: Falling into a gap costs time while a crane lifts the car back. Turbo is rationed per race, and damage from hard landings, crashes and collisions can wreck the car. A single-player league of four divisions builds towards winning division one.
trivia: Two Amigas or Atari STs — or one of each — could be linked by cable for head-to-head races.
In the US it was called Stunt Track Racer.
devStory: Crammond designed it, and MicroProse published it under its MicroStyle label in 1989 for the Amiga, Atari ST, Commodore 64, MS-DOS and ZX Spectrum. Critics widely praised it, especially the Commodore 64 version's 3D vector graphics.

title: Kick Off
description: Kick Off (1989) is Dino Dini's football game for Anco, in which the ball is not stuck to the player's feet but knocked ahead, so control takes skill.
longDescription: Instead of the ball sticking to whoever has it, players knock it ahead as they run, which makes control a matter of skill. It was developed first for the Atari ST and then ported to the Amiga.
trivia: It won a 1989 Golden Joystick Award for Best 16-bit Product.
Amiga Power's Stuart Campbell disliked the series.
devStory: Dini created it, and Anco published it in 1989. It was followed by Player Manager and Kick Off 2 in 1990; Dini later left Anco and made Goal! for Virgin in 1993.

title: Loom
description: Loom (1990) is Brian Moriarty's adventure for Lucasfilm Games, in which Bobbin Threadbare solves puzzles by playing four-note tunes instead of using items.
longDescription: Bobbin plays four-note "drafts" on his distaff, learning them by watching objects with matching qualities. Some drafts can be reversed, though palindromic ones cannot. On Expert difficulty the notes are not labelled, so drafts must be played by ear.
trivia: Its music adapts Tchaikovsky's Swan Lake, arranged for MIDI by George Sanger.
Computer Gaming World gave it a Special Award for Artistic Achievement.
devStory: Moriarty, formerly of Infocom, led the project. It came out for MS-DOS in 1990, with later Amiga, Atari ST, Mac, FM Towns and TurboGrafx-CD versions. It was a critical success but did not sell well enough to warrant sequels.

title: Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis
description: Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis (1992) is LucasArts' SCUMM adventure in which Indy races Nazis to Atlantis, playable by one of three paths: team, wits or fists.
longDescription: In 1939, Indy and Sophia Hapgood search for Atlantis, while Nazi agents including Klaus Kerner and Dr. Hans Ubermann want its power for war. Early on the player chooses a path: Team, with Sophia as a partner; Wits, with harder puzzles; or Fists, with more action.
trivia: A CD-ROM "talkie" edition with full voice acting followed in 1993.
It sold over a million copies, LucasArts' most successful adventure up to that point, according to Noah Falstein.
devStory: Hal Barwood led the project and wrote the story and script, and Noah Falstein devised the three paths. It came out in June 1992 for DOS, Amiga and Mac, and several publications named it the best adventure game of the year.

sources.title: Indiana Jones and the Fate of Atlantis

title: Star Control II
description: Star Control II (1992) is Toys for Bob's space adventure across more than 500 stars, with branching conversations with 25 alien races and real-time ship battles.
longDescription: The player explores a galaxy of over 500 stars and 3,800 planets, gathers resources, builds a fleet and talks to 25 alien races through branching conversations. Ship battles are real-time, carried over from the first Star Control, and a two-player Super Melee mode is included.
trivia: The developers ran a soundtrack contest on an Amiga newsgroup, the home of MOD tracker musicians.
The 3DO version's source code was released in 2002 and became the open-source The Ur-Quan Masters.
devStory: Paul Reiche III and Fred Ford designed it, and Accolade released it for MS-DOS in 1992, with a 3DO version in 1994. It won awards including Pelit's 1993 Game of the Year and has since appeared on many lists of the greatest games.

title: Master of Orion
description: Master of Orion (1993) is Steve Barcia's turn-based space strategy game for MicroProse, the first game described as "4X".
longDescription: The player leads one of ten races through a randomly generated galaxy, researching six independent fields of technology. Victory comes by wiping out rivals or winning a galactic vote for peaceful unification.
trivia: Alan Emrich's preview in Computer Gaming World summed it up as "4X": explore, expand, exploit, exterminate.
It won Computer Gaming World's Strategy Game of the Year.
devStory: Barcia designed it at SimTex, with music by David Govett. MicroProse released it for MS-DOS in September 1993, and it sold over 100,000 copies; a Mac version followed in 1995.

title: The Settlers
description: The Settlers (1993) is Volker Wertich's Blue Byte economy game, in which carriers move goods along roads to build a working settlement and an army.
longDescription: Serfs carry goods along roads, and placing flags adds more carriers to speed things up. Territory grows by building military buildings near the border, which knights garrison and use to attack the enemy. There are 30 missions and a free-play mode.
trivia: In North America it was sold as Serf City: Life is Feudal.
About 70,000 lines of 68000 assembly were written before the graphics work began.
devStory: Wertich, its designer and programmer, turned the idea from a god game into an economic simulation. It came out on the Amiga in Germany in June 1993 and on MS-DOS in 1994, and sold over 400,000 copies by 1998. Critics praised the economy but not the combat.

title: Frontier: Elite II
description: Frontier: Elite II (1993) is David Braben's sequel to Elite, a plotless space game with Newtonian flight and planets and star systems at true scale.
longDescription: The game begins in 3200 with a grandchild of Commander Jameson, 100 credits and an Eagle fighter, amid a tense cease-fire between the Federation and the Empire. With no plot and no way to win, the player trades, takes missions or turns pirate. Ships obey Newtonian physics, so momentum has to be cancelled to stop.
trivia: It was the first game to use procedurally generated star systems.
Manual-based copy protection came as police spot-checks: three wrong answers meant arrest.
devStory: Braben developed and designed it, with Chris Sawyer helping port the code to 80286 assembly and music by David Lowe. It came out in October 1993 for the Amiga, Atari ST and MS-DOS, and sold about 500,000 copies. CU Amiga gave it 97%.

title: Transport Tycoon
description: Transport Tycoon (1994) is Chris Sawyer's business simulation, written entirely in assembly language, in which the player builds a transport empire by road, rail, sea and air.
longDescription: The player runs a transport company from 1930 to 2030 on a randomly generated map, building routes to carry passengers and cargo for profit.
trivia: OpenTTD, a free reverse-engineered recreation of Transport Tycoon Deluxe, was first released in 2004.
Reviewers compared it favourably with Railroad Tycoon and SimCity 2000.
devStory: Sawyer designed and programmed it in x86 assembly, with music by John Broomhall. MicroProse published it for MS-DOS in November 1994, and Transport Tycoon Deluxe followed a year later. PC Gamer gave it 91/100, though reviewers criticised the manual and the computer opponents.

title: Hexen: Beyond Heretic
description: Hexen (1995) is Raven Software's sequel to Heretic, a fantasy shooter with three character classes and hub levels full of switch and item puzzles.
longDescription: The player picks the Fighter Baratus, the Cleric Parias or the Mage Daedolon, each with their own weapons and abilities. Hub levels link to side levels, and the player returns to the hubs to solve puzzles by collecting items or throwing switches.
trivia: Its modified Doom engine added jumping, looking up and down, and a scripting system.
The PC version sold over 250,000 copies, but the console ports were poorly received.
devStory: Raven developed it, and id Software published it for MS-DOS in October 1995. The Deathkings of the Dark Citadel expansion followed in 1996, and the source code was released in 1999. Critics praised the non-linear levels and the class choice.

title: Total Annihilation
description: Total Annihilation (1997) is Chris Taylor's real-time strategy game for Cavedog, with height-mapped terrain, streaming resources and an orchestral score by Jeremy Soule.
longDescription: Players build bases and armies, drawing Metal and Energy as a continuous stream rather than in batches. Its terrain is a height-mapped surface. Jeremy Soule's score, played by the 95-piece Northwest Sinfonia, changes with combat and construction.
trivia: Cavedog released free downloadable units, maps and scenarios from 1997.
GameSpot named it 1997's Game of the Year.
devStory: Taylor was lead designer and Ron Gilbert producer. It came out in September 1997, and two expansions followed in 1998. It had sold over 1.5 million copies by 2002.

title: Unreal
description: Unreal (1998) is Epic MegaGames and Digital Extremes' first-person shooter, the debut of the Unreal Engine, set on the alien world of Na Pali.
longDescription: A prisoner whose transport ship crash-lands on Na Pali must escape while fighting the Skaarj, an alien empire that has enslaved the native Nali.
trivia: Epic made it freeware in 2024.
Critics praised its graphics, music and bots but criticised its laggy online play.
devStory: Tim Sweeney was lead programmer, with James Schmalz and Cliff Bleszinski designing. GT Interactive released it in May 1998, and it had sold about 1.5 million copies by 2002. Its engine went on to power the Unreal series.

title: Thunder Force IV
description: Thunder Force IV (1992) is Technosoft's Mega Drive shooter, released in North America as Lightening Force, with playfields that scroll vertically as well as sideways.
longDescription: The first four of its ten stages can be played in any order. The player can scroll up and down to reveal larger playfields and hidden power-ups, and halfway through gains the Thunder Sword attack, which needs two satellite ships.
trivia: The sound team, led by Naosuke Arai, used distortion effects on the Mega Drive's FM chip to imitate an electric guitar.
IGN called it "the pinnacle of Genesis shooters".
devStory: Technosoft released it in Japan in 1992, with Sega publishing it in the West. It was the series' last Mega Drive game. Critics praised its graphics and scrolling while some found the play unoriginal; GameFan scored it 96.5%.

title: Heroes of Might and Magic
description: Heroes of Might and Magic (1995) is Jon Van Caneghem's turn-based strategy spin-off from the Might and Magic role-playing series, and the start of its own long series.
longDescription: It is a turn-based strategy game for one player or several. The 1996 Windows version added a map editor, a random map generator, CD audio and new scenarios.
trivia: The Windows CD included King's Bounty as a bonus.
Next Generation called it "easy to learn, but difficult to master".
devStory: Van Caneghem designed it at New World Computing, with Phil Steinmeyer programming. It came out for DOS in September 1995, and 100,000 copies had shipped by mid-November. Computer Gaming World gave it 5/5 and made it joint Strategy Game of the Year.

sources.title: Heroes of Might and Magic: A Strategic Quest

title: Twisted Metal
description: Twisted Metal (1995) is SingleTrac's PlayStation car-combat game, in which drivers fight in Calypso's tournament for the prize of a wish.
longDescription: Twelve vehicles battle with missiles, mines and oil slicks across six arenas, with three lives and health stations to restore damage. Drivers are invited by email reading "WILL YOU DRIVE?", and the last one standing gets a wish. A two-player Duel mode is included.
trivia: It is set on Christmas Eve 2005, during the tournament's tenth running in Los Angeles.
Electronic Gaming Monthly named it its 1995 Game of the Year.
devStory: Michael D. Jackson directed it, with David Jaffe and Mike Giam designing. It came out in North America in November 1995 and sold over a million copies there. Critics liked the action and variety but found the single-player mode short.

title: Blast Corps
description: Blast Corps (1997) is Rare's Nintendo 64 demolition game, in which the player smashes buildings out of the path of a runaway nuclear missile carrier.
longDescription: The carrier keeps moving, and the player uses a range of vehicles to demolish whatever stands in its way. If it hits anything, the level is lost. There are 57 levels.
trivia: It sold close to a million copies.
It was included in Rare Replay in 2015.
devStory: Paul Mountain and George Andreas directed it, with Martin Wakeley designing and Graeme Norgate composing. Nintendo released it in March 1997, and it scored 90% on Metacritic.

title: Mischief Makers
description: Mischief Makers (1997) is Treasure's Nintendo 64 platformer, in which the robot maid Marina Liteyears grabs, shakes and throws objects.
longDescription: Marina crosses five worlds and 52 levels by grabbing, shaking and throwing objects. It plays in 2D with pre-rendered 3D graphics, and was the Nintendo 64's first 2D side-scrolling single-player platformer.
trivia: GamesRadar called it "possibly the most underrated and widely ignored" Nintendo 64 game.
Enix published it in Japan and Nintendo elsewhere.
devStory: Treasure released it in Japan in June 1997 and abroad later that year. Critics praised its invention and bosses but criticised its short length, low difficulty and sound; later reviews were kinder.

title: Croc: Legend of the Gobbos
description: Croc (1997) is Argonaut's 3D platformer that grew from a Yoshi prototype Nintendo turned down, in which a crocodile rescues the Gobbos from Baron Dante.
longDescription: Croc explores 3D levels to free the captive Gobbos and defeat Baron Dante. Critics praised its visuals and music but criticised the controls and camera.
trivia: It sold over 3 million copies on the PlayStation, one of Argonaut's best sellers.
A remaster came out in 2025.
devStory: Argonaut pitched a 3D platformer prototype starring Yoshi to Nintendo, which rejected it, and reworked it as an original game. Fox Interactive released it in 1997 for the PlayStation, Saturn and Windows.

title: Carmageddon
description: Carmageddon (1997) is Stainless Games' racing game in which wrecking every rival or running down every pedestrian wins as well as finishing first — and was censored or banned in several countries.
longDescription: Across 36 tracks in 11 locations, a race can be won by finishing the course, wrecking all the other cars or killing all the pedestrians. Time bonuses come from pickups, damaging rivals and running people over.
trivia: In Germany and briefly the UK, pedestrians became green-blooded zombies or robots; the BBFC later passed the original after a ten-month appeal.
SCi tried for the Mad Max licence before securing Death Race 2000.
devStory: Stainless began it as a prototype called 3D Destruction Derby, and added pedestrian kills to set it apart and to court controversy. It came out in June 1997, and reviews were generally positive, with GameSpot giving it 8.8/10.

title: Einhänder
description: Einhänder (1997) is Square's PlayStation shooter, in which the player's fighter uses a mechanical arm to grab guns dropped by destroyed enemies.
longDescription: The ship's manipulator arm picks up gunpods left by enemies, each with its own power, ammunition and range, and can hold them above or below the ship.
trivia: It was never released in Europe.
Kenichiro Fukui's soundtrack is mostly techno and trance.
devStory: Tatsuo Fujii directed it. Square released it in Japan in November 1997 and Sony in North America in 1998. Critics praised its gameplay and graphics but noted its short length and lack of two-player mode; it scored 89 on Metacritic.

title: Bust a Groove
description: Bust a Groove (1998) is Metro's PlayStation dance game, in which rival dancers match button prompts to the beat and knock each other off rhythm.
longDescription: Players press direction and button prompts on the beat, and chaining eight moves opens up more complex, higher-scoring routines. Rivals can fire "Jammer" attacks, dodged with a somersault. Ten dancers, including Heat, Frida and Hamm, each have their own song, with four more hidden.
trivia: In Japan it was called Bust a Move, renamed abroad to avoid a trademark clash with Bust-A-Move, the Western name of Puzzle Bobble.
The Western release removed Hiro's cigarette and changed a hip flask into a soda can.
devStory: Metro developed it, and Enix released it in Japan in January 1998, with 989 Studios and Sony handling the West. Next Generation gave it four stars, saying it "is definitely an idea whose time has come".

title: Vigilante 8
description: Vigilante 8 (1998) is Luxoflux's car-combat game set in an alternate 1975, where trucker Convoy's Vigilantes fight an oil cartel's gang across the American West.
longDescription: The Vigilantes battle the Coyotes, mercenaries working for the Oil Monopoly Alliance Regime, across stages in the western United States. Every vehicle has a machine gun and can carry up to three of five weapon types.
trivia: Vigilante 8: 2nd Offense followed in 1999.
A remake, Vigilante 8 Arcade, came to Xbox Live Arcade in 2008.
devStory: Activision published it on the PlayStation in June 1998, followed by Nintendo 64 and Game Boy Color versions. The PlayStation and N64 versions were well reviewed, at 86% and 83% on GameRankings.

title: Space Station Silicon Valley
description: Space Station Silicon Valley (1998) is DMA Design's Nintendo 64 platformer, in which a robot reduced to a microchip takes over animals to use their abilities.
longDescription: Evo, reduced to a microchip, takes control of animals, each with different abilities, to solve puzzles and beat enemies.
trivia: IGN named it Game of the Month for October 1998 and its Most Innovative Game.
A PlayStation version was released in Europe as Evo's Space Adventures.
devStory: DMA Design developed it and Take-Two published it in October 1998. Critics praised its mechanics, level design and humour, but it sold poorly and got no sequel.

title: Legacy of Kain: Soul Reaver
description: Soul Reaver (1999) is Amy Hennig's Crystal Dynamics action-adventure, in which the wraith Raziel shifts between material and spectral realms to take revenge on Kain, with no loading times.
longDescription: Raziel, once Kain's vampire lieutenant, is killed by Kain and revived by the Elder God as a soul reaver. Shifting between the material and spectral realms changes the layout and what can be used, which drives the puzzles. Combat is hack-and-slash, and Raziel takes his brothers' powers after defeating them.
trivia: Hennig said the team had "over-designed the game" and split the story in two, which explains its cliffhanger.
It is set 1,500 years after Blood Omen: Legacy of Kain.
devStory: Hennig directed, co-wrote and co-designed it, with music mostly by Kurt Harland. Delays forced cuts, including extra powers and a third battle with Kain. It came out in August 1999 and scored 91 on Metacritic; critics loved its atmosphere and voice acting but found the play repetitive.

title: Homeworld
description: Homeworld (1999) is Relic's first game, a real-time strategy game fought in full 3D space, whose fleet carries over from mission to mission.
longDescription: Battles take place in a fully three-dimensional sphere rather than on a flat map. Players gather resources and build a fleet around a mothership, and the fleet carries over across the campaign's 16 missions.
trivia: Its music includes Samuel Barber's Adagio for Strings and a closing song by Yes.
Metacritic lists it as the highest-rated computer game of 1999.
devStory: Relic developed it and Sierra published it in September 1999, with a score by Paul Ruskay. It sold over 500,000 copies in six months. Critics praised the graphics and multiplayer, while the story and difficulty drew mixed reviews.

title: Medal of Honor
description: Medal of Honor (1999) is the Steven Spielberg-created PlayStation shooter that popularised World War II first-person shooters, with a score by Michael Giacchino.
longDescription: Set from mid-1944 to mid-1945, the player carries out Office of Strategic Services missions such as rescuing a downed pilot and sabotaging the Nazi war effort. It also has split-screen deathmatch.
trivia: Spielberg was partly inspired by watching his son play GoldenEye 007.
The Congressional Medal of Honor Society objected at first, until producer Peter Hirschmann persuaded its president the project was serious.
devStory: Spielberg created it with producer Peter Hirschmann at DreamWorks Interactive, with Dale Dye as military adviser. Work began in November 1997, and EA released it in November 1999. It scored 92 on Metacritic and won an award for sound design.

title: Balloon Fight
description: Balloon Fight (1984) is Nintendo's Joust-like balloon battle game, programmed by Satoru Iwata, which gained a Balloon Trip mode on the NES.
longDescription: In the main mode, one or two players clear the screen of enemy Balloon Fighters. The NES version adds Balloon Trip, a scrolling stage of dodging lightning sparks and collecting balloons that the arcade original does not have.
trivia: Its gameplay is similar to Williams' Joust (1982).
A sequel, Balloon Kid, came out on the Game Boy in 1990.
devStory: Yoshio Sakamoto designed it under producer Gunpei Yokoi, with Satoru Iwata of HAL programming and Hirokazu Tanaka composing. VS. Balloon Fight reached arcades in 1984, and the Famicom version followed in Japan in January 1985.

title: Wrecking Crew
description: Wrecking Crew (1984) is Nintendo's demolition puzzle game, in which Mario, too weighed down by his hammer to jump, must knock down every target in 100 levels.
longDescription: Mario (or Luigi for a second player in the arcade) smashes every target object in each level, while the foreman Spike knocks things down to get in his way. A level editor lets players build up to four levels of their own.
trivia: Custom levels could only be saved with the Famicom Data Recorder, sold only in Japan.
It was a North American launch title for the NES in October 1985.
devStory: Satoru Okada directed it under producer Gunpei Yokoi, with Yoshio Sakamoto and Makoto Kanoh designing and Hirokazu Tanaka composing. VS. Wrecking Crew came to arcades in July 1984, followed by the single-player Famicom version in 1985.

title: Ice Climber
description: Ice Climber (1985) is Nintendo's two-player platformer, in which Popo and Nana climb 32 icy mountains to win back vegetables stolen by a giant condor.
longDescription: Popo and Nana smash through layers of ice with mallets to climb each mountain, fending off Topis, Nitpickers and White Bears. One or two can play.
trivia: Popo and Nana became fighters in Super Smash Bros. Melee (2001) and Ultimate (2018).
An arcade version, VS. Ice Climber, also came out in 1985.
devStory: Kenji Miki directed it, with Masayuki Uemura and Shigeru Miyamoto producing and Akito Nakatsuka composing. It came out on the Famicom in January 1985 and in North America that October.

title: Shadowgate
description: Shadowgate (1987) is ICOM Simulations' point-and-click adventure, in which a torch must always be kept burning and most wrong moves end in a grisly death.
longDescription: Torches are limited and the player must keep one lit, so they work as a time limit. Many puzzles are trial and error, and most wrong actions are fatal, which makes frequent saving necessary.
trivia: It was part of ICOM's MacVenture series.
The NES version replaced hints in books with vague clues about each room.
devStory: ICOM made it for the Macintosh in black and white in 1987, followed by colour versions for the Amiga and Atari ST. Kemco brought it to the NES in 1989, and remakes followed on the Game Boy Color in 1999 and Windows in 2014.

title: Tecmo Bowl
description: Tecmo Bowl (1987) is Tecmo's American football game, whose NES version was the first console game with real NFL players, licensed through the players' union.
longDescription: Twelve teams each have four plays. Without an NFL league licence, teams go by city or state names, though their rosters match real NFL teams. The arcade version takes up to four players and the NES version two.
trivia: Its sequel, Tecmo Super Bowl (1991), was the first of several.
Sinclair User called the arcade version "superb".
devStory: Tecmo released it in arcades in December 1987, and the NES version came out in North America in February 1989. Nintendo Power ranked it 30th in its 1997 list of the best games.

title: Faxanadu
description: Faxanadu (1987) is Hudson Soft's side-scrolling action RPG spun off from Falcom's Xanadu, set on the World Tree.
longDescription: The hero returns to his home town of Eolis to find it under attack by Dwarves and the Elves' fountain run dry, with the Evil One, who came from a meteorite, behind it. The quest takes place across four areas of the World Tree.
trivia: The name combines "Famicom" and "Xanadu", though it shares little of Xanadu's play.
IGN called it a "hidden gem" in 2011.
devStory: Hitoshi Okuno designed it, with music by Jun Chikuma. Hudson released it in Japan in November 1987, and Nintendo published it in North America in 1989, where Nintendo Power ranked it sixth in its November 1989 chart.

title: R.C. Pro-Am
description: R.C. Pro-Am (1988) is Rare's isometric radio-controlled car racer for the NES, one of the first games to mix racing with car combat.
longDescription: Players race against three rivals, and the top three go through. Along the track they collect power-ups, weapons and letters spelling NINTENDO. There are 32 tracks built from twelve layouts.
trivia: It sold about 2.3 million copies.
A Genesis version, Championship Pro-Am, followed in 1992 with six cars per race.
devStory: Rare developed it and Nintendo published it in North America in February 1988. Computer and Video Games gave it 90%. Super R.C. Pro-Am (1991) and R.C. Pro-Am II (1992) followed.

title: Castlevania III: Dracula's Curse
description: Castlevania III (1989) is Konami's NES return to the original Castlevania's action, in which Trevor Belmont takes one of three companions on branching routes to Dracula.
longDescription: Trevor can be joined by one partner at a time — Sypha Belnades, Grant Danasty or Alucard. Two main routes run through its sixteen stages, and there are several endings depending on the player's choices.
trivia: The Japanese cartridge had a VRC6 sound chip adding three extra channels; the American version's music was reworked for the standard five.
IGN ranked it fifth among the best NES games.
devStory: Konami released it in Japan in December 1989 and in North America in September 1990. AllGame called it "the greatest Castlevania game to ever grace the NES".

title: Crystalis
description: Crystalis (1990) is SNK's post-apocalyptic NES action RPG, set in 2097, a century after a nuclear war, where four elemental swords fight enemies and clear the way.
longDescription: Played from above, it gives the hero swords of wind, fire, water and thunder, which serve as weapons and also open paths past obstacles. A fifth sword, Crystalis, waits in the final dungeon.
trivia: A Game Boy Color version in 2000 was criticised for its lower resolution and altered story and music.
It was included in the SNK 40th Anniversary Collection.
devStory: SNK released it in Japan in April 1990 and in North America that July. Critics praised its graphics, music and story but found the combat repetitive.

title: Dr. Mario
description: Dr. Mario (1990) is Nintendo's falling-capsule puzzle game, in which the player drops two-coloured capsules into a bottle to wipe out red, yellow and blue viruses.
longDescription: Lining up four of the same colour destroys capsules and viruses, and a level ends when every virus is gone. The game is lost if capsules block the bottle's neck. Two players can compete head-to-head.
trivia: In North America it sold 2.5 million copies within six weeks.
ACE called it a "plagiarism" of Tetris, and some parents objected to the medicine theme.
devStory: Gunpei Yokoi produced it, with Takahiro Harada programming and Hirokazu Tanaka composing. It came out on the NES and Game Boy together in Japan in July 1990 and sold about 3.86 million copies there.

title: Snake Rattle 'n' Roll
description: Snake Rattle 'n' Roll (1990) is Rare's isometric NES platformer, in which snakes Rattle and Roll eat Nibbley Pibbleys so they can ring a weigh-in bell.
longDescription: Across 11 levels, the snakes eat Nibbley Pibbleys so they can ring the weigh-in bell. One or two players can play.
trivia: A Mega Drive version, released only in Europe, added a 12th level.
Game Players gave it its 1990 NES Excellence Award.
devStory: Tim Stamper designed it, Mark Betteridge programmed it and David Wise composed the music. Nintendo released it in North America in July 1990, and Mean Machines gave it 94%.

title: StarTropics
description: StarTropics (1990) is Genyo Takeda's Western-only NES adventure, in which Mike Jones fights with a yo-yo — and a real letter in the box had to be dipped in water to progress.
longDescription: Mike Jones explores from a top-down view, fighting with a yo-yo. At one point the player must dip the physical letter packed with the game in water to reveal a code. Critics compared it to The Legend of Zelda.
trivia: It was never released in Japan.
Its sequel was Zoda's Revenge: StarTropics II (1994).
devStory: Takeda produced, wrote and directed it at Nintendo R&D3 with Locomotive. It came out in North America in December 1990 and in Europe in 1992. IGN ranked it 35th among the best NES games.

title: Little Nemo: The Dream Master
description: Little Nemo: The Dream Master (1990) is Capcom's NES platformer based on the animated film of Winsor McCay's comic strip, in which Nemo feeds candy to animals to ride them.
longDescription: Nemo gives candy to animals such as a frog, a gorilla or a mole, then rides them to use their abilities. Each level needs a set number of keys, and how many is only revealed at the exit.
trivia: Its composer, Junko Tamiya, is credited as "Gonzou".
Gaming Bus called it "punishingly difficult at times, even by NES games standards".
devStory: Capcom made it from the 1989 film Little Nemo: Adventures in Slumberland and released it in North America in September 1990. Reviews were generally positive; IGN later ranked it 68th among the best NES games.

title: Gimmick!
description: Gimmick! (1992) is Sunsoft's late Famicom platformer, in which the little green Yumetaro rides his own bouncing star, released only in Japan and Scandinavia.
longDescription: Yumetaro chases a girl who has been taken to another dimension by her toys. His star attack defeats enemies and can be ridden like a platform to reach places he could not otherwise get to. Six stages each end with a boss, and finding every hidden item without continuing opens a secret stage.
trivia: The Japanese cartridge used Sunsoft's 5B chip for three extra sound channels.
The Japanese original has become a collector's item.
devStory: Tomomi Sakai directed, designed and programmed it, with music by Masashi Kageyama. It came out in Japan in January 1992 and in Scandinavia in 1993 as Mr. Gimmick, in small numbers. Critics found it hard at release, and later reviews have been warmer.

title: Mario Paint
description: Mario Paint (1992) is Nintendo's drawing, animation and music-making package for the Super NES, sold with the Super NES Mouse, and one of the console's best sellers.
longDescription: It combines a paint program with 15 colours, 75 patterns and 120 stamps, a simple animation tool of four to nine frames, a music composer with 15 instrument sounds and Gnat Attack, a minigame of swatting flies.
trivia: Nintendo Power named it the most innovative game of 1992.
It sold over 2.3 million copies.
devStory: Hirofumi Matsuoka directed it under producer Gunpei Yokoi, with music by Hirokazu Tanaka, Ryoji Yoshitomi and Kazumi Totaka. It came out in Japan in July 1992 and was later followed by the Mario Artist series on the 64DD.

title: Axelay
description: Axelay (1992) is Konami's Super NES shooter, alternating side-on stages with top-down ones warped for a pseudo-3D effect.
longDescription: Like Life Force, it switches between vertical and horizontal stages, and the top-down stages are warped to look three-dimensional. The pilot sets out to recover weapons taken by the invaders, gaining new ones stage by stage rather than from power-ups.
trivia: Electronic Gaming Monthly praised its Mode 7 effects.
Famitsu reported only 4,625 copies sold in Japan.
devStory: Kazumi Kitaue produced it and Taro Kudo composed the music. Konami released it in Japan and North America in September 1992 and in Europe a year later. It averaged about 81% on GameRankings.

title: The Magical Quest Starring Mickey Mouse
description: The Magical Quest (1992) is Capcom's Super NES platformer, in which Mickey changes into magician, firefighter and climber outfits to rescue Pluto from Emperor Pete.
longDescription: Mickey defeats enemies by jumping on them or throwing blocks, and changes outfits for new powers: a magician's, a firefighter's that sprays water, and climbing gear with a grappling hook. The whole adventure turns out to be a dream.
trivia: It sold 1.2 million copies.
A Game Boy Advance remake in 2002 added Minnie as a playable character.
