devStory: Capcom released it in Japan in November 1992 and in North America that December. Critics praised its graphics and outfits but found it short and easy. Two sequels followed, and a planned Mega Drive version was dropped.

sources.title: The Magical Quest Starring Mickey Mouse

title: Zombies Ate My Neighbors
description: Zombies Ate My Neighbors (1993) is LucasArts' two-player monster-movie run and gun, in which Zeke and Julie save their neighbours with bazookas, weed-whackers and soda cans.
longDescription: Zeke and Julie rescue neighbours from the monsters of Dr. Tongue across 48 stages, seven of them optional bonus levels. Weapons include bazookas, weed-whackers, exploding soda cans and fire extinguishers.
trivia: In Europe it was called Zombies, and chainsaw-wielding enemies became axe-wielding lumberjacks.
Nintendo of America had the blood and gore removed.
devStory: Mike Ebert designed it, with music by Joe McDermott and George Sanger, and Konami published it on the Super NES and Genesis in 1993. Reviewers praised its humour and two-player mode, and it became a cult classic. Ghoul Patrol followed in 1994.

title: Plok!
description: Plok! (1993) is the Pickford brothers' Super NES platformer, in which a hooded hero throws his own arms and legs at enemies, with music by Tim and Geoff Follin.
longDescription: Plok fires his detachable limbs at enemies. They fly back when they hit a target and take longer to return when they miss.
trivia: It began as a coin-op called Fleapit at Zippo Games, which was cancelled in 1990.
A Mega Drive version was planned but never released.
devStory: Ste and John Pickford designed it, reviving the idea at Software Creations, with John Buckley programming. Tradewest published it in North America in September 1993 and Nintendo in Europe. Critics praised its limb mechanics, variety and music.

title: Goof Troop
description: Goof Troop (1993) is Capcom's two-player puzzle adventure based on the Disney cartoon, an early design by Shinji Mikami before Resident Evil.
longDescription: Goofy and Max explore five areas of Spoonerville Island, alone or together. Levels are built around puzzles using items such as a grappling hook, a bell and shovels, and bosses are fought by throwing objects.
trivia: Reviewers liked it in co-op but found it easy and tedious alone.
It was included in The Disney Afternoon Collection.
devStory: Satoshi Murata and Shinji Mikami designed it, with music by Yuki Iwai. Capcom released it in North America in July 1993. Nintendo Power found the challenge "fairly low" but the game still fun.

title: Kirby's Dream Course
description: Kirby's Dream Course (1994) is HAL's isometric mini golf game in which Kirby is the ball, reworked from an unreleased game called Special Tee Shot.
longDescription: Players aim and launch Kirby towards the hole, knocking out enemies on the way to collect stars. Some defeated enemies give Kirby powers, such as a tornado or a UFO form.
trivia: HAL designed it in 1992 as Special Tee Shot with its own characters, then shelved it after Kirby's success on the Game Boy.
In Japan it was called Kirby Ball.
devStory: HAL and Nintendo EAD made it, and Nintendo released it in Japan in September 1994. Critics praised its unusual design and humour, though some found it frustrating. IGN ranked it 38th among the best SNES games.

title: Live A Live
description: Live A Live (1994) is Square's Super Famicom role-playing game told in seven chapters across different eras, each lead designed by a different manga artist.
longDescription: Seven main scenarios run from prehistory to the distant future. Finishing them opens a Middle Ages chapter and then a final chapter that ties all the stories together.
trivia: It stayed in Japan until an HD-2D remake reached the Switch worldwide in 2022.
It was Yoko Shimomura's first major score after joining Square.
devStory: Takashi Tokita directed it, his first time directing, at Square's Development Division 5. It came out in September 1994 but sold only about 270,000 copies and was seen as a commercial failure; critics praised its storytelling but found it short.

title: Wild Guns
description: Wild Guns (1994) is Natsume's science-fiction western shooting gallery for the Super NES, in which Annie and bounty hunter Clint take revenge on the Kid family.
longDescription: Annie, whose family the Kid gang killed, hires Clint to help her. The player dodges enemy bullets while shooting enemies. Six levels of two stages each lead to a final boss, and two can play together.
trivia: Original cartridges became rare collector's items.
An enhanced version, Wild Guns Reloaded, came out from 2016.
devStory: Natsume released it in Japan in August 1994; the North American release slipped to July 1995. Reviews were positive, and it is now called a cult classic.

title: Mega Man X2
description: Mega Man X2 (1994) is Capcom's sequel, in which X battles the three X-Hunters to win back the parts of Zero's body, using the Cx4 chip for wireframe 3D effects.
longDescription: The X-Hunters Serges, Agile and Violen taunt X with Zero's remains, and beating each earns one of his parts. Collecting all three before the end changes the finale.
trivia: The Cx4 chip let the cartridge rotate and scale objects and draw simple 3D wireframes.
IGN ranked it 31st among the best SNES games.
devStory: Tokuro Fujiwara produced it, with Keiji Inafune among the designers and artists. It came out in Japan in December 1994. Critics praised its graphics and sound, though some wanted more change from the first Mega Man X.

title: Mega Man 7
description: Mega Man 7 (1995) is the original series' Super NES entry, made in about three months, which introduced Bass and his robot wolf Treble.
longDescription: Only four Robot Masters can be chosen at first, with the rest unlocking after they fall. Auto runs a shop where bolts buy items, and a password opens a hidden two-player fighting mode. Bass and Treble appear as allies but turn out to be working for Dr. Wily.
trivia: Keiji Inafune handed his role to Hayato Kaji, who became head illustrator.
Ten people worked on the music.
devStory: Yoshihisa Tsuda directed it under producer Tokuro Fujiwara, on a schedule of about three months. It came out in Japan in March 1995. Reviewers liked its presentation and challenge but felt it did little new.

title: Tetris Attack
description: Tetris Attack (1995) is Intelligent Systems' block-swapping puzzle game, Panel de Pon in Japan, given a Yoshi's Island look abroad and no connection to Tetris.
longDescription: Players swap side-by-side blocks to line up three or more of a colour, and the blocks that fall can set off chains, while clearing several at once scores combos. The stack rises steadily, and the game ends when it reaches the top.
trivia: The Japanese version stars fairies; the Western one swapped in characters from Yoshi's Island.
Despite the name, it has nothing to do with the Tetris series.
devStory: Gunpei Yokoi produced it, and Nintendo released it in Japan in October 1995, in North America in 1996, and on the Game Boy a year later. It averaged about 90% on GameRankings.

title: Secret of Evermore
description: Secret of Evermore (1995) is the only Square game made by North American designers, an action RPG starring a boy and his shape-shifting dog, never released in Japan.
longDescription: The player switches between the boy and his dog in real-time battles. Spells come from alchemy, which combines pairs of ingredients, and the dog can sniff out hidden ones.
trivia: It was Jeremy Soule's first video game score.
A Japanese release was planned but cancelled.
devStory: Alan Weiss and George Sinfield designed it at Square USA, and it came out in North America in October 1995. Critics praised its graphics and alchemy but found the battles awkward and the story less memorable than Square's Japanese RPGs.

title: Bahamut Lagoon
description: Bahamut Lagoon (1996) is Square's Japan-only tactical RPG, in which each squad's dragon grows by being fed weapons, armour and items.
longDescription: Byuu leads squads of four against the Granbelos Empire. Each of the six squad leaders has a dragon that evolves according to what it is fed. The dragons are not controlled directly; the player gives orders such as "Go!" or "Wait!".
trivia: It was originally titled Final Fantasy Tactics.
Fans translated it into English in 2002 and again in 2021.
devStory: Kazushige Nojima directed it, with Motomu Toriyama writing and Noriko Matsueda composing. Square released it in Japan in February 1996, and it sold over 474,600 copies that year. Edge gave it 9/10.

title: Alleyway
description: Alleyway (1989) is Gunpei Yokoi's Breakout-style Game Boy launch title, in which a paddle bounces a ball to clear walls of bricks.
longDescription: The player keeps the ball from falling into the pit while clearing every brick in the stage. There are 24 regular levels plus bonus stages, 32 in all. Players start with five paddles and earn more with points.
trivia: The original box showed an unnamed pilot in a spacesuit; later international releases replaced that character with Mario.
Critics compared it unfavourably with Arkanoid for its repetition and lack of power-ups.
devStory: Yokoi designed it and Kenji Yamamoto composed the music. It launched with the Game Boy in Japan in April 1989. Reviews were mostly mixed to negative, though AllGame called it "fun to play".

title: Castlevania: The Adventure
description: Castlevania: The Adventure (1989) is the first handheld Castlevania, a four-stage Game Boy game starring Simon's ancestor Christopher Belmont, with no sub-weapons.
longDescription: Christopher's whip can be upgraded to a chain whip and then a flame whip, but enemy hits knock it back down. Hearts restore health rather than powering sub-weapons, which this game lacks.
trivia: Some EGM reviewers called it the best Game Boy game they had reviewed so far.
It was remade for WiiWare as Castlevania: The Adventure ReBirth.
devStory: Konami released it in Japan in October 1989. Contemporary reviews praised its graphics for a Game Boy game, but later critics were harsher about its slow pace; Nintendo Life gave it 3/10.

title: The Final Fantasy Legend
description: The Final Fantasy Legend (1989) is Square's first Game Boy game and the first SaGa game, renamed in the West to tie it to Final Fantasy, and Square's first million-seller.
longDescription: Characters are humans, mutants or monsters, and monsters change form by eating meat dropped in battle. A chainsaw kills instantly — even the final boss, the Creator.
trivia: Satoshi Tajiri cited it as an influence on Pokémon.
It had shipped 1.37 million copies worldwide by 2003.
devStory: Akitoshi Kawazu directed and co-wrote it, and Nobuo Uematsu composed the music. Square released it in Japan as Makai Toushi SaGa in December 1989 and in North America in 1990. Reviews were mixed, though Famitsu praised it.

title: Balloon Kid
description: Balloon Kid (1990) is Nintendo's Game Boy sequel to Balloon Fight, in which Alice collects balloons left by her brother Jim, built on Balloon Fight's Balloon Trip mode.
longDescription: Alice collects the balloons left by her brother Jim while dodging enemies, with four bosses along the way. In two-player mode she races her rival Samm to collect the most balloons.
trivia: It never came out on the Game Boy in Japan; it appeared there as the Famicom game Hello Kitty World, and later as Balloon Fight GB.
IGN's Lucas M. Thomas called it a "solid little adventure game".
devStory: Yoshio Sakamoto directed it under producer Gunpei Yokoi, with music by Hirokazu Tanaka and help from Pax Softnica. Nintendo released it in North America in October 1990.

title: The G.G. Shinobi
description: The G.G. Shinobi (1991) is Sega's Game Gear ninja game, in which the Red Shinobi rescues four fellow ninjas and can then switch between them, with music by Yuzo Koshiro.
longDescription: Joe Musashi, the Red Shinobi, must free four kidnapped ninjas held in different stages. Each one rescued joins as a playable character with their own weapon, ninjutsu and ability. It is loosely based on The Revenge of Shinobi.
trivia: Retro Gamer called it "unquestionably a classic slice of ninja heaven", if "notoriously difficult".
A sequel, The G.G. Shinobi II: The Silent Fury, followed in 1993.
devStory: Katsuhiro Hasegawa and Masahide Kobayashi designed it, and Sega released it in Japan in April 1991 and abroad that summer.

title: Final Fantasy Adventure
description: Final Fantasy Adventure (1991) is Square's Game Boy action RPG, a Final Fantasy spin-off that began the Mana series, followed by Secret of Mana.
longDescription: Laid out much like The Legend of Zelda, it adds experience levels, magic and a power gauge that affects attack strength. Players could even attack townspeople, unusual for a role-playing game of the time.
trivia: In Japan it was Seiken Densetsu, and in Europe Mystic Quest.
It was remade as Sword of Mana (2003) and Adventures of Mana (2016).
devStory: Koichi Ishii directed it, co-wrote it with Yoshinori Kitase and designed the characters, and Kenji Ito composed most of the music. Square released it in Japan in June 1991 and claimed 700,000 copies sold worldwide.

title: Defenders of Oasis
description: Defenders of Oasis (1992) is Sega's Game Gear role-playing game drawn from the Thousand and One Nights, in which the Prince of Shadam fights an empire reviving the dark god Ahriman.
longDescription: The prince gathers three companions and fights in command-based battles seen from above. The game saves automatically.
trivia: In Japan it was called Shadam Crusader: The Far Kingdom.
Sega Force gave it 90% and called the plot "highly original and entertaining".
devStory: Sega released it in Japan in September 1992 and in North America that December, where it stayed in Babbage's top ten Game Gear titles for five months.

title: Sonic Chaos
description: Sonic Chaos (1993) is Aspect's Game Gear and Master System Sonic game, in which players can choose Sonic or Tails, who can fly and hover.
longDescription: Sonic or Tails crosses six zones collecting the Chaos Emeralds from Dr. Robotnik. Tails plays as his own character, able to fly and hover.
trivia: In Japan it was called Sonic & Tails.
Its direct sequel, Sonic Triple Trouble, followed in 1994.
devStory: Aspect developed it and Sega released it in November 1993. Early reviews praised its levels and the inclusion of Tails; later ones were cooler about its level design and frame rate.

title: Mario's Picross
description: Mario's Picross (1995) is Nintendo's Game Boy picture-logic puzzle game, a hit in Japan whose poor Western sales kept its sequels there until Picross DS.
longDescription: Number clues show which squares of a 5×5, 10×10 or 15×15 grid to fill in to reveal a picture. Each puzzle has 30 minutes, and mistakes cost 2, then 4, then 8 minutes. There are 256 puzzles.
trivia: The next Picross released in English-speaking countries was Picross DS in 2007.
Critics praised its length but wished for bigger grids and more Mario.
devStory: Jupiter and Ape developed it, and Nintendo released it in March 1995 in Japan and North America. It sold well in Japan but poorly in English-speaking regions.

title: Donkey Kong Land
description: Donkey Kong Land (1995) is Rare's Game Boy version of the Donkey Kong Country formula, sold on banana-yellow cartridges, and the best-selling Donkey Kong game on the system.
longDescription: Donkey Kong and Diddy Kong cross 30 levels to recover the banana hoard stolen by King K. Rool, in a game adapted from the SNES Donkey Kong Country.
trivia: It sold about 3.91 million copies.
GamePro named it the best Game Boy game of 1995.
devStory: Rare developed it and Nintendo released it in North America in June 1995, and in Japan as Super Donkey Kong GB. Critics praised how well it carried over Country's play, visuals and music.

title: Wario Land II
description: Wario Land II (1998) is Nintendo's Game Boy platformer in which Wario cannot die: enemy hits cost him coins or transform him, and some transformations open new paths.
longDescription: Captain Syrup and the Black Sugar Gang steal Wario's treasure, and he sets off to get it back. There are no timers, health or lives. Hidden exits lead to different endings, and finding every treasure unlocks five alternate endings and a "Really Final Chapter".
trivia: Electronic Gaming Monthly made it Game of the Month in May 1998.
A Game Boy Color version followed later in 1998.
devStory: Takehiko Hosokawa directed it at Nintendo R&D1, and it came out in March 1998. The colour version averaged 88% on GameRankings.

title: Dragon Warrior Monsters
description: Dragon Warrior Monsters (1998) is the Game Boy Dragon Quest spin-off in which Terry recruits monsters with meat and breeds them into stronger ones.
longDescription: Terry sets out to rescue his sister Milly, kidnapped when they were children. Instead of defeating monsters, he wins them over by offering meat in battle, and can breed two monsters into a stronger one.
trivia: Critics often compared it to Pokémon; GameSpot said it lacked Pokémon's "cutesy, over-merchandised appeal" but praised its play.
It sold about 2.35 million copies in Japan, but only about 60,000 in North America by April 2000.
devStory: Tose developed it and Enix released it in Japan in September 1998 as Dragon Quest Monsters: Terry no Wonderland. Eidos published it in the West in 2000.

title: Pokémon Pinball
description: Pokémon Pinball (1999) is the Game Boy Color pinball game in which the ball is a Poké Ball and players catch all 151 Pokémon across two tables.
longDescription: Hitting the bumpers six times reveals a Pokémon, and hitting it four more times catches it. Evolution Mode needs three items collected from targets. The Pokédex is saved between games, and the cartridge has a built-in rumble.
trivia: It sold 262,000 copies in 20 days, the fastest-selling Game Boy game at the time.
It was the fourth best-selling US video game of 1999.
devStory: Jupiter and HAL developed it, with Tsunekazu Ishihara producing and Go Ichinose composing. It came out in Japan in April 1999 and averaged about 82% on GameRankings.

title: SNK vs. Capcom: The Match of the Millennium
description: SNK vs. Capcom: The Match of the Millennium (1999) is SNK's Neo Geo Pocket Color crossover fighter, with 26 characters from both companies and the best seller on the system in Japan.
longDescription: Fighters battle one-on-one, in tag teams of two or in teams of three. Players choose between three meter systems, one Capcom-style, one SNK-style and one neutral. An Olympic mode of minigames earns points that unlock extras in other games, including on the Dreamcast.
trivia: IGN gave it 10/10.
It lost a GamePro Readers' Choice Award to Pokémon Yellow.
devStory: SNK developed and published it in December 1999. It sold about 75,000 copies in Japan, and was re-released on Switch and Windows in 2021.
